Repo (hyzhang24/DuplexSLA): "MIT License"; "Inference code, model checkpoints, and DuplexSLA-Bench are coming soon — stay tuned."; "The backbone is initialised from Step-Audio-2-mini (~7B parameters)".
results.correction: The claim sentence itself is supported verbatim (160 ms chunk, rate-limited textual action channel, control labels interrupt/backchannel/response, planning text, JSON-formatted tool calls, explicit contrast with 'externally attaching another semantic VAD'). One number in the numbers field is wrong: DuplexSLA-Bench is 1,200 turn-taking cases (300 x normal/pause/interrupt/backchannel) plus 900 tool-call cases = 2,100 cases total, not '2,100 turn cases + 900 tool cases' (which would be 3,000). Two smaller notes: the action channel also carries 'delayed transcript text' (omitted in the claim); and although the abstract says the project page, demos and DuplexSLA-Bench 'are publicly available', the GitHub README states that inference code, checkpoints AND DuplexSLA-Bench are all 'coming soon', so at present only the repo/report/demo page is out — consistent with 'only the repo, not weights, is out'.

results.claim: RoboEgo (FLM-Ego) is a 7B omnimodal model with native full duplexity that runs six parallel streams (contextual vision, streaming vision, speaking audio, listening audio, text, action tokens) with 80 ms theoretical duplex latency and was deployed on a LEJU Kuavo humanoid for locomotion and collaborative games.
results.evidence_quote: "RoboEgo incorporates a backbone architecture and algorithms that natively support full duplexity, achieving a theoretical duplex latency of 80 ms." / "Our backbone model is a 7-billion-parameter autoregressive LLM" / "At each time step, the model processes the following inputs: contextual visual embeddings v1...m^context or time-aligned visual embeddings v_t^stream (depending on the task), all prior audio tokens from both the speaking and listening channels a~t-1^speak, a~t-1^listen, and all preceding textual tokens w~t-1^text" / "The visual stream can be flexibly utilized either as contextual information through TDM—leveraging cross-attention in the backbone—or integrated directly into the parallel streams, depending on the specific task." / "At each time step, lightweight decoders for audio, language, and action modalities generate their respective tokens based on a shared hidden state produced by the backbone model." / "This parallel processing approach eliminates the need for time-slice sharing via time-division multiplexing (TDM)" / "we deploy RoboEgo on LEJU Kuavo robots and assess its performance on two embodied tasks: Locomotion and the Telepathy Challenge... In the Telepathy Challenge, the robot participates in a collaborative game where it is shown an image that is hidden from its human teammate." / Table 5: RoboEgo (SFT) Locomotion 96.5%, "Telepathy Challenge" 97.2%.
results.correction: 7B, native full duplexity, 80 ms theoretical duplex latency, LEJU Kuavo deployment, locomotion (96.5%) and a 'collaborative game' (Telepathy Challenge, 97.2%) are all verbatim in the paper. The 'six parallel streams' enumeration is not: the paper never gives a stream count, and contextual vision and streaming vision are task-dependent ALTERNATIVES ('contextual visual embeddings ... OR time-aligned visual embeddings (depending on the task)'), with contextual vision routed 'through TDM—leveraging cross-attention', i.e. explicitly not a parallel stream. Action tokens are outputs of an action decoder from the shared hidden state that are merged back as input at the next step, alongside speaking-channel audio, listening-channel audio and text. Corrected statement: 'RoboEgo merges, at each step, a visual stream (contextual via TDM/cross-attention or time-aligned streaming, per task), speaking- and listening-channel audio tokens, text tokens and previously generated action outputs, and decodes audio, text and action tokens in parallel from one hidden state.' On availability: the paper contains no release/weights/GitHub/HF statement (only lejurobot.com is linked), so 'no weights released' is consistent with the paper but could not be independently verified (web-search budget was exhausted).

sweeps.topic: Safe online / interactive learning of robot behavior from sparse human feedback (preference RL, TAMER/COACH, contextual bandits, in-context RL, LLM/VLM reward and language corrections, safe RL shields on legged robots, continual learning, and what pet robots actually learn) — for Parcel's "chuckle when funny" and "look back when lost" targets

findings.claim: Canonical RLHF-for-control baseline: a NEW motor behaviour learned from scratch via preferences needs ~10^3 comparisons; human labels cover <1% of environment interactions.
findings.source_title: Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences (Christiano et al.)
findings.numbers: MuJoCo 350/700/1,400 synthetic comparisons, 700 real-human; Atari 5,500 comparisons, 3-5 s each, 30 min-5 h total; Hopper backflip 900 queries in <1 h; Half-Cheetah 800; Enduro ~1,300; clips 1-2 s; reward net 2x64 leaky ReLU (alpha 0.01).
findings.relevance: Sets the order of magnitude every later method is trying to cut; too many labels for a home owner.

findings.claim: With off-policy learning, unsupervised pre-training and reward relabeling, a single easy-to-judge expressive behaviour was taught by real humans in 50-200 comparisons and under an hour.
findings.source_title: PEBBLE: Feedback-Efficient Interactive RL via Relabeling Experience and Unsupervised Pre-training (Lee, Smith, Abbeel, ICML 2021)
findings.numbers: Human experiments: Cart-pole waving 50 queries, Quadruped leg-waving 200 queries, Hopper backflip 50 queries, <=1 h, 1-second clips. Simulated: Walker/Quadruped/Cheetah 400/700/1,400 queries; Meta-world 2,500/5,000/10,000; Drawer Open & Sweep Into 25k/50k; segment 50 steps (DMC)/10 (MW); reward ensemble 3; 10K pre-training steps; matches SAC at 1,400 queries where Preference PPO cannot at 2,100.
findings.relevance: Chuckle/look-back are exactly 'wave a leg'-class primitives: tens to low hundreds of comparisons if the agent already has diverse behaviour data.

findings.claim: Pseudo-labelling unlabeled clip pairs plus temporal-crop augmentation cuts preference labels ~6x (400 vs 2,500 queries to match SAC on Window Open).
findings.source_title: SURF: Semi-supervised Reward Learning with Data Augmentation for Feedback-efficient Preference-based RL (ICLR 2022)
findings.numbers: SURF with 400 queries = SAC on Window Open vs PEBBLE needing 2,500 (~6x); ~100% success with 'a few hundred' queries vs ~50% baseline; tau 0.99/0.999; unlabeled ratio mu=4 (10x unlabeled sampled per session); ablation N in {50,100,200,400}; Walker-walk with 100 queries.
findings.relevance: Cheap, orthogonal saving: the dog produces an unlimited unlabeled stream of its own clips.

findings.claim: Preference RL breaks under mildly noisy teachers (mistake prob 0.1 already degrades PEBBLE/PrefPPO); benchmark defines irrational-teacher parameters.
findings.source_title: B-Pref: Benchmarking Preference-Based Reinforcement Learning (NeurIPS D&B 2021)
findings.numbers: Teacher params: rationality beta (Oracle -> inf, Stoc beta=1), myopia gamma 1.0 (0.9), mistake epsilon 0 (0.1), skip/equal thresholds; budgets DMC 2000/200, 1000/100, 500/50; Meta-world 20K/100, 10K/50; 'existing methods often suffer from poor performance when teachers provide wrong labels'.
findings.relevance: Owner 'was that funny' signals will be far noisier than 10%; naive preference learning will fail without denoising.

findings.claim: Real non-expert annotators produced ~40% label error; a KL-based sample filter (RIME) recovers most performance at 30% synthetic noise.
findings.source_title: RIME: Robust Preference-based Reinforcement Learning with Noisy Preferences
findings.numbers: epsilon in {0.1..0.3}; at 0.3: Walker PEBBLE 431+/-157 vs RIME 741+/-139; Button Press 22.0 vs 80.0 %; Hammer 8.6 vs 58.5 %; budgets Walker 500-1000, Button 10-20K, Hammer up to 80K; 5 non-expert humans on Hopper ~40% error.
findings.relevance: Plan for ~40% label error on implicit owner feedback; filter low-confidence events before updating.

findings.claim: A meta-learned (MAML) reward prior from prior tasks cuts online preference queries 20x vs PEBBLE; humans trained tasks with 36-100 queries; transfers to a real Franka.
findings.source_title: Few-Shot Preference Learning for Human-in-the-Loop RL (Hejna, Sadigh, CoRL 2022)
findings.numbers: 20x fewer queries than PEBBLE (PEBBLE up to 25,000; this ~100-500 sim); human budgets 36-100 queries/task; real Franka Panda reach (2.5 cm) and push (5 cm) with sim-pretrained reward priors.
findings.relevance: The 'pretrain the prior in simulation, adapt with tens of owner labels' recipe is the only preference-RL route whose count fits a household.

findings.claim: LLM-authored reward functions ranked by a human need only 49 preference queries (>30x fewer) and beat PEBBLE with 15k queries; 17/20 people preferred the result on a novel humanoid-jump task.
findings.source_title: ICPL: Few-shot In-context Preference Learning via LLMs
findings.numbers: 49 queries (K=6 rewards x 2 comparisons x 5 iterations - 1) vs 150/1,500/15,000; Ant 12.04 vs PrefPPO-49 0.743 vs PEBBLE-15k 8.543; Humanoid 9.227 vs 0.457 vs 6.162; 9 IsaacGym tasks + HumanoidJump; GPT-4-0613 / GPT-4o; 7 labelers, 20 evaluators, 17/20 preferred ICPL; <1 day per experiment.
findings.relevance: Pattern for the hosted text-model budget: a handful of LLM calls per iteration writing reward code, owner ranks videos.

findings.claim: Per-owner social-motion parameters on a Unitree Go1 (CPG amplitude/frequency/stiffness/duration) were learned from 10 binary comparisons per user; 76% of 25 subjects were happy with the result.
findings.source_title: Learning Human-Robot Handshaking Preferences for Quadruped Robots (Chappuis, Bellegarda, Ijspeert)
findings.numbers: 10 binary choices/user; 25 subjects (11 female per text); 76% happy, 20% neutral; APReL active preference learning; optimized handshakes had lower amplitude/frequency error and DTW than random/test handshakes (33%/51%/47% amplitude errors quoted for comparison handshakes).
findings.relevance: Direct evidence on the same robot class that per-owner styling of an expressive primitive takes ~10 comparisons.

findings.claim: Human feedback is policy-dependent (people reward improvement, silence is meaningful); COACH interprets feedback as advantage and taught 5 TurtleBot behaviours in under 2 minutes each, while TAMER-style reward modelling unlearns behaviours.
findings.source_title: Interactive Learning from Policy-Dependent Human Feedback (COACH; MacGlashan et al., ICML 2017)
findings.numbers: 5 TurtleBot behaviours, each <2 min including verification; feedback delay d=6 steps=0.198 s; eligibility traces lambda 0.95 (+/-1) and 0.9999 (+4); TAMER window 0.2-0.8 s; TAMER failed compositional/lure training and forgot behaviours.
findings.relevance: Owner praise/laughter must be treated as an advantage-like signal relative to the dog's usual behaviour, with a ~0.2-2 s credit window, not as absolute reward.

findings.claim: Scalar human reinforcement with delay-based credit assignment lets lay users teach Tetris to 65.89 lines/game by game 3, versus 50 lines after ~120 games for the best prior learner.
findings.source_title: Interactively Shaping Agents via Human Reinforcement: The TAMER Framework (Knox, Stone, K-CAP 2009)
findings.numbers: 9 Tetris trainers, 19 Mountain Car trainers, >=1/4 non-programmers; TAMER 65.89 lines by game 3 vs RRL-KBR 50 lines after 120 games, Sarsa(lambda) ~30 lines after hundreds; credit gamma(2.0,0.28) or Uniform(0.2,0.6) s; actions every ~150 ms in Mountain Car.
findings.relevance: Establishes that a few episodes of praise suffice in small decision spaces; motivates the delay window for crediting laughter.

findings.claim: Thompson sampling for linear contextual bandits has near-optimal regret: O~(d^{3/2} sqrt(T)) against a lower bound of Omega(sqrt(dT)).
findings.source_title: Thompson Sampling for Contextual Bandits with Linear Payoffs (Agrawal, Goyal, ICML 2013)
findings.numbers: Regret O~((d/sqrt(eps)) sqrt(T^{1+eps})) for eps in (0,1); lower bound Omega(sqrt(dT)); resolves Chapelle-Li COLT 2012 open problem.
findings.relevance: With a d~32-64 context and a few arms, cumulative wrong-chuckle count grows only like sqrt(T).

findings.claim: For neural contextual bandits, a Bayesian linear head on a learned representation (NeuralLinear) and exact-posterior linear models beat all approximate-posterior deep methods; partially optimised uncertainty is catastrophic online.
findings.source_title: Deep Bayesian Bandits Showdown (Riquelme, Tucker, Snoek, ICLR 2018)
findings.numbers: 8 real datasets + synthetic; 25+ variants; ~10,000 contexts per run; 50 runs; NeuralLinear and exact linear best; 'partially optimized uncertainty estimates can lead to catastrophic decisions'.
findings.relevance: Implementation choice for the on-robot learner: closed-form Bayesian linear head over frozen embeddings, honest uncertainty from sample one, trivial on Orin CPU.

findings.claim: A public social robot ran Beta-Bernoulli Thompson sampling over 6 speech-style arms for 12 days / 1,400+ encounters; ~480 pulls per reward condition produced clearly separated arm posteriors, and the reward DEFINITION changed which behaviour was learned.
findings.source_title: What you reward is what you learn: Comparing rewards for online speech policy optimization in public HRI (Song, Okafuji, Ariu, Koike)
findings.numbers: Sota robot, shopping mall, 12 days x ~8 h, >1,400 encounters; 6 arms (3 speech rates x 2 verbosity); alpha=beta=1 prior; 30 cold-start (5 pulls/arm) + 450 bandit-active = 480 per reward; rewards Ru (Likert>=6/7), Rc (closing routine), Rt (>=2 turns); Ru: Normal-Concise 63.3% success; Rc: NC 39.2% success/30.8% selection, Slow-Detailed & Fast-Detailed 0%; Rt: Fast-Detailed 59.8%, Slow-Concise 42.4% selection; context (group size, crowd) modulates.
findings.relevance: Closest published analogue of learning WHICH social behaviour to emit from sparse binary outcomes; fixes the sample scale (~tens of pulls per arm) and warns that the reward definition is the design.

findings.claim: In-home RL personalisation of a socially assistive robot for 17 children converged in ~25-50 episodes (feedback controller) and ~100 episodes (challenge controller) over ~41 days.
findings.source_title: Long-Term Personalization of an In-Home Socially Assistive Robot for Children With Autism Spectrum Disorders (Clabaugh et al., Frontiers Robotics & AI)
findings.numbers: 17 children (3-7 y), avg 41 days, 14.10 sessions/child, 13.27 games/session; hierarchical Q-learning; challenge 1-5, feedback 1-4; convergence ~100 episodes (challenge), 25-50 (feedback); engagement 65% (70% when robot speaking); math +7.0 / +7.125; all 16 completers improved (p<0.01, d~0.54); USC news: 90% engagement-detection accuracy on 7 participants.
findings.relevance: Realistic weeks-long time-scale and episode count for learning owner-specific behaviour at home.

findings.claim: A tiny causal transformer (4 layers, 64-dim) trained on RL learning histories improves its policy in-context within 2-4 episodes without weight updates, but needs thousands of simulated learning histories.
findings.source_title: In-context Reinforcement Learning with Algorithm Distillation (Laskin et al., DeepMind)
findings.numbers: 4 layers, 64 emb, 4 heads, FF 2048; context 2-4 episodes needed; Dark Room 20-step & Key-to-Door 50-step: 2,000 A3C histories (100 actors); Watermaze: 4,000 DQN histories; 2,048 tasks x 2,000 episodes single-stream; matches RL^2 on Dark Room, within 13% on Watermaze; more data-efficient than the source algorithm.
findings.relevance: Shows the on-robot learner can be minuscule if an owner-reaction simulator supplies learning histories; ICRL survey notes no sim-to-real evidence yet.

findings.claim: LLMs perform in-context RL from scalar rewards alone: concatenating prior responses + rewards raised Game-of-24 success from 47% (Long-CoT) to 90%, even with the same LLM as the reward model.
findings.source_title: Reward Is Enough: LLMs Are In-Context Reinforcement Learners (Song, Moeini et al., ICLR 2026)
findings.numbers: GPT-4.1 as policy and reward: Game of 24 CoT 6%, Long-CoT 47%, Reflexion 44%, Best-of-N 49%, Self-Refine 47%, ICRL Preset 90%, ICRL Autonomous 84%; creative-writing LC win rates 59.48% vs Reflexion, 78.36% vs Best-of-N, 86.32+/-3.03 vs Self-Refine; keeps improving over +50 episodes; ScienceWorld 30 tasks with GPT-4.1-mini.
findings.relevance: Zero-training path for the hosted text model: keep the last N (joke, outcome) pairs in the prompt to steer humour choices; not a motor learner.

findings.claim: A VLM answering pairwise preference queries can replace the human labeller for reward learning; RL-VLM-F matched or beat ground-truth-preference training on 6/7 tasks.
findings.source_title: RL-VLM-F: Reinforcement Learning from Vision Language Foundation Model Feedback (ICML 2024)
findings.numbers: Gemini-Pro (GPT-4V for cloth); 40-100 VLM queries per session every 1,000-5,000 steps; caps 500 (cloth) to 20,000 (drawer/soccer/sweep); beats VLM-score, CLIP, BLIP-2, RoboCLIP on all 7 tasks; label accuracy rises with image difference.
findings.relevance: Use a VLM/LLM as the labeller for simulation pre-training of the chuckle/look-back primitives (10^3-10^4 offline calls).

findings.claim: Spoken corrections routed into a hierarchical high-level policy gave 15->50% real-time gains and 15->45% after fine-tuning, using correction data that was only 4-11% of the base dataset.
findings.source_title: Yell At Your Robot: Improving On-the-Fly from Language Corrections (Shi et al.)
findings.numbers: ALOHA 14-D 50 Hz; base 1,170/317/265 trajectories; post-training data 2,028/292/348 segments = 4.8%/4.2%/10.8% of base over 2-3 iterations; real-time 15->50%; fine-tuned 15->45%; per-task +15-45 pts; 20 trials/eval; HL policy every ~4 s (ViT+frozen CLIP+DistilBERT), LL ACT (EfficientNet-b3, FiLM); Whisper via USB mic; saves 2 s pre-intervention context.
findings.relevance: 'Look at me when you lose me' is a high-level language correction; tens-to-hundreds of such events move a high-level policy 20-45 points.

findings.claim: Language-motion corrections are far more sample-efficient than teleoperated corrections: 30 correction episodes per task lifted success 40->63%, whereas teleop corrections degraded it 25->13%.
findings.source_title: RT-H: Action Hierarchies Using Language (Belkhale et al., RSS 2024)
findings.numbers: PaLI-X 55B (frozen 22B ViT); ~100K demos (70K kitchen, 30K diverse); >2,500 language motions; +15% avg over RT-2 on 8 tasks; near-perfect with live language intervention; RT-H-Intervene 40->63%; RT-2-IWR 25->13%; 30 episodes/task (240 total); corrections typed via keyboard/hotkeys.
findings.relevance: Data-shape lesson: collect corrections as language over primitives, not as joint-level takeovers.

findings.claim: An LLM relabels the 1-2 s before a verbal correction with a better action and a 19M-parameter policy is retrained; ~80-100 corrections gave +20 points on average (real Franka 35.3->73.5%).
findings.source_title: Interactive Robot Learning from Verbal Correction (OLAF; Liu et al.)
findings.numbers: GPT-4 temp 0.5, one query per correction; BC-transformer ~19M params (ResNet-18, GMM head, history 10); sim M=50 demos + N=100 corrections: Coffee Machine 16.0->51.0, Square 41.0->59.0, Threading 53.3->60.5, PickPlaceCan 73.6->84.6; real M=40+N=80: PickPlace-Bin 35.3->73.5, Drawer-Basket 52.9->70.6; avg +20.0 (verbal-only +17.8); 1-2 s human reaction window.
findings.relevance: Template for turning the owner's spoken corrections into policy-head updates with the hosted text model at one call per event.

findings.claim: Online learning on a real quadruped is safe when a fixed recovery policy has final authority: fewer than 5 falls in 115 minutes of hardware learning, 48.6% fewer falls in sim.
findings.source_title: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Legged Locomotion (Yang, Zhang, Luu, Ha, Tan, Yu)
findings.numbers: 48.6% fewer falls in simulation; <5 falls over 115 min of real-robot learning; learned gaits: 34% more energy efficient, catwalk 40.9% narrower feet, two-leg balance 2x longer; switch to recovery policy on imminent constraint violation, 'minimally intervening'.
findings.relevance: Justifies keeping Parcel's deterministic safety layer as the shield while the behaviour selector learns; learned outputs stay within pre-vetted primitives.

findings.claim: A learned reach-avoid safety value plus recovery policy runs onboard a Unitree Go1 with a Jetson Orin NX at 3.1 m/s with 9-10/10 real-world success.
findings.source_title: Agile But Safe: Learning Collision-Free High-Speed Legged Locomotion (He et al., RSS 2024)
findings.numbers: Go1; peak 3.1 m/s; V_threshold=-0.05 switch; RA net on 200k episodes; Isaac Gym 1,280 envs, PPO; 9-10/10 success on three testbeds; Jetson Orin NX; ray-prediction ResNet-18 9 ms; Kp=30, Kd=0.65.
findings.relevance: Orin-class boards can host a learned safety value alongside the deterministic layer if a learned shield is ever wanted.

findings.claim: Small scratch policies forget badly under sequential learning (NBT 0.245 with 20% replay) while 3B pretrained VLAs barely forget (0.027); EWC is worse than replay.
findings.source_title: Pretrained Vision-Language-Action Models are Surprisingly Resistant to Forgetting in Continual Learning (Liu, Kim, Liu, Liu, Zhu)
findings.numbers: LIBERO, 10 sequential tasks; 20% replay (1,000 samples): GR00T N1.5 (~3B) 0.919 SR / 0.027 NBT; pi0 (~3B) 0.768 / -0.016; BC-Transformer (~15M) 0.585 / 0.245; BC-ViT 0.508 / 0.193; 2% replay: VLAs 0.1-0.2 NBT vs scratch 0.4-0.5; Sequential+EWC NBT 0.6-0.8; pi0 recovers in 6.2-10.5% of steps vs BC-Transformer 33-187%; sim only.
findings.relevance: Do not fine-tune the whole motion policy online; learn a small head over a frozen backbone and always replay past owner episodes.

findings.claim: Sony documents aibo's personality drifting with owner interaction and a ~3-year growth curve steered by compliments/scolding, but gives no mechanism, no evaluation and no claim of learning a context-conditioned behaviour.
findings.source_title: Sony aibo ERS-1000 Help Guide: aibo's growth and change (also personality page TP0001970096 and desires page TP0001970094)
findings.numbers: 'about 3 years for aibo to reach the maturity stage'; personalities e.g. 'Clingy' and 'Wild' shown in the My aibo app; 'the pattern of tricks and the strength of desires change'; 'give a lot of compliments ... teach it a lesson'; emotions 'delight, anger, sorrow and pleasure'.
findings.relevance: No shipped pet robot publishes a verifiable learned behaviour; Parcel can differentiate by logging posteriors and reward definitions.

findings.claim: MiRo's product architecture is a layered brain-inspired controller with basal-ganglia-style action selection; no owner-specific online learning is documented in the platform paper.
findings.source_title: MiRo: An Animal-like Companion Robot with a Biomimetic Brain-based Control System (Prescott, Mitchinson, Conran, HRI 2017)
findings.numbers: six senses, eight DOF, 6 h+ battery, 3B-CS layered control with centralised action selection; responds to stroking and sound; positioned as a platform for 'learning from reward' research.
findings.relevance: Confirms the pet-robot field ships hand-authored behaviour selection, not learned owner-specific behaviour.

findings.claim: KEYi's Loona marketing claims it 'learns from you and evolves over time' on a 5 TOPS BPU with a 720P camera, with no mechanism or data.
findings.source_title: What Is Loona Petbot? A Complete Guide (KEYi vendor blog)
findings.numbers: 5 TOPS BPU; 720P RGB camera; '95% accuracy rate for spotting human feelings'; 'over 1,000 unique movements'; 'over 200 signals every minute'; ChatGPT-backed chat.
findings.relevance: Baseline of unverifiable competitor claims; not evidence of learning.

findings.claim: An MIT-licensed PyTorch laughter detector (Switchboard-trained, Interspeech 2021) is available off the shelf with a 0.5 probability threshold and 0.2 s minimum segment.
findings.source_title: jrgillick/laughter-detection (Robust Laughter Detection in Noisy Environments)
findings.numbers: MIT license; PyTorch>=1.3.1, librosa>=0.8.1; threshold default 0.5; min_length 0.2 s; Switchboard training, AudioSet eval annotations. (Interspeech 2024 LaughterSegmentation: 1.26 GB model, research-only weights, torch 2.1.2, 16 kHz.)
findings.relevance: Provides the binary 'owner laughed within the window' reward event for the chuckle bandit; untested with the XVF3800 and the dog's own speaker echo.

design_implications: Reframe both targets as DECISIONS over existing safe primitives (fire chuckle / look-back, with a few style parameters), not as new continuous motion learning; every learned output stays inside the set the deterministic safety layer already vets (Yang 2022 recovery-policy pattern; Agile-But-Safe shows learned safety values run on Orin NX).

On-robot learner = contextual Thompson-sampling bandit with a NeuralLinear head (Bayesian linear regression over a frozen d~32-64 context embedding built from the duplex voice state, owner-model facts, perception, and a laughter detector). Closed-form updates, honest uncertainty from sample one, sqrt(T) regret (Riquelme 2018; Agrawal-Goyal 2013). Cold-start each arm ~5 pulls as Song 2026 did.

Fix the reward definitions up front, because the reward IS the learned policy (Song 2026): chuckle success = owner laughter onset (or explicit positive utterance) within a 0.2-3 s window after the owner's utterance ends; look-back success = owner re-acquired (face/voice bearing) within N s or a positive utterance. Interpret feedback as advantage-like relative to the owner's baseline (COACH), not absolute reward; silence is informative.

Budget for ~40% implicit-label noise (RIME human study; B-Pref shows epsilon=0.1 already hurts): filter low-confidence events, use conservative priors, and pseudo-label the unlabeled clip stream only above a high confidence threshold (SURF tau 0.99-0.999).

Expect ~30-100 labelled events per behaviour per owner for a separated posterior (Song: 480 pulls over 6 arms; Clabaugh: 25-100 episodes; PEBBLE humans: 50-200 comparisons) and ~10 pairwise comparisons for per-owner styling of the primitive parameters (Chappuis 2024 on a Go1). At a few events/day this is 1-3 weeks, so simulation pre-training of the prior is mandatory.

Simulation/training plan: build an LLM-driven owner-reaction simulator (jokes/non-jokes/getting-lost with a B-Pref-style irrational-teacher model beta/gamma/epsilon) to pre-train the context encoder and a meta-learned prior for the bandit head (Hejna-Sadigh 20x reduction; ICPL 49-query pattern); use VLM preference labels (RL-VLM-F) to tune chuckle/look-back primitive parameters in MuJoCo/Isaac before an owner sees them; optionally distil the learning process into a 4-layer/64-dim Algorithm-Distillation head that adapts within 2-4 episodes, but treat ICRL as an experiment lane since the ICRL survey reports no sim-to-real evidence.

Route spoken owner corrections ('look at me when you lose me', 'don't laugh at that') through a YAY/OLAF-style channel: transcribe, relabel the previous ~2 s of context with the hosted text model (one call per event), append to a small replay dataset that refits the bandit priors and later a high-level policy head; expect 20-45 point gains from tens-to-hundreds of corrections that are single-digit percent of base data.

Continual-learning rule: only the bandit/policy heads update online; backbone and the 50 Hz body-intent policy stay frozen; keep a replay buffer of all labelled owner episodes (2-20%) and refit from it rather than sequentially (Liu 2026: 15M scratch policies lose 20-25% with 20% replay; EWC is worse than replay).

Hosted-budget fit: on-robot learning is closed-form CPU math; hosted text-model calls occur per owner event (a few/day) plus offline simulation runs on the desktop; an 8B VLM reward model (Large Reward Models) fits Orin 64 GB only for batched offline labelling, not the 50 Hz lane.

Do NOT run PEBBLE/SAC-style preference RL on the real dog (10^2-10^3 clips + exploration), do NOT fine-tune the whole motion policy from owner feedback, do NOT adopt Vintix-class ICRL (300M, no weights, 31-47% on novel tasks), and do not claim 'personality learning' the way aibo/Loona do without a logged posterior and an A/B-able reward definition.

trainable_options.name: NeuralLinear contextual Thompson-sampling bandit (behaviour trigger head)
trainable_options.what_it_is: Bayesian linear regression head (per primitive: chuckle, look-back) over a frozen context embedding; Thompson sampling over a few discrete arms; the top performer in the Deep Bayesian Bandits Showdown and the model class used in Song et al.'s 12-day HRI deployment (Beta-Bernoulli).
trainable_options.size_params: O(d x arms) parameters, d~32-64; closed-form posterior
trainable_options.inputs: frozen embedding of voice-LLM utterance state, owner-model facts, perception (owner bearing, lost flag), laughter-detector event
trainable_options.outputs: arm choice = fire/not fire primitive (and style bucket) with posterior sample
trainable_options.train_recipe: Cold-start ~5 pulls per arm; Bernoulli/Gaussian posterior update per labelled event; priors meta-learned from an LLM-driven owner simulator; RIME-style filtering of low-confidence labels; replay-refit from stored episodes
trainable_options.license: algorithm; Agrawal-Goyal and Riquelme papers are ICML/ICLR proceedings
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Trivial: microsecond CPU updates, no GPU

trainable_options.name: PEBBLE + SURF preference-based RL (simulation-only pre-training of primitives)
trainable_options.what_it_is: Off-policy SAC with a learned reward from pairwise clip preferences, unsupervised pre-training, replay relabeling; SURF adds pseudo-labels and temporal cropping for ~6x fewer labels.
trainable_options.size_params: reward ensemble of 3 small MLPs + SAC actor/critic (sub-10M)
trainable_options.inputs: state/proprioception segments (50 steps DMC) and pairwise preference labels from a human or VLM
trainable_options.outputs: a reward model and a policy for the primitive (e.g. chuckle body motion, look-back turn)
trainable_options.train_recipe: Humans: 50-200 comparisons for one expressive behaviour in <1 h (PEBBLE); in sim use VLM labels (RL-VLM-F, 40-100 queries/session) and SURF pseudo-labelling; run on the desktop RTX 5000 Ada in MuJoCo
trainable_options.license: papers ICML 2021 / ICLR 2022 (code repo rll-research/BPref referenced by B-Pref)
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Training on desktop only; the resulting small policy runs on Orin; not for online learning on the real dog

trainable_options.name: Few-shot preference learning with a meta-learned (MAML) reward prior
trainable_options.what_it_is: Pre-train a preference reward model across many task variants so a new task adapts from tens of queries; 20x fewer online labels than PEBBLE; transferred to a real Franka.
trainable_options.inputs: trajectory segments + pairwise preferences
trainable_options.outputs: adapted reward model for a new owner/behaviour variant
trainable_options.train_recipe: Meta-train on simulated owner-reaction variants; adapt with 36-100 human queries per task (their human study), ~100-500 in sim
trainable_options.license: CoRL 2022 paper
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Adaptation step is a few gradient steps on a tiny MLP: feasible on Orin CPU/GPU

trainable_options.name: ICPL: LLM writes candidate reward functions, human ranks rollouts
trainable_options.what_it_is: GPT-4 proposes K=6 reward functions per iteration, policies are trained, a human ranks videos, the LLM revises; 49 human queries total, >30x fewer than PEBBLE/PrefPPO.
trainable_options.size_params: depends on the hosted LLM (GPT-4/4o in the paper) + IsaacGym PPO policies
trainable_options.inputs: task description + human pairwise/ranking feedback over rollout videos
trainable_options.outputs: executable reward code and a trained policy
trainable_options.train_recipe: N=5 iterations x K=6 rewards; <1 day per experiment; fits Parcel's hosted text-model budget as a handful of calls per iteration
trainable_options.license: paper CC-BY style arXiv; hosted LLM usage costs
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Training happens on the desktop; only the resulting policy/primitive goes to Orin

trainable_options.name: YAY-Robot / OLAF-style language-correction learning for the high-level policy
trainable_options.what_it_is: Hierarchical policy where spoken corrections override the high-level command in real time and are appended (with the last ~2 s of context, LLM-relabelled in OLAF) to fine-tune a small high-level policy head.
trainable_options.size_params: OLAF policy ~19M params (ResNet-18 BC-transformer); YAY HL policy ViT+frozen CLIP+DistilBERT
trainable_options.inputs: images/context + transcribed correction (Whisper)
trainable_options.outputs: high-level skill/primitive command
trainable_options.train_recipe: Real-time correction data was 4-11% of base data over 2-3 iterations (YAY); OLAF used 80-100 correction trajectories with one GPT-4 call each; expect +20-45 points
trainable_options.license: papers 2023/2024 (YAY code at yay-robot.github.io per paper)
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Small head fine-tuning feasible on Orin GPU offline; inference well within budget

trainable_options.name: Algorithm Distillation in-context RL head (experimental lane)
trainable_options.what_it_is: A causal transformer trained on simulated learning histories that improves a discrete behaviour choice in-context after 2-4 episodes without weight updates.
trainable_options.inputs: across-episode context of (context features, arm, reward)
trainable_options.outputs: next arm choice
trainable_options.train_recipe: Needs 2,000-4,000 simulated learning histories of the same task family (owner-reaction simulator); ICRL survey: no sim-to-real evidence, so preregister an evaluation
trainable_options.license: paper (DeepMind, ICLR 2023)
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Trivial to run; risk is transfer, not compute

trainable_options.name: Laughter detector (jrgillick/laughter-detection)
trainable_options.what_it_is: Pretrained PyTorch laughter segmenter (Switchboard-trained) producing laugh segments with a probability threshold; supplies the 'owner laughed' reward event.
trainable_options.size_params: not stated in README (small CNN/ResNet-class model file)
trainable_options.inputs: 16 kHz mono audio
trainable_options.outputs: laugh segments (start/end s) above threshold 0.5, min length 0.2 s
trainable_options.train_recipe: Use as-is; optionally fine-tune on owner audio with consent
trainable_options.license: MIT (2024 LaughterSegmentation alternative: code MIT, weights research-only, 1.26 GB)
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Runs on CPU/GPU in real time; untested with XVF3800 beamformer and speaker echo

trainable_options.name: Large Reward Models (Qwen3-VL-8B LoRA reward generator)
trainable_options.what_it_is: A VLM fine-tuned with LoRA into a frame-level reward generator (temporal contrastive, progress, completion) used as a frozen online reward engine every K=10 steps.
trainable_options.inputs: frames + task text
trainable_options.outputs: dense scalar reward
trainable_options.train_recipe: Trained on 24 data sources (OXE, HOI4D, EgoDex, LIBERO, RoboCasa) via DPO/SFT; real pick-and-place 38.3->51.7% in 30 RL iterations
trainable_options.license: arXiv 2026 paper; weights availability not stated in the read text
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Fits Orin 64 GB memory for batched/offline reward labelling; not usable in the 50 Hz lane

trainable_options.name: Vintix cross-domain ICRL action model (not recommended)
trainable_options.what_it_is: 300M-parameter Algorithm-Distillation action model over 87 tasks in 4 domains that learns in-context; weak transfer to genuinely new tasks.
trainable_options.inputs: multi-episode context of states/actions/rewards
trainable_options.outputs: actions
trainable_options.train_recipe: 1.6M episodes / 222.7M transitions; ~0.95-0.97 normalised on training tasks; 31-47% of expert on new tasks
trainable_options.license: paper CC BY 4.0; code 'to be released', weights not stated available
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Runs on Orin GPU but no weights and poor novel-task transfer; excluded

open_questions: Real event rates in a home (jokes/day, owner-lost episodes/day) are unknown; they set wall-clock time to reach the 30-100 labelled events per behaviour the literature implies.
Laughter detection on the reSpeaker XVF3800 while the dog's own speaker is active (echo/AEC) is unmeasured; the MIT detector was trained on Switchboard telephone speech.
Owner feedback is policy-dependent (COACH) and context-dependent (Song 2026): does the bandit need discounting, contextual arms for time-of-day/mood, or a non-stationary model?
What is the humour label-noise rate for a single owner? RIME's ~40% human error was on a motion task; humour judgments may be noisier, which changes the required prior strength.
Does a hosted-LLM 'was that funny' judge agree with actual owner laughter? A small paired dataset is needed before using the LLM as a simulator or labeller.
How should 'lost' be defined and simulated (LiDAR track loss, face absence > t s) and can MuJoCo/Isaac plus an owner-motion generator produce believable lost episodes for pre-training?
Consent and privacy: reward logs of owner laughter and corrections must be covered by the existing owner-model consent mechanism.
In-context RL has no published sim-to-real result; an AD-style head must get its own preregistered evaluation before it replaces the Bayesian bandit head.
Which reward definition to commit to for each behaviour (laughter vs verbal praise vs continued engagement), since Song 2026 shows the definition changes the learned policy.

results.claim: With off-policy learning, unsupervised pre-training and reward relabeling, a single easy-to-judge expressive behaviour was taught by real humans in 50-200 comparisons and under an hour.
results.evidence_quote: "Cart agent swinging a pole (using 50 queries)" ... "Quadruped agent waving a front leg (using 200 queries)" ... "Hopper performing a backflip (using 50 queries)" ... "a maximum of one hour of human time is required" ... "each trajectory segment is presented to the human as a 1 second video clip" ... "given a budget of 1400 queries, PEBBLE (green) reaches the same performance as SAC (pink) while Preference PPO (purple) is unable to match PPO (black)"
results.correction: No correction needed. All numbers verified on ar5iv + Appendix B: DMControl budgets 1400/700/400; Meta-world budgets 2500/5000/10000 (Drawer Close, Window Open, Door Open, Button Press) and 25000/50000 (Sweep Into, Drawer Open); segment length 50 (DMC) / 10 (Meta-world); ensemble of three reward models; 10K pre-training timesteps; Preference PPO given 2100 or 1400 queries. Minor wording: paper says 'a maximum of one hour' (i.e. <= 1 h) rather than strictly 'under an hour'. Note the quadruped leg-wave, the closest analogue to the Parcel primitives, is the 200-query case, not 50.

results.claim: Preference RL breaks under mildly noisy teachers (mistake prob 0.1 already degrades PEBBLE/PrefPPO); benchmark defines irrational-teacher parameters.
results.evidence_quote: "they often suffer from poor performance when teachers can provide the wrong labels (Mistake and Stoc). This suggests opportunities for further investigations and development of techniques that can improve the robustness to corrupted labels." ... "Mistake: SimTeacher(beta -> inf, gamma = 1, epsilon = 0.1, delta_skip = 0, delta_equal = 0)" ... "Stoc: SimTeacher(beta = 1, ...)" ... "Myopic: SimTeacher(..., gamma = 0.9, ...)" ... "Maximum budget / # of queries per session: 2000/200, 1000/100, 500/50 (DMControl); 20K/100, 10K/50 (Meta-world)"
results.correction: No correction needed; the abstract sentence is 'We find that existing methods often suffer from poor performance when teachers provide wrong labels'. Two details for precision: (1) the degradation under the epsilon=0.1 Mistake teacher is shown only in Figure 2 curves, the paper gives no numeric drop in text; (2) the Skip and Equal thresholds are not fixed numbers but adaptive (delta_adapt(epsilon_adapt, t)) because reward scales differ per environment.

results.claim: A meta-learned (MAML) reward prior from prior tasks cuts online preference queries 20x vs PEBBLE; humans trained tasks with 36-100 queries; transfers to a real Franka.
results.evidence_quote: "Previous works in preference based RL have required up to fifty-thousand artificial queries in order to solve some of the Meta-world tasks [18]. Our approach generally achieves the same performance using 20x fewer queries." ... "we adopt the MAML algorithm [49] for learning new reward functions" ... Figure 3 panels: "Point Mass, 36 / Reacher, 48 / Window Close, 64 / Door Close, 100" ... "We pre-train reward models with artificial queries and learn policies in simulation. We then transfer the learned policies to the real world and test on unseen goal locations." ... "For the Reach task we define success as being within 2.5cm of the goal and for the Block push task we define it to be within 5 cm."
results.correction: Headline (MAML prior, 20x vs PEBBLE, human budgets 36/48/64/100, real Franka reach 2.5 cm / push 5 cm) is supported. The supporting numbers are off: PEBBLE needed up to 50,000 artificial queries (25k is the drawer-open figure), not 'up to 25,000'; the Few-Shot simulated Meta-world budgets were 200 (Window Close, Door Close), 500 (Button Press), 1,000 (Drawer Open) and 2,500 (Sweep Into), not '~100-500' (the '~100 queries' convergence figure comes from a DM Control feedback-schedule ablation). Caveats: the human study used 'a single expert human subject' familiar with preference RL (plus three more users on Reacher only) taking ~22 min to ~1 h per task; on the Franka no human preferences were collected on the real robot: reward priors were adapted with artificial queries and policies trained in PyBullet, then transferred; the 20x claim held 'in all tasks, except Button Press'.

results.claim: Per-owner social-motion parameters on a Unitree Go1 (CPG amplitude/frequency/stiffness/duration) were learned from 10 binary comparisons per user; 76% of 25 subjects were happy with the result.
results.evidence_quote: "we parameterize handshakes with a Central Pattern Generator consisting of an amplitude, frequency, stiffness, and duration. Through 10 binary choices between handshakes, we learn a belief model to fit individual preferences for 25 different subjects. Our results show that this is an effective strategy, with 76% of users feeling happy with their identified optimal handshake parameters, and 20% feeling neutral. Moreover, compared with random and test handshakes, the optimized handshakes have significantly decreased errors in amplitude and frequency, lower Dynamic Time Warping scores" ... full text: "quadruped robots such as the Unitree Go1"; "APReL - a library for active preference-based reward learning"; "25 participants (11 female and 14 male) aged 20-35"
results.correction: The claim sentence itself is verbatim-supported (Go1, CPG amplitude/frequency/stiffness/duration, 10 binary choices, 25 subjects, 11 female, 76% happy / 20% neutral, APReL). The parenthetical in 'numbers' is wrong: 33%/51%/47% are the amplitude errors of three illustrative handshakes A/B/C (frequency errors 3%/42%/3%, DTW 12.62/51.71/31.07 m), not the comparison baseline, and the optimized handshakes still had 'a residual error of 49% in amplitude and 14% in frequency', i.e. higher amplitude error than A and C. The paper's actual improvement figures are a 15% then further 7% decrease in amplitude error from learning-phase to test to optimized handshakes and a 25% total decrease in frequency error, reported descriptively without a stated significance test.

results.claim: Human feedback is policy-dependent (people reward improvement, silence is meaningful); COACH interprets feedback as advantage and taught 5 TurtleBot behaviours in under 2 minutes each, while TAMER-style reward modelling unlearns behaviours.
results.evidence_quote: "COACH is based on the insight that the advantage function ... provides a better model of human feedback, capturing human-feedback properties like diminishing returns, rewarding improvement, and giving 0-valued feedback a semantic meaning that combats forgetting." ... "COACH was able to successfully learn all five behaviors ... Each of these behaviors were trained in less than two minutes, including the time spent verifying that a behavior worked." ... "eligibility traces with lambda = 0.95 for feedback +1 and -1, and lambda = 0.9999 for feedback +4. The feedback-action delay d was set to 6, which is 0.198 seconds." ... "human feedback is typically delayed by about 0.2 to 0.8 seconds" ... "we constructed a well-defined scenario in which TAMER consistently unlearns behavior" ... "TAMER only successfully learned the behaviors using the flat training methodology and failed to learn the compositionally trained behaviors. In all cases, TAMER tended to forget behavior"
results.correction: No correction needed; all quotes come from the PDF linked on the given page (proceedings.mlr.press/v70/macglashan17a/macglashan17a.pdf), since the abstract page itself carries only the policy-dependence and 'multiple behaviors on a physical robot' statements. Minor precision: the 0.2-0.8 s figure is cited from Knox (2012) as the typical human reaction delay and used as TAMER's credit-assignment window; the TurtleBot trainer was one of the co-authors (n=1), so the 'under 2 minutes' is an expert-trainer qualitative result, and 'TAMER also failed to learn from lure training because TAMER does not allow reinforcing a long history of behaviors'.

results.claim: For neural contextual bandits, a Bayesian linear head on a learned representation (NeuralLinear) and exact-posterior linear models beat all approximate-posterior deep methods; partially optimised uncertainty is catastrophic online.
results.evidence_quote: "In these cases, we found that partially optimized uncertainty estimates can lead to catastrophic decisions and poor performance. Second, and while it deserves further investigation, it seems that decoupling representation learning and uncertainty estimation improves performance. The NeuralLinear algorithm is an example of this decoupling." ... "No single algorithm bested the others in every bandit problem, however, we observed some general trends. We found that dropout, injecting random noise, and bootstrapping did provide a strong boost in performance on some tasks, but was not able to solve challenging synthetic exploration tasks. Other algorithms, like Variational Inference, Black Box alpha-divergence, and minibatch Markov Chain Monte Carlo approaches, strongly couple their complex representation and uncertainty estimates. This proves problematic when decisions are made based on partial optimization of both" ... "making decisions according to a Bayesian linear regression on the representation provided by the last layer of a deep network offers a robust and easy-to-tune approach"
results.correction: The 'partially optimized uncertainty is catastrophic online' half is a verbatim finding, and NeuralLinear / exact linear posteriors are the paper's recommended robust choice. 'Beat all approximate-posterior deep methods' is overstated: the paper says 'No single algorithm bested the others in every bandit problem'; in the Table 1 mean ranks (52 rows incl. Uniform, 50 trials) the best are exact linear LinFullPost 13.9, LinFullDiagPrecPost 14.3, LinDiagPrecPost 15.8, LinPost 16.4 and NeuralLinear-SL 17.4, but base NeuralLinear (22.0) is level with BootstrappedNN (22.4) and behind Dropout-MR (20.3), ParamNoise-SL (20.9) and SGFS-MR (21.8); Constant-SGD 'comes out as the winner on Covertype'. What is robustly beaten are the coupled approximate-posterior methods (Bayes-by-Backprop, BB alpha-divergence, minibatch MCMC) and, on the exploration-heavy Wheel bandit, everything ('NeuralLinear is probably the best algorithm ... almost an order of magnitude better than any RMS algorithm'). Also '~10,000 contexts per run' is wrong: horizons are dataset-specific, n = 3,713 (Financial), 19,181 (Jester), 43,500 (Statlog), 45,222 (Adult), 50,000 (Mushroom), 150,000 (Covertype), 250,000 (Census, Song); '25+ variants' undercounts (~50 configurations).

sweeps.topic: Coupling speech with body motion in real time: co-speech gesture generation, robot gesture systems, full-duplex backchannel/laughter timing, listener-motion generation, and a timing architecture for a full-duplex listen-speak-move loop on a companion quadruped

findings.claim: Human turn transitions have a cross-language mean offset of +208 ms (mode 0 ms; Japanese +7 ms to Danish +469 ms), and visible responses (nods, gestures) are produced faster than vocal responses in all 10 languages studied. This sets the latency budget for a reacting robot body (~200 ms) and voice (~300-500 ms).
findings.source_title: Stivers et al., Universals and cultural variation in turn-taking in conversation (PNAS)
findings.numbers: 10 languages; mean +208 ms; mode 0 ms; language means +7 ms (Japanese) to +469 ms (Danish); confirmations 100-500 ms faster than disconfirmations; visible responses faster than vocal in all languages
findings.relevance: Defines the timing envelope the 10 Hz reaction lane and 50 Hz body lane must hit; licenses body-first, voice-second reactions

findings.claim: Voice Activity Projection predicts the next 2 s of both parties' voice activity as a 256-state distribution from stereo audio with a CPC encoder + 4-layer 256-d transformer, trained self-supervised on Switchboard; it reaches backchannel-prediction F1 0.723 and shift-prediction F1 0.733, and code is MIT-licensed.
findings.source_title: Ekstedt & Skantze, Voice Activity Projection: Self-supervised Learning of Turn-taking Events (Interspeech 2022); code github.com/ErikEkstedt/VoiceActivityProjection
findings.numbers: 2 s window; bins 200/400/600/800 ms; 4 bins/speaker -> 256 states; CPC at 100 Hz; transformer hidden 256, 4 layers, 4 heads; Switchboard 2438 dialogs, 11-fold; weighted F1: S/H .899, S/L .786, S-pred .733, BC-pred .723 (majority .333); MIT license
findings.relevance: The trainable local 'when to react' primitive; needs no labels so Parcel can train on its own conversation logs

findings.claim: VAP runs in real time on CPU: with transformer context cut to 1 s, balanced accuracy on shift/hold is 76.16% (vs 74.20% at 20 s) at 14.61 ms per 20 ms frame (RTF 0.73) on a Xeon Gold 6128; the companion VAP-Realtime repo ships 5/10/20 Hz VAP, backchannel (VAP-BC) and a nodding model predicting nods 500 ms ahead.
findings.source_title: Inoue, Ekstedt, Skantze, Real-time and Continuous Turn-taking Prediction Using Voice Activity Projection (IWSDS 2024); repo github.com/inokoj/VAP-Realtime
findings.numbers: Train 92.5 h Japanese travel dialogue; 1-layer channel transformer + 3-layer cross transformer, 256 units, 4 heads; context 20 s: 74.20% / 273.84 ms (RTF 13.69); 10 s: 75.73% / 94.93 ms; 5 s: 75.01% / 33.66 ms (1.68); 1 s: 76.16% / 14.61 ms (0.73); 0.5 s: 75.41%; 0.3 s: 71.50%; 0.1 s: 62.81%; VAP-Realtime: models at 5/10/20 Hz, 2.5-5 s context; nodding model 10 Hz, 10 s context, outputs p_nod_short/p_nod_long/p_nod_long_p 500 ms ahead; code MIT, weights academic-only; input 160 samples @16 kHz per cycle
findings.relevance: Shows the reaction predictor fits on Orin CPU and that listener-gesture (nod) heads already exist in this family

findings.claim: Fine-tuning VAP with one extra linear layer predicts backchannels 500 ms before they occur: timing F1 42.85 (zero-shot VAP 15.11, prior baseline 36.37), continuer F1 38.11, assessment F1 31.76, running at 10 Hz with RTF 0.194 on an Intel i7-11700 CPU.
findings.source_title: Yeah, Un, Oh: Continuous and Real-time Backchannel Prediction with Fine-tuning of Voice Activity Projection (NAACL 2025)
findings.numbers: Positive frames 500 ms before backchannel; pre-training ~35 h Japanese dialogue; fine-tune 109 WOZ sessions (7-8 min each), 11,371 training utterances; F1 timing 42.85 vs 15.11 zero-shot; continuer 38.11 vs 34.13; assessment 31.76 vs 19.74; RTF < 1.0 on i7-11700, 0.194 at 5 s context, 10 Hz; Japanese only
findings.relevance: The exact recipe (extra head, 500 ms lead, 10 Hz) to add 'amused', 'nod', 'look-at-owner' heads for the dog

findings.claim: A shared-laughter system on the android ERICA detects laughs (BiGRU, F1 82.6), decides whether to laugh back (logistic regression, F1 30.3 vs 16.2% chance) and picks mirthful vs social laugh type (macro-F1 70.2), responding within 2 s; raters scored it significantly higher on empathy, naturalness and human-likeness than never- or always-laughing baselines.
findings.source_title: Inoue, Lala, Kawahara, Can a robot laugh with you?: Shared laughter generation for empathetic spoken dialogue (Frontiers in Robotics and AI)
findings.numbers: 82 speed-dating sessions (10-15 min); 2,453 laugh IPUs (8.2%): 1,611 solo + 842 speech laughs; 268 shared-laughter positives vs 1,389 negatives; laugh detector 2-layer BiGRU 256 hidden on 40-d mel: P 78.2 R 87.6 F1 82.6; shared-laughter LR on 80-d acoustic + 12-d prosodic: P 21.2 R 53.4 F1 30.3 (random 16.2%); laugh type macro-F1 70.2; response window 2 s; raters n=30-41 per scenario; empathy p=0.003, naturalness p<0.001, human-likeness p<0.001
findings.relevance: Closest existing system to 'learn to chuckle if the joke was funny'; shows audio-only decision is the weak link and that the 2 s window matters

findings.claim: GENEA 2023 (12 submissions + 2 baselines, dyadic Talking-With-Hands data): best system reached human-likeness median 69 vs mocap 71, but speech-appropriateness MAS 0.39 vs 0.81 for mocap, and interlocutor-appropriateness of every submission was at best 0.09 vs 0.63 for mocap, i.e., reacting to the other party was essentially unsolved.
findings.source_title: Kucherenko, Nagy, Yoon et al., The GENEA Challenge 2023: A large-scale evaluation of gesture generation models in monadic and dyadic settings (ICMI 2023)
findings.numbers: 41 one-minute test chunks (+29 mismatched); ~20 h 49 min TWH data; human-likeness medians NA 71, SG 69, SF 65, SJ 51, ... SC 9; speech-appropriateness MAS NA 0.81±0.06 (73.6% pref. matched), SG 0.39±0.07 (61.8%), SJ 0.27, BM 0.20, SF 0.20±0.06 (55.8%); interlocutor MAS NA 0.63±0.08 (67.9%), best submission SA 0.09, SG -0.09, SH -0.21; SF = DiffuseStyleGesture+ (1000 steps, 132 h on one V100); KTH CSMP+diffusion reports highest human-likeness and speech appropriateness (matches SG)
findings.relevance: Tells Parcel that realism is not the problem; listener/interlocutor appropriateness (the dog's core job) is the open frontier and is a timing/prediction problem

findings.claim: GENEA 2022 (18 h mocap, 10 teams, ~20,600 ratings) was the first time synthetic gestures were rated more human-like than mocap (FSA median 71 vs FNA 70), yet all synthetic motion was vastly less appropriate for speech (best 60.5% matched vs 74.0% for mocap) and FGD correlated only weakly with ratings.
findings.source_title: Kucherenko, Wolfert, Yoon et al., Evaluating gesture generation in a large-scale open challenge: The GENEA Challenge 2022 (ACM TOG)
findings.numbers: 18 h full-body mocap from Talking With Hands 16.2M (50 h audio); 30 fps; 10 teams; 9,196 full-body + 11,400 upper-body ratings; full-body medians FNA 70, FSA 71, FSC 53, FSI 46; appropriateness % matched FNA 74.0, FSH 60.5, FSA 57.1; upper-body UNA 63, USQ 69; UNA 75.4%, USQ 59.7%; FGD Kendall tau ~ -0.5
findings.relevance: Canonical evidence for separating realism from appropriateness and for distrusting FGD

findings.claim: A 2025 community re-evaluation of six gesture models on BEAT2 (600+ raters, 16,000 votes) found motion realism saturated (four models at 41-46% win rate vs mocap) while speech-gesture alignment of several claimed-SOTA models sits at ~50% (chance) versus 74% for mocap.
findings.source_title: Towards Reliable Human Evaluations in Gesture Generation: Insights from a Community-Driven State-of-the-Art Benchmark
findings.numbers: Models: DiffuseStyleGesture, Semantic Gesticulator, ConvoFusion, RAG-Gesture, AMUSE, HoloGest; realism Elo: mocap 1133, ConvoFusion 1102, RAG-Gesture 1088, HoloGest 1084, Semantic Gesticulator 1070, AMUSE 824, DiffuseStyleGesture 701; alignment (audio mismatch) mocap ~74%, DSG and HoloGest ~60%, Semantic Gesticulator ~57%, AMUSE/ConvoFusion/RAG-Gesture ~50%; >600 evaluators, >16,000 pairwise votes on Prolific
findings.relevance: Confirms: do not optimize realism/FGD for the dog; invest in alignment and timing

findings.claim: Moshi is a 7B full-duplex speech-text model over a 12.5 Hz / 1.1 kbps codec with 160 ms theoretical / 200 ms practical latency; its paralinguistics (92 speaking styles including 'laughs') and backchanneling were learned from ~20k h of LLM-scripted synthetic dialogue plus 2,000 h Fisher, and it reproduces human pause/gap/overlap statistics; weights CC-BY-4.0, needs ~24 GB GPU un-quantized.
findings.source_title: Défossez et al., Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue (Kyutai); code github.com/kyutai-labs/moshi
findings.numbers: Helium 7B (2.1T tokens); Depth Transformer 6 layers, dim 1024; Mimi 12.5 Hz, 1.1 kbps, 80 ms frame; latency 160 ms theory, 200 ms on L4; 7M h audio pretrain; Fisher 2000 h; 170 h natural conversations; >20k h synthetic; Table 19: 92 styles incl. laughs/amused/joking; prompts 'Use some backchanneling. Use short turns.'; turn-taking per minute (temp 1.0): IPU 50.8 s, Pause 7.0 s, Gap 4.5 s, Overlap 4.1 s vs GT 51.1/6.4/4.2/3.3; code MIT/Apache, weights CC-BY 4.0; PyTorch needs 24 GB GPU; MLX int4/int8
findings.relevance: Shows paralinguistic reactions can be learned from LLM-tagged synthetic data (a reusable recipe for dog reaction tokens) but that 7B is too heavy for the Orin reaction loop

findings.claim: On Full-Duplex-Bench the best open full-duplex model (Moshi) turn-takes with 0.265 s latency and handles interruptions in 0.257 s, but almost never backchannels (frequency 0.001, JSD 0.957); Freeze-Omni and Gemini Live are 1-1.4 s.
findings.source_title: Full-Duplex-Bench: A Benchmark to Evaluate Full-duplex Spoken Dialogue Models on Turn-taking Capabilities
findings.numbers: Pause handling TOR: dGSLM 0.934, Moshi 0.985, Freeze-Omni 0.642, Gemini Live 0.255; backchannel (ICC, 55 samples): Moshi freq 0.001 JSD 0.957, dGSLM 0.015/0.934, Gemini Live 0.012/0.896; smooth turn-taking (Candor, 119): Moshi TOR 1.000 latency 0.265 s, dGSLM 0.352 s, Freeze-Omni 0.953 s, Gemini Live 1.301 s; interruption (200 synthetic): Moshi 0.257 s, Freeze-Omni 1.409 s, Gemini Live 1.183 s
findings.relevance: Even an end-to-end full-duplex model needs a dedicated backchannel/reaction head; justifies the separate 10 Hz VAP lane

findings.claim: F-Actor shows a 1B-parameter (Llama-3.2-1B) full-duplex model trained on only ~2,000 h of synthetic Behavior-SD dialogue can follow explicit instructions controlling the number of backchannels and interruptions per dialogue, with turn-taking statistics matching its training data; model and code are released.
findings.source_title: F-Actor: Controllable Conversational Behaviour in Full-Duplex Models; code github.com/MaikeZuefle/f-actor
findings.numbers: Llama3.2-1B-Instruct backbone, frozen audio encoder, 4 DAU streams per audio stream; Behavior-SD 2,164 h synthetic (CosyVoice); instruction 'backchannels: 2 / interruptions: 1'; per-minute IPU 59.3 s, Pause 10.4 s, Gap 3.0 s, Overlap 5.4 s vs GT 55.8/10.8/3.8/3.0; LLM judge vs human ranking tau 1.00; interruptions avg 0.9 per dialogue so control is directional
findings.relevance: Template for a desktop-trainable speech model that accepts a per-turn 'reaction budget' from the hosted text model

findings.claim: Learning to Listen generates listener facial motion from speaker audio+motion as discrete VQ tokens (K=200) predicted 8 frames (267 ms) at a time at 30 fps, trained on 72 h of in-the-wild dyadic video; 75.3% of 150 evaluators preferred it over nearest-neighbour retrieval.
findings.source_title: Ng et al., Learning to Listen: Modeling Non-Deterministic Dyadic Facial Motion (CVPR 2022)
findings.numbers: 72 h from 6 YouTube channels; 30 fps; 53 expression coeffs + jaw + 3D head rotation; VQ-VAE K=200, d=256; window w=8, T=64; L2 33.16 expr / 4.75 rot; FD 3.55 / 0.81; 75.3% preferred over NN (n=150), 71.1% over a+m ablation; code/data released
findings.relevance: Direct template for a discrete 'dog reaction token' model over head/ears/tail/posture

findings.claim: A text-only listener model (GPT2-Medium, 345M) that emits VQ listener-motion tokens interleaved with the speaker's timestamped words produces semantically timed reactions: 92.8% preferred over unconditioned, 55.7% over the audio-based L2L, and 49.7% vs ground truth; initializing from a text-pretrained LM was critical.
findings.source_title: Ng et al., Can Language Models Learn to Listen? (ICCV 2023); code github.com/sanjayss34/lm-listener
findings.numbers: GPT2-Medium 24 layers 345M params; one listener (Trevor Noah); 2366 train / 222 val / 543 test segments up to 8 s; FD 18.22 vs GT 2.59; preference 92.8% vs Uncond, 55.7% vs L2L, 49.7% vs GT
findings.relevance: Mechanism for 'chuckle because the joke was funny' (semantic) rather than 'because prosody rose' (acoustic); fits the hosted/local text-model tier

findings.claim: Real-time dyadic head generation is achieved by ARIG with frame-wise autoregressive continuous diffusion (15 steps) at 31 fps, trained on 200+ h and explicitly modelling seven conversational states (speaking, listening, receiving feedback, pausing, interrupted, waiting, giving feedback); INFP (200+ h DyConv) switches speaking/listening implicitly from dual-track audio.
findings.source_title: ARIG: Autoregressive Interactive Head Generation for Real-time Conversations (ICCV 2025); companion INFP arXiv 2412.04037
findings.numbers: ARIG: 31 fps; 15 diffusion steps; >200 h (MultiDialog, ViCo, RealTalk); vs DIM on RealTalk SyncScore 7.218 vs 4.192, FID 21.64 vs 26.29, SID 2.428 vs 1.083. INFP: DyConv >200 h; vs DIM SSIM 0.834 vs 0.651, FID 15.727 vs 34.361, SID 2.613 vs 0.766; 20-participant study naturalness 4.38 vs 2.71; CC BY-NC-SA
findings.relevance: Validates a single dual-audio-conditioned generator with implicit speak/listen state at ~30 fps as the shape of the motion lane

findings.claim: Two-rate factorisation works for conversational body motion: a VQ transformer emits guide poses at 1 fps and a diffusion model in-fills details at 30 fps, conditioned on both speakers' audio; 70% of evaluators preferred it over a diffusion baseline. Moshi-Face similarly emits face tokens at the 12.5 Hz codec rate inside a full-duplex speech model.
findings.source_title: Ng et al., From Audio to Photoreal Embodiment: Synthesizing Humans in Conversations (CVPR 2024); Moshi-Face arXiv 2606.21970
findings.numbers: 8 h from 4 participants (2 h each dyadic); guide poses 1 fps; diffusion at 30 fps; 104 joint angles + 256-d face codes; FD_g 2.94±0.2, FD_k 0.96±0.07; 70% preference vs LDA. Moshi-Face: face tokens at 12.5 Hz (25 fps video /2); 180 h / 3,400 dialogues from Seamless Interaction; 5,143-vertex meshes; LSE-D 8.76
findings.relevance: Directly supports Parcel's per-utterance / 10-12.5 Hz / 30-50 Hz split

findings.claim: Meta's Seamless Interaction dataset provides 4,065 h of dyadic face-to-face interaction (4,284 participants, 64,739 interactions, 30 fps video, 48 kHz lapel audio) with body/face parametric representations, released on Hugging Face under CC BY-SA 4.0, plus dyadic motion models with emotion/expressivity control and LLM-guided gesture codebooks.
findings.source_title: Seamless Interaction: Dyadic Audiovisual Motion Modeling and Large-Scale Dataset (Meta)
findings.numbers: 4,065 h; 4,284 participants; 64,739 interactions; 5,098 sessions; Naturalistic 2,745 h / Improvised 1,320 h; 2160x3840 @30 fps; 48 kHz/16-bit; CC BY-SA 4.0 (arXiv header); audio-only and audiovisual dyadic models; emotion/expressivity/semantic-gesture control; model sizes not exposed
findings.relevance: The pretraining corpus for a human listener-reaction model to distil into dog reaction tokens

findings.claim: Uni-Mo / Quad-Imaginarium provides 7,488 language-annotated expressive quadruped motions (18.5 h) generated from a fine-tuned video diffusion model, lifted to 3D and tracked by a PPO policy, with 96.7% deployment success on a Unitree Go2.
findings.source_title: Unleashing Infinite Motion: Scaling Expressive Quadrupedal Motion via Generative Video Priors (Uni-Mo); data github.com/GaoLii/Quad-Imaginarium
findings.numbers: 7,488 motions, 18.5 h; Wan2.2 video backbone with LoRA + identity-consistency loss; PPO tracking; 96.7% success over 392 hardware motions; 97.6% in sim; CC BY 4.0 header; no latency numbers
findings.relevance: The missing expressive 'gesture library' for the Go2 body; text-conditioned selection can be driven by the reaction-token layer

findings.claim: Published legged/humanoid conversational robots couple body to speech only at per-utterance granularity with multi-second latency: Boston Dynamics' Spot tour guide (GPT-4 + Whisper + ElevenLabs) reported ~6 s question-to-answer latency and produced 'mouth' motion by low-pass-filtering the TTS envelope into a gripper trajectory; LLM-authored humanoid gestures (EMOTION, GPT-4o) take 26.8 s per sequence; cascaded Pepper LLM systems took 3.84-8.96 s.
findings.source_title: Boston Dynamics, Robots That Can Chat (blog); EMOTION arXiv 2410.23234; Pepper framework arXiv 2603.21013
findings.numbers: Spot: gpt-3.5 then gpt-4, BLIP-2 VQA, Whisper, ElevenLabs, Respeaker V2 on EAP 2; latency 'sometimes 6 seconds or so'; arm turned toward nearest person; gripper driven by low-passed speech. EMOTION: GR-1 humanoid, gpt-4o-2024-05-13, 22 participants, 26.8 s initial / 21.2 s per revision. Pepper: prior systems 3.84-8.96 s vs 1-2 s target; S2S APIs (gpt-realtime etc.) with function calling; MIT code
findings.relevance: Establishes the baseline Parcel already matches (command-picking from an LLM) and why a local sub-second reaction lane is the gap

findings.claim: Co-speech gesture generators that run per-frame are far faster than real time: ZeroEGGS (GRU decoder with a VAE style embedding from a 4-8 s example clip) infers at 4 ms/frame at 60 fps versus 29 ms for MoGlow, trained on 135 min of 19-style mocap; but its license is Ubisoft-proprietary. DiffuseStyleGesture (MIT) reaches MOS 4.11 vs 4.15 ground truth but needs 1000 diffusion steps per 4-s clip.
findings.source_title: Ghorbani et al., ZeroEGGS: Zero-shot Example-based Gesture Generation from Speech (CGF 2023); DiffuseStyleGesture arXiv 2305.04919 / github.com/YoungSeng/DiffuseStyleGesture
findings.numbers: ZeroEGGS: 67 monologues, 135 min, 19 styles, 60 fps, 75 joints; 80-ch mel, 12.5 ms hop; style clip 256-512 frames; 2-layer GRU 1024; 4 ms/frame vs MoGlow 29 ms; 131 participants; naturalness ~56.3±22.2 vs 11.8±12.2; '© Ubisoft All Rights Reserved'. DSG: WavLM-Large, 4 s clips at 20 fps (N=80), 8-frame seed, T=1000 steps; MOS human-likeness 4.11±0.08 vs GT 4.15±0.11; MIT; RTX 2080 Ti
findings.relevance: Fixes the shape (recurrent per-frame decoder with a style vector) and the licensing constraint for the 50 Hz motion lane

findings.claim: EMAGE/BEAT2 is the standard holistic co-speech dataset and model: 60 h from 25 speakers (from 76 h/30 speakers raw), SMPL-X+FLAME, with a masked audio-gesture transformer over four compositional VQ-VAEs that accepts partially specified gesture hints; FGD 5.512 vs TalkSHOW 6.209 and 52.7% user preference; weights on Hugging Face.
findings.source_title: Liu et al., EMAGE: Towards Unified Holistic Co-Speech Gesture Generation via Expressive Masked Audio Gesture Modeling (CVPR 2024); github.com/PantoMatrix/PantoMatrix
findings.numbers: BEAT raw 76 h / 30 speakers; BEAT2 60 h / 25 speakers (12 F, 13 M); BEAT2-standard 27 h, additional 33 h; 1762 sequences avg 65.66 s; FGD x1e-1 5.512, BC 7.724, Diversity 13.06, MSE 7.680e-8, LVD 7.556e-5; TalkSHOW 6.209/6.947/13.47; user study 60 participants x 40 pairs of 10 s; holistic preference 52.7% vs 34.9% vs 12.4%; paper CC BY-NC-SA
findings.relevance: Masked-hint conditioning is the pattern for a motion generator that must accept safety-layer overrides mid-sequence

findings.claim: Laughter can be placed at frame-level inside synthesized speech (ELaTE: 335M flow-matching TTS fine-tuned on 460 h of laughing speech, laughter timing correlation 0.673, WER 2.2) but weights are not released, so a system on a hosted Realtime API cannot control laugh placement and must use a local sound bank or local TTS.
findings.source_title: Kanda et al., Making Flow-Matching-Based Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech Laugh as You Like (ELaTE, Microsoft)
findings.numbers: 335M params, 24 Transformer layers; LibriLight 60k h pretrain; 459.8 h laughter fine-tune (AMI, Switchboard, Fisher); control by start/end times or example laugh; LibriSpeech WER 2.2, SIM-o 0.662; laughter timing correlation 0.673, similarity 0.796; no weights
findings.relevance: Determines where the chuckle sound must come from in Parcel's hosted-speech architecture

findings.claim: Sony aibo's product behaviour model is an internal state of four desires (affection, curiosity, sleep, expressing feelings) and emotions (delight, anger, sorrow, pleasure) triggered by events such as compliments, petting and loud sounds, expressed through eye/tail movement and tricks, with mood shifts affecting long-term growth; no timing numbers are published.
findings.source_title: Sony aibo ERS-1000 Help Guide: aibo's desires and emotions
findings.numbers: 4 desires; 4 emotion families; triggers: compliment, favorite object, no playmate, loud sound; expression via eyes, tail, tricks; no latency or model numbers
findings.relevance: The only shipped companion-dog spec; supports an explicit affect state modulating reaction priors rather than direct LLM command selection

findings.claim: As of 2026 there is no peer-reviewed quadruped system with measured speech-affect-driven reaction timing: the Go2 'LLM-powered interactive action synthesis' paper (Whisper small + Qwen3:0.6b) reports a single anecdote and no numbers, and a 2026 Frontiers quadruped review contains no social/affective behaviour coverage, listing latency and safety as VLA barriers.
findings.source_title: LLM-Powered Interactive Robotic Action Synthesis from Multimodal Speech, Gestures, and Music (Go2); Frontiers in Neurorobotics 2026 review 10.3389/fnbot.2026.1855550
findings.numbers: Go2; Whisper 'small'; Qwen3:0.6b via Ollama; beat detection for music; one demo (handstand on fist gesture); no latency, no success rate, no user study, no code. Review: names CognitiveDog, QUAR-VLA, NaVILA; barriers 'reliable grounding, action feasibility, latency, computation load, safety constraints, and hardware validation'
findings.relevance: Negative result: Parcel's evidence base must come from the human/avatar and spoken-dialogue literature; a measured full-duplex dog would be novel

design_implications: Split the loop into three trainable rates, each validated by a published system: per-utterance (0.2-1 Hz) semantic appraisal and 'reaction budget' from a text model (LM-Listener / F-Actor pattern); 10-12.5 Hz 'when to react' predictor (VAP + backchannel/nod/laugh/look-at-owner heads, 500 ms lead); 30-50 Hz continuous body decoder (ZeroEGGS-style GRU or ARIG-style frame-wise AR diffusion, or codebook lookup into Quad-Imaginarium clips tracked by the RL policy) inside the existing 50 Hz body-intent lane with the deterministic safety layer keeping authority.

Latency targets from human data: body reaction onset <= ~200-300 ms after the owner's cue (Stivers: mean gap +208 ms, visible responses precede vocal), audible chuckle <= 1 s and never later than 2 s after the owner's laugh (Inoue), no takeover during owner pauses (Full-Duplex-Bench pause-handling), and stay below the ~500 ms 'L0 external scheduler' ceiling that the full-duplex survey attributes to LLM-in-the-loop designs.

Feed the 10 Hz predictor stereo audio = owner mic channel + the robot's own outgoing TTS stream (VAP models are trained on both parties), plus a small world-state vector (owner bearing/distance, localisation covariance, seconds since last owner utterance) so the same network can emit 'look-at-owner' probabilities when lost.

Make 'chuckle if funny' a two-signal decision: fast acoustic head (laugh detector F1 ~83, shared-laughter decision F1 ~30 from audio alone) triggers a low-amplitude 'amused' body token immediately; the per-utterance text model (which has the joke's semantics and owner history) decides escalation to an audible chuckle; log (context, chuckle?, owner-laughed-within-3-s?, 'stop'?) into skill_outcomes and fit a per-owner bandit/logistic policy, i.e., Inoue's predictor with the text and owner-history features it lacked.

Represent reactions as discrete tokens (K ~ 50-200, ~250 ms per token as in L2L w=8 @30 fps) over head/neck/ears/tail/posture/gait-modulation, emitted at the 10-12.5 Hz rate and interpolated by the 50 Hz decoder; this is the Moshi-Face / Audio-to-Photoreal two-rate factorisation and it makes the safety layer's override a simple token veto.

Do not put a 7B full-duplex model in the Orin reaction loop first (24 GB bf16; Moshi's own backchannel frequency on Full-Duplex-Bench is 0.001); use Moshi's synthetic-dialogue recipe (LLM-written transcripts with style tags such as 'laughs' and 'use some backchanneling') to generate training data, and F-Actor's 1B behaviour-count instruction format as the interface between the hosted text model and local models.

Stop optimising gesture realism or FGD: the GENEA 2022/2023 challenges and the 2025 BEAT2 re-evaluation show realism is saturated and appropriateness (especially reaction to the interlocutor, MAS <= 0.09 vs 0.63 for humans) is where every system fails; Parcel's evaluation should be mismatch-style appropriateness tests and reaction-onset latency, not FGD.

Because the hosted Realtime speech API cannot place laughter at frame level (ELaTE shows this needs control of the TTS), the dog's chuckle and other vocal reactions must come from a local sound bank or local TTS triggered by the reaction layer, synchronised with the body token.

Sim/training plan for 'look back when lost': train the look-at-owner head in MuJoCo with a reward for owner-gaze events that precede re-acquisition, using the owner-bearing/localisation-covariance features; fine-tune on real logs; validate that the safety layer can pre-empt any reaction token within one 50 Hz tick.

Licensing guardrails: retrain VAP-family models from the MIT code (Kyoto's released weights are academic-only); do not ship ZeroEGGS code (Ubisoft proprietary) or INFP/EMAGE under CC BY-NC-SA in a product path; Seamless Interaction (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Quad-Imaginarium (CC BY 4.0) are the usable open datasets.

trainable_options.name: Voice Activity Projection (VAP) with reaction heads
trainable_options.what_it_is: Self-supervised stereo-audio model predicting the next 2 s of both parties' voice activity (256 states); fine-tuned with one extra linear layer per reaction (backchannel, nod, laugh-back, look-at-owner) at 500 ms lead, per the Kyoto NAACL 2025 recipe
trainable_options.size_params: CPC encoder + 4-layer 256-d transformer (order of a few million trainable params; frozen CPC)
trainable_options.inputs: 16 kHz stereo audio (owner mic + robot TTS stream), optional VA history and world-state vector
trainable_options.outputs: p_now/p_future per speaker; 256-state VAP distribution; per-head probabilities 500 ms ahead at 5-20 Hz
trainable_options.train_recipe: Pretrain on Switchboard-style dialogue (2438 dialogs) or any stereo conversation (no labels); fine-tune heads on ~35 h + ~13 h labelled events (Kyoto used 109 WOZ sessions); positives 500 ms before event; 1-5 s transformer context
trainable_options.license: MIT code; Ekstedt checkpoint in repo; Kyoto VAP-Realtime weights academic-only
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: High: 14.6 ms/frame (RTF 0.73 at 50 fps) with 1 s context on a Xeon CPU; RTF 0.19 at 10 Hz with 5 s context on an i7; CPU-only viable on Orin

trainable_options.outputs: System audio stream (+ optional text stream)

trainable_options.license: Code and model released (see repo)

trainable_options.outputs: Moshi audio stream + time-aligned text tokens

open_questions: Does a VAP-family predictor trained on human-human stereo audio transfer to the owner-mic + robot-TTS channel pair on the Go2 (motor/fan noise, far-field XVF3800 pickup)? Kyoto ships noise-augmented 'robot dialogue' variants, implying the gap is real; needs measurement.

What is the achievable reaction-onset latency on the Jetson AGX Orin for the full chain mic -> 10 Hz head -> 50 Hz body lane -> safety layer -> motor, and does it fit the ~200-300 ms visible-response window? No published quadruped number exists.

How large a dog 'reaction codebook' is perceptually sufficient (L2L used K=200 for faces; a quadruped with head/ears/tail/posture may need far fewer), and how should tokens map onto Quad-Imaginarium clips vs continuous decoder output?

Can the shared-laughter decision (F1 ~30 from audio alone) be pushed materially higher by adding the hosted text model's humour appraisal and owner history, and how many owner-labelled events (owner laughed within 3 s of a chuckle) are needed before a per-owner policy beats the prior?

Is Moshi (7B, CC-BY) runnable at usable throughput on Orin 64 GB in int8, and if so is the extra paralinguistic fidelity worth replacing the hosted Realtime API within the <= $300/mo budget? Only the 24 GB bf16 desktop requirement is documented.

What licence terms govern Seamless Interaction's model weights and Kyoto's VAP-BC/nod weights for product use (dataset CC BY-SA and academic-only weights, respectively) — retraining from MIT code may be mandatory.

How should 'look back when lost' be labelled: from simulated localisation-covariance spikes, from owner-absence timers, or from human listener-gaze events in Seamless Interaction retargeted to a dog? No source covers this behaviour on a robot.

Which appropriateness evaluation (GENEA mismatch protocol adapted to dog reactions) can be run cheaply enough in the 12-hour window without crowd raters — e.g., owner-only A/B of matched vs mismatched reaction streams in the MuJoCo viewer?

results.claim: Human turn transitions have a cross-language mean offset of +208 ms (mode 0 ms; Japanese +7 ms to Danish +469 ms), and visible responses (nods, gestures) are produced faster than vocal responses in all 10 languages studied. This sets the latency budget for a reacting robot body (~200 ms) and voice (~300-500 ms).
results.evidence_quote: "we compared data from video recordings of informal natural conversation in 10 languages from 5 continents" ... "The mean response offset for the full dataset is +208 ms, and the language-specific means fall within ≈250 ms either side of this cross-language mean" ... "a unimodal distribution with a mode offset for each language between 0 and +200 ms, and an overall mode of 0 ms" ... "Danish has the slowest response time on average (+469 ms) and Japanese has the fastest (+7 ms)" ...
