"confirmations are delivered faster than disconfirmations in all languages, between 100 and 500 ms faster on average" ... "When visible responses occurred in response to a question, they were faster than speech in every language" ... "This reached significance in 7/10 of the languages even though there was substantial variation"
results.correction: All numbers check out. Two nuances: (1) visible responses were faster than speech in every language as point estimates, but the difference reached statistical significance in only 7 of 10 languages; (2) the '~200 ms body / ~300-500 ms voice' latency budget is the claimant's design inference, not a figure stated by the paper (the paper only notes ~208 ms is roughly the length of one English syllable).

results.claim: Voice Activity Projection predicts the next 2 s of both parties' voice activity as a 256-state distribution from stereo audio with a CPC encoder + 4-layer 256-d transformer, trained self-supervised on Switchboard; it reaches backchannel-prediction F1 0.723 and shift-prediction F1 0.733, and code is MIT-licensed.
results.evidence_quote: "we limit the number of bins to 4 for each speaker, resulting in 8 total bits, or 256 different possible states" ... "we define a VAP window of 2 seconds ... bin durations of 200, 400, 600 and 800ms" ... "pre-trained CPC [22] model that outputs frame representations h_speech,t ∈ R256, at 100Hz" ... "transformer [23] using a hidden size of 256, 4 layers, 4 heads and 0.1 dropout" ... "We train on the Switchboard dataset [24] containing a total of 2438 dialogs ... 11 pairs of train/validation sets" ... "The dialog waveforms are volume normalized, resampled to 16kHz and, unlike prior work [14], mixed to a single channel." ... Table 1: "Discrete (ours) .899 (.510) .786 .733* .723*" / "Majority class .843 (0) .565 .333 .333". GitHub ErikEkstedt/VoiceActivityProjection: License: MIT.
results.correction: Every number (2 s window; 200/400/600/800 ms bins; 256 states; CPC at 100 Hz; 256-d, 4-layer, 4-head transformer; Switchboard 2438 dialogs, 11-fold; F1 S/H .899, S/L .786, S-pred .733, BC-pred .723; majority .333) is in the paper and the VoiceActivityProjection repo is MIT-licensed. But the input is NOT stereo in this paper: the two speakers' waveforms are 'mixed to a single channel' (mono). Stereo (per-channel) input was introduced in later VAP variants (e.g., Ekstedt & Skantze SIGDIAL 2022 / Inoue et al. 2024). Also note the paper itself links github.com/ErikEkstedt/vap_turn_taking and conv_ssl, not the VoiceActivityProjection repo.

results.claim: Fine-tuning VAP with one extra linear layer predicts backchannels 500 ms before they occur: timing F1 42.85 (zero-shot VAP 15.11, prior baseline 36.37), continuer F1 38.11, assessment F1 31.76, running at 10 Hz with RTF 0.194 on an Intel i7-11700 CPU.
results.evidence_quote: "we marked the positive sample frames as occurring 500 milliseconds before the actual backchannel utterances" ... "a new linear layer is introduced on top of the VAP model, complementing the existing layers for VAP and VAD" ... "the pre-training data amounted to about 35 hours" ... "we recorded 109 dialogue sessions, each lasting approximately 7 to 8 minutes" ... "11,371 utterances for training, 1,139 for validation, and 1,091 for testing" ... Table 1: "Zero-shot 15.11 ... Baseline 36.37 ... MT w/ PT 42.85"; Table 2 (continuer): "Baseline 34.13 ... MT w/ PT 38.11"; Table 3 (assessment): "Baseline 19.74 ... MT w/ PT 31.76" ... "we adjusted the frame rate to 10 Hz, which is sufficient for real-time prediction systems, and retrained the models accordingly. Therefore, note that the results in this section would be different from the ones so far." ... "only a CPU was utilized, specifically an Intel Core i7-11700 @ 2.50 GHz" ... Table 5 (context 5 s): "36.57 30.08 0.194" ... "This study was evaluated solely on a Japanese dialogue dataset"
results.correction: All individual numbers are in the paper, but the sentence conflates two experiments: continuer F1 38.11 / assessment F1 31.76 come from the main (full-frame-rate) experiment; the real-time experiment retrained the models at 10 Hz, where the 5 s-context model achieved RTF 0.194 with continuer F1 36.57 and assessment F1 30.08 (RTF ranged 0.157-0.229 across 1-20 s contexts). Also, 34.13/19.74 are the CPC+linear 'Baseline', not zero-shot VAP (zero-shot was only reported for the timing task). Japanese-only data.

results.claim: A shared-laughter system on the android ERICA detects laughs (BiGRU, F1 82.6), decides whether to laugh back (logistic regression, F1 30.3 vs 16.2% chance) and picks mirthful vs social laugh type (macro-F1 70.2), responding within 2 s; raters scored it significantly higher on empathy, naturalness and human-likeness than never- or always-laughing baselines.
results.evidence_quote: "82 dialogue sessions" of "10 to 15 min"; "2,453 IPUs (8.2%)"; "solo laughs (1,611) or speech laughs that ended with laughter (842)"; "268 shared laughter samples were extracted as positive samples" vs "1,389 were labeled as negative samples"; BiGRU "2" layers, "256" hidden, "40-dimensional Mel-filterbank": "Precision 78.2", "Recall 87.6", "F1 score of 82.6%"; logistic regression on "80 dimensions" + "12 dimensions": "Precision 21.2, Recall 53.4, F1 score 30.3" vs "16.2%" random; laugh type "Macro F1 score" "70.2"; "if ERICA responded to a laugh sample with a laugh within 2 s after the end of the initial laugh, this sample was annotated as shared laughter"; Scenario 1 (n=41) proposed vs reactive: "empathy (p = 0.003), naturalness (p < 0.001), human likeness (p < 0.001), and understanding (p = 0.003)" but no significant difference vs no-laugh; Scenario 3 (n=30): "the second baseline (reactive) showed significantly higher scores than the proposed system on empathy (p = 0.002) and human likeness (p = 0.037)"; abstract: "The proposed system improved the impression of the dialogue system such as empathy perception compared to a naive baseline without laughter and a reactive system that always responded with only social laughs."
results.correction: Model numbers (82.6 / 30.3 vs 16.2% / 70.2), dataset counts, and rater n (41, 31, 30, 30) all check out. Two details are off: (1) 'responding within 2 s' is the corpus annotation criterion for labelling shared laughter, not a measured system response latency; (2) the significance claim is overgeneralized. The cited p-values (empathy 0.003, naturalness <0.001, human-likeness <0.001) are from Scenario 1 versus the always-laughing (reactive) baseline only; in that scenario there was no significant difference versus the no-laugh baseline. Scenario 2 showed significance only for understanding vs no-laugh (p=0.046); in Scenario 3 the reactive baseline significantly beat the proposed system on empathy and human-likeness; Scenario 4 favoured the proposed system over no-laugh on all scales and over reactive on naturalness and human-likeness. Correct statement: the proposed system was rated significantly higher than one or both baselines on several scales in 3 of 4 scenarios, and was beaten by the always-laughing baseline in one.

results.claim: GENEA 2023 (12 submissions + 2 baselines, dyadic Talking-With-Hands data): best system reached human-likeness median 69 vs mocap 71, but speech-appropriateness MAS 0.39 vs 0.81 for mocap, and interlocutor-appropriateness of every submission was at best 0.09 vs 0.63 for mocap, i.e., reacting to the other party was essentially unsolved.
results.evidence_quote: "We evaluated 12 submissions and 2 baselines together with held-out motion-capture data" ... "the original Talking With Hands (TWH) data [29]" ... "a core test set consisting of 41 chunks of approximately one minute each ... extended the test set with 29 additional chunks in which the two sides of the conversation were mismatched" ... Human-likeness table: "NA 71 ∈ [70, 71]", "SG 69 ∈ [67, 70]", "SF 65 ∈ [64, 67]", "SJ 51 ∈ [50, 53]", "SC 9 ∈ [9, 9]" ... Speech appropriateness: "NA 0.81±0.06 73.6%", "SG 0.39±0.07 61.8%", "SJ 0.27±0.06", "BM 0.20±0.05", "SF 0.20±0.06 55.8%" ... Interlocutor appropriateness: "NA 0.63±0.08 67.9%", "SA 0.09±0.06 53.5%", "SG −0.09±0.08", "SH −0.21±0.07" ... "The effect of the interlocutor is even more subtle, with submitted systems at best performing barely above chance." ... "the challenge entries were labelled SA–SL. These labels are anonymous and have no relationship to the team names or identities."
results.correction: The claim as written is fully supported (12+2 systems, TWH dyadic data, HL medians 69 vs 71, speech MAS 0.39 vs 0.81, interlocutor MAS best 0.09 vs 0.63, 'at best barely above chance'). Caveats on the auxiliary numbers only: the challenge paper anonymizes conditions, so the identifications 'SF = DiffuseStyleGesture+ (1000 steps, 132 h on one V100)' and 'KTH CSMP+diffusion = SG' are not in this paper and must be sourced from the respective team papers; the '~20 h 49 min' dataset duration was not found in this paper's text either.

sweeps.topic: Language- and affect-conditioned expressive motion generation for legged robots and characters (label/text/latent -> Go2 whole-body motion)

findings.claim: SayTap bridges natural language and a quadruped controller through a 4xT foot-contact-pattern matrix produced by GPT-4; the PPO contact-tracking policy trains in ~15 min and transfers to a real Unitree A1 without fine-tuning, but the style space is gait-level only.
findings.source_title: SayTap: Language to Quadrupedal Locomotion
findings.numbers: GPT-4 at temperature 0.5; 4xT contact matrix, window Lw=5; Unitree A1, 12 outputs, 50 Hz; MLP [512,256,128] ELU, 65-D input; PPO in IsaacGym, 1000 iterations, ~15 min on one V100; cycle T in [24,28] = 0.48-0.56 s; 5 gait types; >50% contact-pattern prediction success; solves 10 more of 30 tasks than alternatives; paper CC BY 4.0; no code linked on project page
findings.relevance: Cheapest language->gait bridge; usable as a tempo/gait channel inside a richer command vector, not as the whole affect->motion answer.

findings.claim: Disney's bipedal robotic character separates an artist-driven animation engine (background loops + triggered clips + joystick procedural modification) from RL tracking policies that consume a small command vector (head/torso offsets, 2-D velocity + yaw rate, or phase), and ran ~10 h across three robots without a fall.
findings.source_title: Design and Control of a Bipedal Robotic Character (RSS 2024)
findings.numbers: 14 DoF (5/leg + 4 head/neck), 15.4 kg, 0.66 m; leg actuators 34 N m peak / 20 rad/s; PPO, Isaac Gym, 8192 envs x 24 steps, 100,000 iterations (~22 days on RTX 4090) per policy; MLP 3x512 ELU; 50 Hz policy, 600 Hz actuator loop; tracking MAE 0.035 rad standing, 0.123 rad walking, 0.027-0.043 rad episodic; max 0.7 m/s fwd, 0.4 m/s lateral, 1.8 rad/s turn; ~10 h runtime, no falls; clips: happy dance, excited, jump, tantrum, yes/no, scanning; no code
findings.relevance: The reference architecture for expressive + robust + interruptible motion: style lives in a kinematic animation layer, balance in a tracker; the interface is a tiny command vector. Direct template for Parcel's expression layer over a Go2 tracker.

findings.claim: AMOR trains one policy conditioned on a reward-weight vector over 7 objectives (Pareto front), so style/smoothness trade-offs are tuned after training on the real robot character without retraining.
findings.source_title: AMOR: Adaptive Character Control through Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning (SIGGRAPH 2025, Disney)
findings.numbers: 20-DoF biped; 7 objectives (upper body, lower body, feet, rigid-body poses, root pose, root velocities, smoothness); MOPPO; Isaac Gym 8192 envs at 250 Hz on RTX 4090; ~5 days (300k iterations) per character; 4-layer MLP 1024 ELU; double pirouette needed ~1 day manual weight tuning on hardware; no code
findings.relevance: Cleanest published mechanism for continuous, runtime-steerable 'intensity' knobs (calmer/smoother/more energetic) on a single policy.

findings.claim: Apple's ELEGNT study shows expressive (vs purely functional) movement roughly doubles user ratings of a non-anthropomorphic robot, with the gain concentrated in social/conversational tasks; movements were hand-authored, not learned.
findings.source_title: ELEGNT: Expressive and Functional Movement Design for Non-anthropomorphic Robot
findings.numbers: 6-DoF WidowX 250S lamp; N=21 (ages 26-51), within-subject, 6 tasks (3 function, 3 social); 0-100 ratings: expression M=56.16 vs function M=28.77 (SD 27.15), Welch t=19.85, p<0.0001; per-metric t: character 10.58, human-likeness 9.32, engagement 8.80, connection 8.50, willingness 7.37, intelligence 5.22; no significant gain on intelligence/willingness/engagement for function tasks; age effect p<0.001; non-roboticists higher p=0.006
findings.relevance: Quantitative justification that affect-driven motion matters most in exactly Parcel's context (conversation), plus a primitive vocabulary (intention/attention/attitude/emotion x kinesics/proxemics) that maps to a neckless dog via body Euler, tempo, pauses, approach/withdraw.

findings.claim: Apple's EMOTION generates humanoid gesture keyframes from GPT-4o with 2 in-context demos and users rate them as natural as human-designed ones, but generation takes ~27 s per gesture, so it is an offline authoring tool rather than a live controller.
findings.source_title: EMOTION: Expressive Motion Sequence Generation for Humanoid Robots with In-Context Learning
findings.numbers: Fourier GR-1; 22 values/timestep, T=10 keyframes; GPT-4o (gpt-4o-2024-05-13); 2 demos (Vision Pro); 10 gestures; N=22 valid of 30; EMOTION vs human oracle n.s. (p=0.267 naturalness, 0.528 understandability); EMOTION++ > EMOTION (p=0.0014 / 0.019), > human on understandability (p=0.003); avg 1.9 feedback iterations; latency 26.8+/-4.0 s initial, 21.2+/-3.7 s per refinement; prompts only released
findings.relevance: Template for LLM-authored clip libraries and for a feedback loop (owner reaction -> refine); confirms hosted-LLM latency rules it out for full-duplex runtime.

findings.claim: ExBody2 runs a single whole-body tracking policy conditioned on reference keypoints/joints/root velocity on a Unitree G1 with a Jetson Orin NX at 50 Hz, trained on ~1.9k CMU clips filtered by tracking error, with ~0.1 rad real joint error.
findings.source_title: ExBody2: Advanced Expressive Humanoid Whole-Body Control
findings.numbers: Unitree G1 + Jetson Orin NX; 50 Hz policy, 18-30 ms command latency, 500 Hz low-level; CMU 1,919 sequences + ACCAD OOD; curation threshold tau=0.15; inputs: 23-DoF proprio, 36 keypoints, 23 DoF refs, root vel/pose; teacher PPO -> student DAgger (10-frame history); Adam lr 1e-4, batch 4096; sim E_vel 0.2930 m/s, MPKPE 0.1000 m, MPJPE 0.1079 rad; real joint error 0.1074 rad; 43-s choreography; no code link found
findings.relevance: Proves the 'one universal reference-conditioned tracker on Orin at 50 Hz' shape Parcel should target instead of per-clip policies.

findings.claim: ExBody decouples expressive upper-body imitation from velocity-tracked legs on a Unitree H1 using 780 keyword-filtered CMU clips (3.7 h) and releases the Isaac Gym training + CMU retargeting code.
findings.source_title: Expressive Whole-Body Control for Humanoid Robots (RSS 2024)
findings.numbers: H1 19 DoF, ~51.5 kg, ~1.8 m; 780 clips, 3.7 h; inputs: 9 upper-body joint angles + 18 keypoint values + root command (lin vel, roll/pitch/yaw, height); PPO 4096 envs Isaac Gym, lr 1e-3; real roll/pitch MAE 0.036-0.075 rad across 14 motion types vs 0.055-0.11 for AMP baseline; code: github.com/chengxuxin/expressive-humanoid (license file present, type not shown)
findings.relevance: The 'expressive posture channel + robust gait channel' decoupling transfers directly to a dog body/head-attitude vs gait split.

findings.claim: Four-and-a-half seconds of German Shepherd mocap used as an adversarial style reward produced natural, energy-efficient gaits with emergent pace->trot->canter transitions on a real Unitree A1, with cost of transport well below a hand-tuned complex reward.
findings.source_title: Adversarial Motion Priors Make Good Substitutes for Complex Reward Functions (IROS 2022)
findings.numbers: Unitree A1; 4.5 s mocap (Zhang & Starke dataset: pace, trot, canter, turn); discriminator on (s,s') joint pos/vel + base lin/ang vel; w_style 0.65, w_task 0.35, gradient penalty 10; distributed PPO, Isaac Gym 5280 envs, 4B steps, 16 h on one V100; CoT 0.93+/-0.04 to 1.12+/-0.1 (0.8-1.6 m/s) vs 1.37+/-0.12 to 1.54+/-0.17 complex reward vs 5.18-14.03 no style; pace at 0.8 m/s, trot/canter at 1.7 m/s; code MIT (escontra/AMP_for_hardware, Isaac Gym Preview 3)
findings.relevance: The cheapest 'make it move like a dog' prior; a few seconds of clip data is enough. Gives style quality, not style selection.

findings.claim: VIM learns one latent-skill-conditioned controller over 11 reference motions (dog mocap, synthesized, trajectory-optimized) on a Unitree A1 and executes trot, jumps and a backflip on hardware without fine-tuning, with a high-level policy choosing latents for tasks.
findings.source_title: Generalized Animal Imitator: Agile Locomotion with Versatile Motion Prior (VIM)
findings.numbers: A1, 12 joints, 25 Hz, PD KP 40 / KD 1.0; latent skill embedding from reference-motion encoder; 11 references (Zhang 2018 dog: walk, trot, canter, pace, jump-while-running, L/R turns; 2 synthesized; backflip + jump from traj-opt); functionality reward exp(-20|e|^2) horiz / exp(-80) vertical / exp(-10) orientation; stylization adversarial early -> joint tracking later; PPO 4096 envs IsaacGym at 200 Hz, 2e9 samples low-level, 4e8 high-level; real: jump height 0.50+/-0.003 m (ref 0.53), jump distance 0.76+/-0.05 m (ref 0.82), trot 1.33+/-0.17 m/s (ref 1.16), backflip 0.62+/-0.01 m; sim root XY error 1.24+/-0.62 m; code not linked
findings.relevance: Closest published latent-conditioned multi-skill dog controller on Unitree hardware; the label->latent selection step is exactly Parcel's missing piece.

findings.claim: CAMP switches among four gaits on a real Unitree Go2 from a one-hot skill vector using a skill-conditioned adversarial motion prior trained on model-based synthetic clips in about 7 GPU-hours on a consumer card.
findings.source_title: Learning Multi-Skill Legged Locomotion Using Conditional Adversarial Motion Priors
findings.numbers: Unitree Go2 (also A1); one-hot skill vector; 4 gaits (trot, pace, bound, pronk); reference clips ~4 s each from a model-based controller (no mocap); PPO, Isaac Gym, 4096 agents, ~7 h on RTX 4060 Ti; 50 Hz; 8 DR categories; joint-tracking accuracy 91.23-91.38%; skill discriminator required for >2 skills; deployed without retuning; code not specified
findings.relevance: Direct evidence that categorical label -> Go2 skill switching is an overnight training job when reference clips exist, even synthetic ones.

findings.claim: Walk Like Dogs learns an 18-D hyperspherical latent + mixture-of-experts synthesizer over unlabeled dog mocap retargeted kino-dynamically to the Go2, with an RL policy mapping velocity commands to latents; emergent gallop/trot/pace transitions were deployed on a real Go2.
findings.source_title: Walk Like Dogs: Learning Steerable Imitation Controllers for Legged Robots from Unlabeled Motion Data
findings.numbers: Unitree Go2; 13,076 dog pose samples (Zhang 2018) + mirrored; IK scale factors alpha_z 0.81, alpha_fwd 0.6, alpha_side 0.6, limb [0.6,0.7,0.81]; MJPC iLQG 2.0 s horizon, 0.01 s; vMF VAE 18-D latent; 6-expert MoE decoder; PPO 4096 envs, [512,256,128], batch 24,576, lr 5e-4; Isaac Lab tracker, Kp 30 / Kd 0.5, 50 Hz; commands 0.6-2.4 m/s, +/-1.0 rad/s; gallop->trot->pace at 1.8->1.2->0.7 m/s; RMS base-velocity error 0.11 (as printed); no code
findings.relevance: A Go2-specific latent-over-dog-data controller with a learned command->latent policy; swapping 'velocity' for 'velocity + affect' is Parcel's style-conditioned gait layer. Also the retargeting recipe to copy.

findings.claim: Multi-Domain Motion Embedding conditions a quadruped policy on a wavelet + VAE embedding of raw (unretargeted) actor motion and reproduces dog motions zero-shot on ANYmal D in real time, trained from ~10 min of dog mocap augmented to ~52 min.
findings.source_title: Multi-Domain Motion Embedding: Expressive Real-Time Mimicry for Legged Robots
findings.numbers: ANYmal D; H1 (sim); Fourier N1 (hardware); db2 wavelet 4 levels (quadruped) / 2 (humanoid) + VAE latent 32-D / 64-D; history buffer 25 frames (quadruped) / 5 (humanoid); AMASS + ~10 min dog (Zhang 2018) -> ~52 min augmented; PPO in Isaac Lab at 50 Hz; outperforms VMP and PAE on reconstruction (figures only); CC BY 4.0; no repo URL
findings.relevance: Shows a continuous embedding (not a label) can steer a quadruped live and generalize to unseen styles; the 'latent' end of the label->latent->motion spectrum.

findings.claim: QuadFM is a 11,784-clip (20.27 h) Go2-native text-annotated motion dataset with an explicit emotion/interaction category, and its Gen2Control system runs a 2 Hz text-to-motion generator plus a single 50 Hz tracker on a Jetson Orin with ~500 ms speech-to-motion latency.
findings.source_title: QuadFM: Foundational Text-Driven Quadruped Motion Dataset (Gen2Control)
findings.numbers: 11,784 clips, 20.27 h, 35,352 descriptions in 3 layers; locomotion 9,390 clips / 11.64 h; interaction & emotion 2,394 clips / 8.63 h; teleop 696 clips / 4.74 h; artist 1,698 clips / 3.89 h; video-generated 1,392 clips / 1.62 h; labels e.g. greeting, cautious/sad pacing, excited bounding, stretching, pouncing toward humans; Go2 X + Jetson Orin; MotionGPT3-based generator (motion VAE + diffusion LM) at 2 Hz, tracker at 50 Hz observing proprio + short future reference window; ~500 ms end-to-end incl. cloud ASR; stage I 48 h on one MI308X; stage II 2xRTX 3090, 20k iterations, 4096 envs; 30 raters, 10 unseen prompts, 0-9: MotionGPT3 5.77/5.62/5.54/6.27 vs Gen2Control 7.40-7.98; dataset CC BY 4.0 'will be released'; GitHub repo Apache-2.0 but empty at fetch
findings.relevance: The published system closest to Parcel's target stack (speech -> generated Go2 motion -> single tracker on Orin, with emotion-labelled data). Design reference only until the data ships.

findings.claim: Uni-Mo shows that 7,488 LLM-prompted, video-diffusion-synthesized Go2 motions (18.5 h) are trackable by per-motion PPO policies trained in MuJoCo, with 96.7% real-robot success over 392 randomly sampled motions.
findings.source_title: Unleashing Infinite Motion: Scaling Expressive Quadrupedal Motion via Generative Video Priors (Quad-Imaginarium)
findings.numbers: Gemini prompts; Wan2.2 I2V fine-tuned with identity-consistency loss on 190 designer motions x 10 views = 1,900 pairs, 56 H20 GPUs, 10 epochs; ViTPose lift + CLIP/geometric/tracking gates; one PPO tracker per motion (BeyondMimic setup), MuJoCo, 4,096 envs on one RTX 3090, MLP (512,256,128), residual joint targets x0.25; 7,488 motions, 18.5 h, 19-D state (paper: 50 Hz; README: 24 fps), clips 5-15 s; sim success 97.6%; real Go2 96.7% over 392 motions x 5 trials (success = no fall / no manual intervention); no text-to-motion model; no latency; dataset unreleased pending acceptance
findings.relevance: Strongest hardware evidence that a large non-gait expressive vocabulary is executable on the Go2, and a zero-mocap data path (synthesize -> lift -> filter in sim) Parcel can copy in miniature with hand-authored clips.

findings.claim: MotionGlot treats robot and human motion as extra tokens of GPT-2 small via per-embodiment VQ-VAE codebooks and instruction-tunes text<->motion tasks across a Spot quadruped (SE(2) velocities) and SMPL humans, including sentiment classification from gaits.
findings.source_title: MotionGlot: A Multi-Embodied Motion Generation Model
findings.numbers: Spot; robot motion = 3-D SE(2) velocities; human 263-D (HumanML3D, 22 joints); VQ-VAE codebooks 128x512 (robot), 512x512 (human), downsample 4; GPT-2 small, vocab 50,257; QUAD-LOCO ~48k trajectories from >1000 teleop trajectories over 2.5 h (mirroring/time-scaling); QUES-CAP 23k prompts; 6 tasks; +35.3% avg; hardware demo; repo has empty README; datasets 'to be released soon'; paper CC BY 4.0
findings.relevance: The recipe for a small trainable text/affect -> motion-token head that fits on an Orin; caveat: its quadruped action space is base velocity only.

findings.claim: OmniMotionGPT releases AnimalML3D, the only open text-annotated animal-motion dataset (SMAL skeleton), and a GPT-style generator that transfers a human-motion prior to animals; code and data are MIT.
findings.source_title: OmniMotionGPT: Animal Motion Generation with Limited Data (CVPR 2024) - code/data repo
findings.numbers: 1,240 sequences, 36 animal identities (922 train / 23 ids; 318 test / 13 ids), 3,720 captions; motions from DeformingThings4D registered to SMAL; MIT license; pretrained weights not explicitly listed
findings.relevance: Open text->animal motion seed data; would need SMAL->Go2 retargeting.

findings.claim: Google's 2020 animal-imitation pipeline (IK retargeting of public dog mocap -> per-clip PPO in PyBullet -> latent-space real-world adaptation from ~50 short trials) is released under Apache-2.0 with retargeted dog clips and pretrained policies for Laikago/A1.
findings.source_title: Learning Agile Robotic Locomotion Skills by Imitating Animals (RSS 2020)
findings.numbers: Laikago 18 DoF (12 actuated); dog mocap (Zhang 2018) + artist clips; IK on keypoint pairs; PPO ~200M samples in PyBullet; DR over 6 parameters; AWR latent adaptation with ~50 real trials of 5-10 s; skills: pace, trot, backward trot, side-steps, spin, turn, hop-turn, in-place stepping; forward running hard; code Apache-2.0 (google-research/motion_imitation) with dog_pace/dog_trot/dog_spin/dog_backward_trot clips + pretrained policies
findings.relevance: Only Apache-licensed source of ready-made retargeted dog clips; canonical retargeting reference.

findings.claim: The canonical dog mocap behind nearly every quadruped imitation paper (Zhang, Starke, Komura, Saito 2018) is distributed via AI4Animation for research/education only, with the motion-capture data under CC BY-NC 4.0.
findings.source_title: AI4Animation (Mode-Adaptive Neural Networks for Quadruped Motion Control dog dataset)
findings.numbers: Project 'only for research or education purposes, and not freely available for commercial use'; mocap data CC BY-NC 4.0; reported as ~10 min (MDME), 4.5 s subset (AMP-hw), 13,076 poses (Walk Like Dogs), 151k frames @60 fps (~42 min) in WalkTheDog; modes: walk, pace, trot, canter, jump, sit, turn, idle
findings.relevance: License gate: Parcel can use it for research prototypes but not commercially; motivates authoring Go2-native clips.

findings.claim: WalkTheDog learns a shared, unsupervised phase manifold between a human and a dog with a vector-quantized periodic autoencoder in ~40 GPU-minutes and releases code, data and a pretrained human-dog model, enabling cross-morphology motion retrieval, transfer and stylization.
findings.source_title: WalkTheDog: Cross-Morphology Motion Alignment via Phase Manifolds (SIGGRAPH 2024)
findings.numbers: Dog 151k frames @60 fps (~42 min); Human-Locomotion 186k frames @60 (~51 min); MOCHA clown/ogre/princess 486-501k frames @120 fps (~68-70 min each); two-layer 1-D convs kernel 23; Adam 1e-4, batch 32, 1-s windows; 40 min on RTX 3090 (dog + human-loco), ~2 h 40 min all; code github.com/PeizhuoLi/walk-the-dog, data + pretrained via Google Drive
findings.relevance: A way to map human performances of an affect ('sad walk') onto a dog skeleton without paired data; kinematic only, needs a tracker.

findings.claim: Spot's Choreography API models expression as a beat-clocked timeline of 54 parameterized moves over 8 independent tracks plus uploadable .cha keyframe animations, requires a special-permissions license, and warns the robot will fall.
findings.source_title: Boston Dynamics Spot SDK - Choreography service
findings.numbers: slice = 1/4 beat; reliable range 250-450 slices/min; 8 tracks (legs, body, arm, gripper, status lights, AV lights, AV buzzer, annotations/music); 54 moves in 8 categories (body 7, step 8, dynamic 8, transition 9, kneel 4, arm 11, face lights 4, AV 3); .cha animations with body/leg/arm/gripper keyframes, time in seconds or frequency, bpm scaling, body_tracking_stiffness 1-11; UploadAnimatedMove RPC; 'The robot will fall down'; flat floor, no payload; special-permissions choreography license
findings.relevance: Mature industrial abstraction (independent tracks + tempo unit + keyframe animation format) worth copying into Parcel's expression layer; the Go2 has no equivalent API.

findings.claim: The Unitree Go2 SDK (BSD-3-Clause) exposes ~40 fixed high-level sport actions and only three continuous expressive channels (Euler body attitude, Move velocity, speed level); anything richer needs low-level joint control with a learned tracker.
findings.source_title: unitree_sdk2 SportClient header (Go2)
findings.numbers: Methods incl. Damp, BalanceStand, StandUp/Down, RecoveryStand, Euler(roll,pitch,yaw), Move(vx,vy,vyaw), Sit, RiseSit, SpeedLevel, Hello, Stretch, Heart, Pose, Scrape, FrontFlip, FrontJump, FrontPounce, Dance1, Dance2, LeftFlip, BackFlip, HandStand, FreeWalk/Bound/Jump/Avoid, ClassicWalk, WalkUpright, CrossStep, StaticWalk, TrotRun, EconomicGait, Content; Python SDK BSD-3 with low-level kp/kd/torque joint control
findings.relevance: Parcel's current five-command list is a subset of this; establishes the ceiling of the no-training path.

findings.claim: Isaac Lab ships Go2 velocity-tracking environments but AMP only for the humanoid and only via skrl; Unitree's own Apache-2.0 unitree_rl_lab adds Go2 training on Isaac Lab 2.3 with MuJoCo sim2sim, and BeyondMimic's MIT tracker (PPO + test-time guided diffusion) is the base Uni-Mo used for Go2.
findings.source_title: Isaac Lab - Available Environments (plus unitree_rl_lab and BeyondMimic repos)
findings.numbers: Isaac-Velocity-Flat/Rough-Unitree-Go2-v0 (rsl_rl, skrl PPO); Isaac-Humanoid-AMP-{Dance,Run,Walk} skrl only; unitree_rl_lab Apache-2.0, Go2/H1/G1-29, Isaac Lab 2.3.0 / Isaac Sim 5.1.0, MuJoCo sim2sim; whole_body_tracking MIT, Isaac Lab 2.1.0, LAFAN1, guidance for inpainting/joystick/obstacles; beyondAMP adds rsl_rl AMP wrapper + mjlab MuJoCo-Warp backend, 'AMP Dog Move' task
findings.relevance: Defines the buildable substrate for the Parcel tracker given the refuted in-repo Go2Env: Isaac Lab + MuJoCo sim2sim, or MuJoCo-native as Uni-Mo did.

design_implications: Adopt the two-layer stack every deployed system uses: a kinematic expression/animation layer that owns style (clips, tempo, Euler/velocity modifiers, layered loops + triggered clips as in Disney RSS 2024) and ONE reference-conditioned RL tracker that owns balance (ExBody2/QuadFM shape: proprio history + short future reference window, 50 Hz). Parcel's existing 50 Hz body-intent lane is the natural home for the tracker's reference stream; the deterministic safety layer stays below it.

The style signal should enter as a categorical/latent clip selector plus 2-3 continuous knobs, not as free-form joint commands: one-hot/latent skill conditioning is proven on Go2/A1 (CAMP ~7 GPU-h for 4 gaits; VIM 11 skills; Walk Like Dogs 18-D latent), and AMOR-style reward-weight or gait-parameter knobs give runtime-tunable intensity (calmer/more energetic) without retraining.

Build a Go2-native clip library (30-100 clips, 3-10 s, tagged category x affect x intensity) as the trainable vocabulary; sources ranked by license: hand-authored MuJoCo keyframes cleaned with IK+MJPC (Walk Like Dogs recipe; Spot .cha-style format), Apache-2.0 motion_imitation dog clips, CC BY-NC Zhang-2018 dog mocap (research only), and QuadFM/Quad-Imaginarium when released. Filter clips by sim trackability (ExBody2 tau threshold, Uni-Mo multi-gate) before they enter the vocabulary.

Expect sim success >=95% on curated clips (Uni-Mo 97.6%) and plan the hardware acceptance test now: N clips x 5 trials, success = complete without fall or intervention (Uni-Mo protocol, 96.7% real). Training budget for a first tracker is overnight on the RTX 5000 Ada (CAMP 7 h on 4060 Ti; AMP-hw 16 h on V100; QuadFM 2x3090 x 20k iterations), not the 22 GPU-days Disney spent per policy.

Add an AMP discriminator on a few seconds of dog motion as a naturalness prior (AMP-hw: 4.5 s, w_style 0.65) so authored clips read as dog-like and energy-efficient; this is orthogonal to style selection.

Hosted LLMs are offline authoring tools, not runtime motion generators: EMOTION needs ~27 s per gesture with GPT-4o; QuadFM's onboard generator runs at 2 Hz with ~500 ms end-to-end. Use the hosted text model to author/refine clips and rules (within the $100/mo budget); run only a small VQ-token head (MotionGlot recipe, GPT-2-small scale) or a lookup on the Orin.

Prioritize expressive behavior in conversational/social moments: ELEGNT shows the rating gain (56 vs 29) is concentrated in social tasks and absent for functional ones, so the reaction arbiter should bias toward expression when the voice module is active and toward plain function during navigation.

'Look back at the owner when lost' and 'chuckle when the joke lands' are selector-learning problems, not motion-generation problems: author the clips (Euler yaw/pitch toward owner bearing + step; rhythmic body bounce), expose world-state features (localization confidence, affect estimate, owner reaction), and learn the trigger/selection policy from owner reactions (EMOTION++ shows ~1.9 feedback rounds significantly improve gesture ratings). No fetched source learns this end-to-end.

Replace the refuted in-repo Go2Env with a substrate the literature actually uses: unitree_rl_lab (Apache-2.0, Isaac Lab 2.3 + MuJoCo sim2sim) or MuJoCo-native RL as Uni-Mo did (4,096 envs on one RTX 3090); Isaac Lab's built-in AMP is humanoid/skrl-only, so bring AMP via beyondAMP or a custom discriminator.

License gate: the Zhang-2018 dog mocap is CC BY-NC 4.0 and Spot choreography needs a special license; Parcel's shippable vocabulary must be authored or generated (QuadFM CC BY 4.0 planned, OmniMotionGPT MIT) rather than derived from the NC mocap.

trainable_options.name: Reference-conditioned universal Go2 tracker (QuadFM Gen2Control / ExBody2 / BeyondMimic pattern)
trainable_options.what_it_is: One PPO policy that tracks any clip from a library given proprioception history + a short future window of reference joints/root pose; the expression layer feeds it clips at 50 Hz.
trainable_options.inputs: Proprio history (joint pos/vel, IMU), future reference window (joint targets, root velocity/pose or keypoints), optional phase
trainable_options.outputs: 12 joint position targets for PD at 50 Hz (Go2)
trainable_options.train_recipe: PPO (asymmetric actor-critic or teacher-student DAgger) with DeepMimic-style tracking rewards + smoothness/energy terms + domain randomization; 4,096 envs in Isaac Lab or MuJoCo; QuadFM: 2xRTX 3090, 20k iterations; ExBody2: teacher privileged PPO then 10-frame-history student; filter untrackable clips by error threshold
trainable_options.size_params: MLP (512,256,128) class (Uni-Mo); ExBody2 unspecified but runs on Orin NX at 50 Hz with 18-30 ms latency
trainable_options.license: BeyondMimic whole_body_tracking code MIT (G1); QuadFM/ExBody2 code not released; unitree_rl_lab Apache-2.0
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: High: ExBody2 runs on Jetson Orin NX at 50 Hz; QuadFM runs generator (2 Hz) + tracker (50 Hz) on a Jetson Orin

trainable_options.name: One-hot / latent skill-conditioned AMP controller (CAMP on Go2, VIM on A1)
trainable_options.what_it_is: Single policy that switches among N skills from a categorical or latent skill vector, with a skill-conditioned discriminator giving a style reward; transitions learned, no per-clip policies.
trainable_options.inputs: Velocity command + one-hot skill (CAMP) or Gaussian skill latent from a reference encoder (VIM) + proprioception
trainable_options.outputs: 12 joint targets at 50 Hz (CAMP) / 25 Hz (VIM)
trainable_options.train_recipe: PPO + skill-conditioned adversarial reward; CAMP: 4096 envs Isaac Gym, ~7 h on RTX 4060 Ti, 4 synthetic ~4 s clips; VIM: 4096 envs, 2e9 samples, adversarial reward early then joint tracking, 11 clips (dog mocap + synthesized + traj-opt)
trainable_options.license: CAMP/VIM code not released; reference implementation AMP_for_hardware MIT (A1, Isaac Gym Preview 3); beyondAMP for Isaac Lab/mjlab
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: High: policies are small MLPs at 25-50 Hz; CAMP deployed on Go2 without retuning

trainable_options.name: Walk-Like-Dogs steerable latent synthesizer (vMF VAE + MoE) + tracker on Go2
trainable_options.what_it_is: Kinematic motion synthesizer over unlabeled dog data with an 18-D hyperspherical latent and 6-expert decoder; a small RL policy maps commands to latents; a separate tracking policy executes.
trainable_options.inputs: Forward/turn velocity commands (extendable to affect labels) -> unit latent; previous pose
trainable_options.outputs: Kinematic joint/root targets -> tracked at 50 Hz
trainable_options.train_recipe: Retarget dog mocap kino-dynamically (constrained IK with scale factors, MJPC iLQG 2 s horizon); train vMF VAE; PPO command->latent policy (4096 envs, batch 24,576, lr 5e-4); PPO tracker in Isaac Lab (Kp 30 / Kd 0.5)
trainable_options.license: No code release; dog data CC BY-NC 4.0
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: High: deployed on a real Go2 with joystick steering on grass

trainable_options.name: Text/affect -> motion-token head (MotionGlot / MotionGPT recipe)
trainable_options.what_it_is: Per-embodiment VQ-VAE motion tokenizer + small LM (GPT-2 small or T5) instruction-tuned on text<->motion pairs; outputs motion tokens decoded to reference trajectories for the tracker.
trainable_options.inputs: Text prompt (and Parcel affect/world-state tokens); optional current pose
trainable_options.outputs: Discrete motion tokens -> decoded joint/root trajectory (MotionGlot Spot: SE(2) velocities; would be 19-D Go2 state for Parcel)
trainable_options.train_recipe: Stage 1 VQ-VAE (codebook ~128x512 for robot), stage 2 LM fine-tune with instruction template on paired data (MotionGlot: ~48k augmented trajectories from 2.5 h teleop; QuadFM: MotionGPT3-style generator, 48 h on one MI308X)
trainable_options.size_params: GPT-2 small (MotionGlot); T5-770M (MotionGPT); QuadFM generator size undisclosed but runs at 2 Hz on Orin
trainable_options.license: MotionGPT MIT (human weights on Hugging Face); MotionGlot repo empty, data 'soon'; OmniMotionGPT MIT (animal, SMAL)
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Medium-high: QuadFM ran an equivalent generator at 2 Hz on Jetson Orin; GPT-2-small scale is trivial for AGX Orin 64 GB

trainable_options.name: Reward-weight-conditioned policy (AMOR) for continuous style intensity
trainable_options.what_it_is: Single tracking policy conditioned on a weight vector over multiple reward objectives (smoothness, root tracking, posture tracking...), letting operators or an affect model dial style trade-offs at runtime.
trainable_options.inputs: Reference motion + weight vector on a simplex (7 objectives in AMOR) + proprioception
trainable_options.outputs: Joint targets (torque-controlled biped in AMOR; PD targets for Go2)
trainable_options.train_recipe: Multi-objective PPO sampling weight vectors; Isaac Gym 8192 envs at 250 Hz; ~5 days on RTX 4090 for a 20-DoF biped (a 12-DoF Go2 with 3-4 objectives should be far cheaper)
trainable_options.license: No code release (Disney)
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: High once trained (single MLP); untested on quadrupeds

trainable_options.name: SayTap contact-pattern policy
trainable_options.what_it_is: PPO gait policy conditioned on a 4xT foot-contact template that an LLM writes from natural language; gives gait/tempo control only.
trainable_options.inputs: Contact-pattern window (Lw=5) + velocity command + proprioception (65-D)
trainable_options.outputs: 12 joint targets at 50 Hz
trainable_options.train_recipe: PPO in IsaacGym, random pattern generator over 5 gait types, 1000 iterations, ~15 min on one V100
trainable_options.license: No code found; paper CC BY 4.0
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: High (tiny MLP; A1 hardware transfer without fine-tuning)

trainable_options.name: Per-clip animal-imitation policies with real-world latent adaptation (motion_imitation)
trainable_options.what_it_is: Google's 2020 pipeline: retarget dog mocap by IK, train one PPO policy per clip in PyBullet, adapt on hardware via AWR over a latent from ~50 short trials; includes 4 retargeted dog clips and pretrained A1/Laikago policies.
trainable_options.inputs: Reference clip phase + proprioception
trainable_options.outputs: 12 joint targets
trainable_options.train_recipe: PPO ~200M samples per clip in PyBullet with 6-parameter DR; real-world AWR adaptation with ~50 trials of 5-10 s
trainable_options.license: Apache-2.0 (google-research/motion_imitation); underlying mocap CC BY-NC 4.0
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: High (small policies); per-clip, no conditioning

trainable_options.name: WalkTheDog VQ periodic autoencoder (human<->dog phase manifold)
trainable_options.what_it_is: Unsupervised shared phase manifold across morphologies used for motion matching, retrieval, transfer and stylization; a kinematic front-end for turning human performances or mocap into dog-skeleton motion.
trainable_options.inputs: 1-s motion windows from any character (human or dog)
trainable_options.outputs: Phase/amplitude codes enabling frequency-scaled motion matching across characters
trainable_options.train_recipe: Two-layer 1-D conv encoder/decoder (kernel 23), Adam 1e-4, batch 32; 40 min on RTX 3090 for dog + human-loco
trainable_options.license: Code on GitHub (license file present, type not shown); data + pretrained human-dog model via Google Drive; dog data CC BY-NC 4.0
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Offline/authoring tool; not a controller

trainable_options.name: Multi-Domain Motion Embedding (wavelet + VAE) retargeting-free mimicry
trainable_options.what_it_is: Policy conditioned on a dual embedding of raw actor motion (periodic wavelet + probabilistic VAE), enabling zero-shot real-time mimicry of unseen styles on a quadruped without retargeting.
trainable_options.inputs: Raw actor motion history (25 frames for quadruped) -> 32-D VAE latent + wavelet coefficients; proprioception
trainable_options.outputs: Joint targets at 50 Hz
trainable_options.train_recipe: PPO in Isaac Lab at 50 Hz; ~10 min dog mocap augmented to ~52 min (mirroring, height scaling); AMASS for humanoids
trainable_options.license: Paper CC BY 4.0; no repository URL in paper
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: High (50 Hz on ANYmal D and Fourier N1 hardware)

open_questions: Will QuadFM (CC BY 4.0 planned, Apache-2.0 repo currently empty) and Quad-Imaginarium (unreleased pending acceptance) actually ship, and in which skeleton/frame-rate convention (Uni-Mo paper says 50 Hz, README says 24 fps)?

Is CC BY-NC 4.0 dog mocap (Zhang et al. 2018, via AI4Animation) acceptable for Parcel's intended use? Every quadruped imitation paper fetched depends on it; a shippable vocabulary would need authored or CC BY data.

Universal tracker vs per-clip policies on the Go2: Uni-Mo used one PPO policy per motion (96.7% real success), QuadFM one tracker for all clips; no fetched source compares both on the same Go2 clip set or reports the universal tracker's real-robot success rate.

What is the actual latency and GPU share of a text/affect->motion head on the AGX Orin 64 GB next to Parcel's other local models? QuadFM reports 2 Hz generation and ~500 ms end-to-end with cloud ASR; nothing reports Orin utilization.

No fetched source learns WHEN to express (outcome-conditioned selection from owner reactions such as 'chuckle if the joke landed'); the closest evidence is EMOTION++'s human-feedback refinement (~1.9 rounds). Whether a contextual bandit over clips converges from sparse owner reactions is untested.

The Go2 has no neck: Disney's 4-DoF head and ELEGNT's gaze primitives carry much of the perceived attention/intention. Whether body Euler (roll/pitch/yaw) plus camera direction reads as 'looking back at the owner' needs a user test.

Two references could not be verified by fetch and were excluded: a canine-inspired emotion-recognition validation study (ResearchGate 397229202, 403) and a 'Roy et al. 2025' LLM gesture-generation paper for quadrupeds; venues for SayTap and MotionGlot could not be confirmed (OpenReview/IEEE pages did not load).

results.claim: Disney's bipedal robotic character separates an artist-driven animation engine (background loops + triggered clips + joystick procedural modification) from RL tracking policies that consume a small command vector (head/torso offsets, 2-D velocity + yaw rate, or phase), and ran ~10 h across three robots without a fall.
results.evidence_quote: "The animation engine procedurally generates the animation command, y_t, based on three layers: background animation, triggered animations, and animations derived from joystick inputs." ... standing command g = (Δh_head, Δθ_head, h_torso, θ_torso); walking command g = (Δh_head, Δθ_head, v^P, ω^P) plus phase signals for periodic/episodic motions ... "At the time of writing, we have conducted several public deployments of the robot with up to three robots simultaneously, resulting in the order of 10 h of robot runtime without a single fall."
results.correction: None needed. All secondary numbers also verified on the page: 5 DoF/leg + 4 DoF neck-head (14 DoF), 15.4 kg, 0.66 m; actuators "peak torque of 34 N m and maximum velocity of 20 rad/s"; "three fully connected layers of 512 hidden units and ELU activation"; "policy actions at a rate of 50 Hz, while our actuator communication operates at 600 Hz"; "Batch size (envs.×steps): 8192×24"; "Each policy is trained for 100,000 iterations ... around 22 days on a Nvidia RTX 4090"; MAE 0.035 rad standing / 0.123 rad walking / 0.027 rad happy dance / 0.043 rad jump; max 0.7 m/s fwd, 0.4 m/s lateral, 1.8 rad/s turn; clips happy dance, excited, jump, tantrum, yes/no, scanning; animations are "artist-designed" and "generated in Maya"; no code release. Minor wording: the paper says "up to three robots simultaneously" rather than a strict total of three.

results.claim: Apple's ELEGNT study shows expressive (vs purely functional) movement roughly doubles user ratings of a non-anthropomorphic robot, with the gain concentrated in social/conversational tasks; movements were hand-authored, not learned.
results.evidence_quote: "The robots with expression-driven movements are rated much higher (M=56.16,std=27.15) than robots incorporating only function-driven movements (M=28.77,std=27.15). Welch's t-test revealed a statistical significance in the difference, t=19.85,p<0.0001." ... "for function-oriented tasks (photograph light, project assistance, failure indication), the two robots show no significant differences in metrics such as Perceived intelligence, Willingness to interact, and Engagement." ... "a team of human-robot interaction researchers and animators iteratively designed and refined pre-recorded robot movement trajectories using the design primitatives"
results.correction: None needed. 56.16 vs 28.77 on a 0–100 scale ("participants rate their perception on a scale from 0 to 100") is a 1.95x ratio, so "roughly doubles" holds. Per-metric t-values (character 10.58, human-likeness 9.32, engagement 8.80, connection 8.50, willingness 7.37, intelligence 5.22), age effect p<0.001, and non-roboticist effect p=0.006 all verified. Minor notes for the numbers field: 30 were recruited and 21 were valid (N=21, ages 26–51); the body text calls the hardware "a re-purposed 6-DOF robotic arm" with WidowX 250S named via the bibliography/controller reference; the paper reports the same SD (27.15) for both conditions.

results.claim: ExBody2 runs a single whole-body tracking policy conditioned on reference keypoints/joints/root velocity on a Unitree G1 with a Jetson Orin NX at 50 Hz, trained on ~1.9k CMU clips filtered by tracking error, with ~0.1 rad real joint error.
results.evidence_quote: "Our real robot employs a Unitree G1 platform, with an onboard Jetson Orin NX acting as the primary computing and communication device." ... "The policy's inference frequency is set at 50 Hz. The commands are sent with a delay kept between 18 and 30 milliseconds. The low-level interface operates at a frequency of 500 Hz." ... "The complete CMU motion-capture repository of 1,919 sequences." ... Table III (real world, Unitree G1): Exbody2(Ours) E_mpjpe 0.1074 ... Abstract: "We observed significant improvement of tracking performance after fine-tuning on a small amount of data, at the expense of the others."
results.correction: Gist holds but two details need tightening. (1) The 1,919 CMU sequences are the pre-curation pool; training uses the subset retained at tracking-error threshold τ=0.15, and the paper does not state how many sequences survive, so "trained on ~1.9k clips" should read "trained on a tracking-error-filtered subset (τ=0.15, count unstated) of the 1,919-sequence CMU repository (plus ACCAD as OOD test)." (2) The 0.1074 rad real-world MPJPE in Table III is the generalist (single) policy, which supports the claim, but the paper's own contribution also includes fine-tuned specialist policies for specific motion groups that improve fidelity "at the expense of the others" — so "single policy" is the headline generalist, not the only policy the paper deploys. Other numbers verified: 36 keypoints, 23 DoF, teacher PPO -> student DAgger with history length 10, Adam lr 1e-4 batch 4096, sim MPKPE 0.1000 m / MPJPE 0.1079 rad / E_vel 0.2930 m/s, 43-s choreography. Project page https://exbody2.github.io exists; no explicit code-release statement.

results.claim: Four-and-a-half seconds of German Shepherd mocap used as an adversarial style reward produced natural, energy-efficient gaits with emergent pace->trot->canter transitions on a real Unitree A1, with cost of transport well below a hand-tuned complex reward.
results.evidence_quote: "The dataset consists of short clips of a German Shepherd pacing, trotting, cantering, and turning in place, with a total duration of 4.5 seconds." ... Table II (simulation): AMP 1.07±0.05 / 0.93±0.04 / 1.02±0.05 / 1.12±0.1 vs Complex Style Reward 1.54±0.17 / 1.37±0.12 / 1.40±0.10 / 1.41±0.09 vs No Style 14.03±0.99 / 8.00±0.44 / 6.05±0.28 / 5.18±0.20 at 0.4/0.8/1.2/1.6 m/s ... Fig. 3 caption: "An agent trained with Adversarial Motion Priors extracts the naturalistic locomotion strategies found in the dataset and can change its gait based on the desired velocity." (pace at 0.8 m/s, trot at 1.7 m/s) ... Sec. IV-C 'Qualitative Performance of Policies in Real': "When the velocity command increases from 1 m/s to 2 m/s, the policy dramatically alters its gait from a pace to a canter."
results.correction: The 4.5-s German Shepherd data, A1 platform, energy-efficient/natural gaits, and CoT advantage are all supported, but the claim conflates sim and real evidence. The real-robot section (IV-C, Fig. 2) documents a pace -> canter switch when the command goes from 1 to 2 m/s; the pace (0.8 m/s) -> trot (1.7 m/s) transition is Fig. 3, whose caption describes 'an agent' and is not explicitly attributed to hardware. So state: 'emergent velocity-dependent gait transitions (pace -> trot in Fig. 3; pace -> canter on the real A1 between 1 and 2 m/s).' The cost-of-transport table (0.93–1.12 for AMP vs 1.37–1.54 for the complex reward vs 5.18–14.03 with no style reward) is measured in simulation (5280 Isaac Gym envs), not on hardware. Training details verified: w_style 0.65, w_task 0.35, gradient penalty 10, 4B steps, 16 h on one V100. Code: github.com/escontra/AMP_for_hardware requires Isaac Gym Preview 3, but its LICENSE is BSD-3-Clause (ETH Zurich/NVIDIA legged_gym inheritance), not MIT.

results.claim: VIM learns one latent-skill-conditioned controller over 11 reference motions (dog mocap, synthesized, trajectory-optimized) on a Unitree A1 and executes trot, jumps and a backflip on hardware without fine-tuning, with a high-level policy choosing latents for tasks.
results.evidence_quote: "Our robot demonstrates diverse agile locomotion skills, including running, jumping, and back-flipping in real using a single motion prior and without fine-tuning." ... "reference motion encoder maps varying reference motions into a latent skill space" ... "high-level policy πhigh outputs high-level latent command for low-level policy" ... Table 5 lists 11 references: Walk, Trot, Jump while Running, Right Turn, Left Turn, Pace, Canter (mocap); Jump Forward Synthetic, Left Turn Synthetic; Backflip Optimization, Jump Forward Optimization ... Table 3 (real): Jump While Running height 0.50±0.003 m (ref 0.53±0.005); Jump Forward distance 0.76±0.05 m (ref 0.82±0.003); Trot 1.33±0.17 m/s (ref 1.16±0.12); Backflip height 0.62±0.01 m (ref 0.60±0.005)
results.correction: None needed for the claim. Numbers verified: A1 with 12 joints at 25 Hz, PD KP=40/KD=1.0; PPO with 4096 parallel envs, 2e9 samples for the low-level prior; sim root XY error 1.24±0.62 m. Clarification for the numbers field: the '0.50 m jump height (ref 0.53)' is specifically the jump-while-running skill; the jump-forward skill's height was 0.44 m (ref 0.59) and its distance 0.76 m (ref 0.82). No code repository is linked; project page is https://rchalyang.github.io/VIM/. arXiv v3 dated May 4, 2025.

results.claim: CAMP switches among four gaits on a real Unitree Go2 from a one-hot skill vector using a skill-conditioned adversarial motion prior trained on model-based synthetic clips in about 7 GPU-hours on a consumer card.
results.evidence_quote: "deployed the trained policy on a real Unitree Go2 robot" ... the skill vector is "designed as a one-hot vector to avoid introducing implicit ordinal biases" ... "four representative quadrupedal gait skills: bounding, pacing, pronking, and trotting" ... "generate quadrupedal locomotion sequences on flat terrain using a model-based control approach, without relying on real-world motion capture data" (each trajectory "approximately 4 seconds") ... "Training is conducted on an NVIDIA RTX 4060Ti GPU and takes approximately 7 hours." ... "In this experiment, the robot autonomously generates and switches among multiple gait skills in response to user commands based on the learned policy."
results.correction: Claim as written is accurate. One fix to the numbers field: the A1 was NOT tested — the paper only says the policy "can be directly deployed on other quadruped robots with similar specifications, such as the Unitree A1 robot" as a stated possibility; drop '(also A1)'. Other numbers verified: PPO, Isaac Gym, 4096 parallel agents, 50 Hz control, 8 domain-randomization categories (Table I), joint tracking accuracy "91.23% and 91.38%" (thigh and calf motors of the rear-left leg, Fig. 5), "when the number of skills exceeds two, the generated behaviors show signs of skill confusion or neutrality" without the skill discriminator, and deployment "does not require additional parameter tuning." No code URL is given.

sweeps.topic: Learning social/affective behaviour from the owner's reactions: reliable, low-cost reward signals for "was that joke funny" and "did the owner approve" (laughter detection, smile/engagement estimation, humor datasets and LLM-judge agreement, RL/preference learning on social robots, backchannel timing)

findings.claim: The canonical open laughter segmenter (ResNet-18-style on spectrograms, 1 s context, 43.1 fps) reaches F1 0.75 on clean Switchboard telephone speech but drops to F1 0.61 (precision 0.51) on in-the-wild AudioSet audio; MFCC-era detectors produced up to 10x more false positives than true laughs in some real recordings.
findings.source_title: Robust Laughter Detection in Noisy Environments (Gillick, Deng, Ryokai, Bamman; Interspeech 2021) + github.com/jrgillick/laughter-detection (MIT)
findings.numbers: Switchboard ~260 h / 543 speakers; AudioSet eval 1,000 manually segmented laughter clips + 1,000 negatives, 95.2% per-frame inter-annotator agreement; ResNet+Aug trained on Switchboard: SWB P .676 R .847 F1 .752; AudioSet P .508 R .759 F1 .608; trained on AudioSet weak labels: AS P .385 R .925 F1 .545; MFCC baseline F1 0.688 on SWB; 8 kHz audio; default threshold 0.5, min length 0.2 s; repo MIT, 291 stars
findings.relevance: Sets realistic expectations for an off-the-shelf laughter reward: ~0.6 F1 and ~0.5 precision in a home unless retrained; precision, not recall, is what a reward signal needs.

findings.claim: Synthesizing laughter into unlabeled base audio (no human annotation) and fine-tuning a wav2vec2-large-xlsr-53 frame classifier gives a segmenter that beats Gillick's model on every test set (detection F1 0.78-0.94 vs 0.58-0.90) and cuts laughter start-time error from 1.5-2.1 s to 0.3-1.1 s; the same synthetic data also improves Gillick's small architecture.
findings.source_title: Robust Laughter Segmentation with Automatic Diverse Data Synthesis (Omine, Akita, Tsuruno; Interspeech 2024)
findings.numbers: ~315 M params (wav2vec2-large-xlsr-53), 7 s input, class every ~0.02 s; trains in ~75 min, segments 1 h of audio in ~1 min on i9-9900K + RTX 2080 Ti; VocalSound 21,024 laughter clips; Spotify podcasts 1,456 episodes from 764 programs as base audio; Detection F1: AMI Gillick 0.583 / Ours 0.784; MAHNOB 0.618 / 0.890; Gillick's AudioSet set 0.844 / 0.865; own set 0.897 / 0.943; Segmentation F1 0.617→0.789, start MAE 1.500 s→0.314 s, end MAE 0.573 s
findings.relevance: The practical recipe to get an owner/room-specific laughter detector with zero labeling; onset accuracy (~0.3 s) is what allows crediting the laugh to the right joke or motion.

findings.claim: Supervised laughter detectors collapse across languages and domains (Gillick F1 as low as 0.13-0.29 on non-English stand-up), while a label-free BYOL-A + Isolation-Forest anomaly detector is more stable and, combined with the Omine model, reaches F1 up to 0.85.
findings.source_title: MultiLinguahah: A New Unsupervised Multilingual Acoustic Laughter Segmentation Method
findings.numbers: Standup4AI 3,617 videos, 7 languages; test 100 videos, 8.53 h, 3,453 laughter events; Kuznetsova RU/EN 10 test videos, 617 laughs; FSD50K 40,966 clips / 80 h; Gillick F1 across conditions 0.130-0.646; MultiLinguahah 0.506 / 0.585 where Gillick 0.456 / 0.439; Omine+MultiLinguahah 0.848 vs Gillick 0.646; RTX 2080
findings.relevance: Confirms domain shift is the main failure mode; a cheap unsupervised detector over a frozen audio embedding is a viable fallback and per-owner calibration is essential.

findings.claim: Laughter type matters: an LLM-based system distinguishes mirthful vs polite vs satirical laughter with F1 0.81 (detection F1 0.97), so a reward that treats every laugh as 'funny' will be fooled by polite laughter.
findings.source_title: SMILE-Next: Teaching Large Language Models to Detect, Classify, and Reason about Laughter
findings.numbers: 3,590 clips, 6,386 QA pairs; detection 2,384 samples (1,565/460/359) F1 0.9674 acc 0.9696; type classification 1,957 samples F1 0.8067 acc 0.8425; reasoning BLEU-4 0.2427 / METEOR 0.2328 / ROUGE-L 0.4168 / SentBERT 0.7828; backbones Vicuna-7B, LLaMA3, Qwen2.5
findings.relevance: Motivates discounting short/polite laughs (duration + smile co-occurrence proxy) in the funniness reward.

findings.claim: Tiny AudioSet taggers expose a per-second 'Laughter' class at negligible cost: YAMNet is 3.7 M params / 69.2 M multiplies per 960 ms frame (balanced mAP 0.306); PANNs MobileNetV1 is 4.8 M params at 0.389 mAP and CNN14 80.8 M at 0.431; AST 86.6 M at 0.459 single-model; BEATs 90 M at 0.506; Whisper-AT adds 527-class tagging to a Whisper ASR encoder for <1% extra compute (mAP 36.5 tiny to 41.7 large-v2).
findings.source_title: YAMNet README (tensorflow/models, Apache 2.0); PANNs arXiv 1912.10211; AST github.com/YuanGongND/ast (BSD-3) + HF card; BEATs arXiv 2212.09058 (size via OpenBEATs arXiv 2507.14129); Whisper-AT github.com/YuanGongND/whisper-at (BSD-2)
findings.numbers: YAMNet 521 classes, 25 ms window/10 ms hop, 0.96 s patches, first output after 975 ms, balanced mAP 0.306, d-prime 2.318; PANNs (AudioSet 1.9 M clips, 527 classes): CNN6 4.84 M/0.343, CNN10 5.22 M/0.380, CNN14 80.75 M/0.431, MobileNetV1 4.80 M/0.389 (3.61 GFLOPs), MobileNetV2 4.08 M/0.383, LeeNet11 0.75 M/0.266, Wavegram-Logmel 81.07 M/0.439; AST 0.459 single, 0.485 6-ensemble, 86.6 M params; BEATs AS-2M mAP 50.6%, ESC-50 98.1%, 90 M params; Whisper-AT mAP tiny 36.5 / base 37.6 / small 39.8 / medium 40.8 / large-v2 41.7
findings.relevance: These give a laughter probability stream that fits on Orin next to the 50 Hz lane; Whisper-AT lets the duplex voice stack's ASR encoder emit the laughter tag for free.

findings.claim: MediaPipe's blendshape model outputs 52 coefficients in [0,1] including mouthSmileLeft (index 44) and mouthSmileRight (45) from 146 face landmarks, under Apache 2.0, giving a continuous on-device smile signal; lightweight FER models top out around 65-66% on 7-class AffectNet (MobileNet 14 MB, 16 ms on a phone).
findings.source_title: MediaPipe Blendshape V2 model card + Face Landmarker task page; HSEmotion (github.com/av-savchenko/face-emotion-recognition, Apache-2.0)
findings.numbers: 52 blendshapes in [0,1]; input 146 of 478 landmarks; bundle: BlazeFace 192x192, FaceMesh-V2 256x256, blendshape 1x146x2, float16; failure above 80 deg rotation or <50% visible; HSEmotion MobileNet 64.71% (7 cls) 14 MB 16±5 ms; EfficientNet-B0 64.63%/60.95% 16 MB 59 ms; EfficientNet-B2 66.34%/63.03% 30 MB 191 ms; Jetson TX2 smile pipeline (arXiv 1807.10570) 20-25 fps, MobileNet a=0.25 0.21 M params 27.3 FPS
findings.relevance: Smile intensity delta (not categorical emotion) is the cheap visual co-signal for both funniness and approval.

findings.claim: A robot-POV engagement regressor (ResNeXt-50 + LSTM) trained on a museum tour-guide robot reaches Spearman 0.63 (0.76 single-party) against 3 coders and transfers zero-shot to a different robot/dataset (UE-HRI) with AUC 0.89, at 5 Hz on a GTX 1060.
findings.source_title: Are You Still With Me? Continuous Engagement Assessment From a Robot's Point of View (Del Duchetto, Baxter, Hanheide; Frontiers Rob. AI 2020)
findings.numbers: 278 days deployed, 556 km, 2,691 tours; ~10 d 16 h video, 5 h 50 min annotated, 94 videos, 227 people; 3 coders, inter-rater rho 0.56-0.72; engagement in [0,1]; test MSE 0.126, rho 0.634; single-party MSE 0.087 rho 0.758; multi-party 0.136 / 0.622; UE-HRI transfer AUC-ROC 0.89; <=200 ms per 10-frame sample, 5 Hz, GTX 1060, 5.4 GB; model+code released
findings.relevance: The state feature for 'the owner is no longer with me' that triggers look-back, and its recovery is the natural reward for the look-back behaviour.

findings.claim: Engagement estimators overfit their recording setup: in MultiMediate'24 OpenFace features fell from 0.81 CCC (val) to 0.28 (NOXI test) and 0.00 on a group dataset, audio (w2v-BERT 2.0) transferred best (0.64 NOXI, 0.41 average), and the challenge winner reached 0.68 average CCC.
findings.source_title: MultiMediate'24: Multi-Domain Engagement Estimation (Muller et al., ACM MM 2024)
findings.numbers: NOXI >25 h (x2), 48 train / 16 test sessions, 2-7 raters (avg 3.6), continuous 0-1; MPIIGroupInteraction 3-4 people, 20 min; baseline MLP 3x136; OpenFace 0.81 val / 0.28 test / 0.00 MPIIGI; w2vbert2 0.77 / 0.64 / 0.09, avg 0.41; eGeMAPS avg 0.39; OpenPose 0.32; XLM-R text 0.23; best MPIIGI baseline 0.15; winner USTC-IAT-United 0.68 avg (+0.27); Li et al. 0.64 avg, NOXI SOTA 0.76
findings.relevance: Any pretrained engagement/affect model must be recalibrated in the owner's home; paralinguistic audio features are the more transferable modality.

findings.claim: Reading face + voice over a whole interaction with multi-instance learning predicts the user's own UX rating better than third-party human observers (70.0% vs 64.0% on 3 classes; 35.1% vs 23.0% on 7), supporting episode-level rather than frame-level approval signals.
findings.source_title: User Experience Estimation in Human-Robot Interaction Via Multi-Instance Learning of Multimodal Social Signals
findings.numbers: 22 participants (21 M/1 F, mean age 21.1), 10 scenarios each, 220 interactions of 30-120 s (~5 turns); Sota robot; 15-item 7-point questionnaire; OpenFace 2.0 (112x112) + mel-spectrogram; Acc.7 35.1% vs 23.0%; Acc.3 70.0% vs 64.0%; attention peaks on mouth elevation/surprise and tonal variation
findings.relevance: Owner approval should be scored per behaviour episode by aggregating face+voice over several seconds, not by a single frame.

findings.claim: In real-world short HRI (54 s average), a zero-shot text LLM over the transcript predicts rapport at CCC 0.58, beating supervised audio (0.46) and video (0.31) embeddings; fusing all three reaches CCC 0.656 / Pearson 0.717, and video collapses with three people present (CCC 0.50 to 0.04).
findings.source_title: Multimodal Rapport Estimation in Real-World HRI
findings.numbers: Japanese drugstore, teleoperated Sota; 131 sessions -> 62 analysed; 97 participants; mean 54.23 s (SD 42.42), 7.06 utterances; CCR-8 rapport 1-5, 3 raters, ICC(2,3)=.85, mean 3.72; Gemini 2.5 Flash text CCC 0.580 PCC 0.665; HuBERT-large 0.460; V-JEPA 2.1 0.310; ST5 0.281; fusion CCC 0.656 PCC 0.717 MAE 0.471; V-JEPA 0.503 (1 person) -> 0.043 (3 people); Gemini 3-person CCC 0.721
findings.relevance: A once-per-session hosted-LLM rapport score is a cheap slow-loop approval term; multi-person scenes need identity gating.

findings.claim: Facial reactions of untrained observers carry enough information to rank an agent's outcomes above chance, but weakly per person: a learned OpenFace-AU mapping beats random ranking (p=0.0024), improves an online policy for 9/10 new users, and ranks 8 robot trajectories with Kendall tau 0.70 only after aggregating across 14 people.
findings.source_title: The EMPATHIC Framework for Task Learning from Implicit Human Feedback (Cui, Zhang, Allievi, Stone, Niekum, Knox; CoRL 2020)
findings.numbers: 17 participants x 3 Robotaxi episodes; 14 participants x 7 robot-sorting trajectories; OpenFace 2.0 head pose + AUs at 30 fps; 7 gestures (smile, pout, brow raise/frown, nod, shake, eye-roll); human-proxy avg tau 0.209 (p=.078), best 0.569 (p=.004); learned mapping vs random p=0.0024 (aux loss) / 0.0207; online 9/10 beat random, 7/10 converged to optimal; sorting tau=0.70 p=0.034; code github.com/Pearl-UTexas/EMPATHIC
findings.relevance: Primary evidence that 'owner approval from the face' works only as an aggregated, per-owner-calibrated ranking signal, not a dense reward.

findings.claim: At scale (561 participants) facial expressions used as TAMER-style evaluative feedback only help an agent when the facial predictor is strong and when trainers are prompted to express and made competitive; unprompted faces are a weak reward.
findings.source_title: Facial Feedback for Reinforcement Learning: A Case Study and Offline Analysis Using the TAMER Framework
findings.numbers: 561 participants; Infinite Mario; CNN-RNN facial model; improvement in positive/negative feedback estimation accuracy when instructed + competitive; simulated agents improve 'significantly' only with strong predictors
findings.relevance: A dog that visibly solicits a reaction (looks back, holds a pose) will get cleaner facial feedback than passive observation.

findings.claim: On physical social robots the working pattern for learning humour/affect from social signals is tabular or linear-FA Q-learning over a tiny action set with reward = mean laugh/smile (or valence/engagement) probability in a fixed post-action window: Weber et al. (Reeti) used laugh+smile probabilities from the SSI framework averaged from punchline to end; Gordon et al. (Tega) used SARSA with Affectiva valence+engagement; Park et al. personalised tabular Q-learning over 6-8 sessions.
findings.source_title: Reinforcement Learning Approaches in Social Robotics (Akalin & Loutfi, survey; cites Weber et al. ICMI 2018, Gordon et al., Park et al., Ritschel et al., Addo & Ahamed) - Weber 2018 primary on ACM DL was not fetchable (403)
findings.numbers: Weber: state = 2-D (P(laugh), P(smile)), actions = sounds, grimaces, 3 joke types + combos, Q-learning with linear function approximation, reward averaged from punchline to end; Gordon: SARSA, reward = weighted valence + engagement (Affectiva); Park: tabular Q-learning, 6-8 sessions, learning-gain reward levels [-100, 0, +50, +100]; Ritschel: reward = change in engagement (Kinect 2 + DBN); Addo & Ahamed: verbal ratings 'very funny'...'not funny' as reward; Zarinbal: r in {-1,0,1} from like/neutral/dislike face
findings.relevance: This is the exact 'learn to chuckle if funny' loop already demonstrated on a robot in 2018; small action set + windowed averaging is what makes it work. Load-bearing but rests on a survey citation of Weber 2018.

findings.claim: Preference-based methods for HRI personalisation work by keeping a pre-trained policy and adapting a latent (PbARL, N=8 user study), by mining users' natural exploratory actions as implicit preferences (CLEA, Kuri robot, N=25/42), and by pairwise human comparisons feeding a Siamese RankNet to learn expressive robot faces (HAPI, 35-DOF android, IROS 2025).
findings.source_title: Personalization in HRI through Preference-based Action Representation Learning (PbARL); CLEA arXiv 2501.01367; HAPI arXiv 2503.17046
findings.numbers: PbARL: conditional-VAE latent action space, MI + preference + KL + dynamics losses, benchmark + real-world N=8; CLEA: N=25 exploratory phase, N=42 evaluation, four metrics (completeness, simplicity, minimality, explainability); HAPI: 35-DOF android, Anger/Happiness/Surprise, 'significantly more realistic and socially resonant' than baseline and expert designs
findings.relevance: Shape of the learner for Parcel's body-intent lane: pre-trained motion stays, preferences steer a latent over a small set of expression variants; safety layer keeps authority.

findings.claim: Commercial companions do not disclose any learned reward: Sony aibo reacts to smiles, petting on head/back/chin and kind vs unkind words and 'may grow clingy or wild' with no algorithm stated; Vector 2.0 lists smile recognition as a planned camera improvement and runs features through a cloud service with no on-device learning described.
findings.source_title: Sony aibo ERS-1000 Help Guide: Getting to know aibo; Vector 2.0 product page (anki.bot)
findings.numbers: aibo: face memorisation without owner intervention; praise/pet channels head, back, under chin; personality 'clingy or wild'; Vector: 2 MP camera, smile detection 'planned software development', subscription cloud
findings.relevance: The commercial baseline is hand-authored reactions to praise/pet/smile detectors; a learned owner-specific reward would be a real differentiator.

findings.claim: Text-only funniness prediction has a low ceiling: with five crowd judges per item, the SemEval-2020 Task 7 winner (RMSE 0.497) beat the predict-the-mean baseline (0.575) by only 13.5%, and on 432k Reddit jokes the best transformer reaches only Pearson 0.47 against log-upvotes.
findings.source_title: SemEval-2020 Task 7: Assessing Humor in Edited News Headlines (Hossain, Krumm, Gamon, Kautz) + The rJokes Dataset (Weller & Seppi, LREC 2020)
findings.numbers: Humicroedit 15,095 edited headlines, 5 judges each, 0-3 scale, 64/16/20 split (9,653/2,420/3,025), FunLines +8,248; 48 teams; baseline RMSE 0.575, Hitachi 0.49725 (13.5% better), BERT+FunLines 0.522; subtask 2 accuracy baseline 49.5% -> 67.43%; judge sigma up to 0.9; rJokes 573,335 jokes, 432,457 for regression, label log-upvotes 0-10, BERT-large RMSE 1.619 / Pearson 0.471 / Spearman 0.430, RoBERTa 1.614 / 0.474 / 0.435, XLNet 1.739 / 0.457 / 0.411; Reddit ToS licence
findings.relevance: Text funniness models are at best a weak prior for joke selection, never the reward.

findings.claim: UR-FUNNY labels humour directly from audience laughter markers in 1,866 TED talks (8,257 pos / 8,257 neg, 90 h) and multimodal fusion adds under 1 point over text (T 64.44% vs T+A+V 65.23%); MUStARD shows sarcasm needs prosody (speaker-independent audio 62.7 F vs text 59.8) and drops to ~60% for new speakers.
findings.source_title: UR-FUNNY: A Multimodal Language Dataset for Understanding Humor (Hasan et al., EMNLP 2019; CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) + MUStARD (Castro et al., ACL 2019; arXiv 1906.01815, MIT)
findings.numbers: UR-FUNNY: 1,866 videos, 1,741 speakers, 417 topics, 90.23 h, punchline avg 16.14 words / 4.97 s; C-MFN accuracy T 64.44, A+V 57.99, T+A 64.47, T+V 64.22, T+A+V 65.23, punchline-only 64.47, context-only 58.45; MUStARD: 690 utterances balanced, 5-fold; speaker-dependent T+A+V 71.5 F (12.9% relative error reduction), speaker-independent T 59.8, A 62.7, T+A 63.1, T+A+V 62.8
findings.relevance: Precedent for using laughter-after-punchline as the ground-truth label; prosody is needed to read sarcastic 'approval'.

findings.claim: Even with 284 million crowd ratings on 2.2 million New Yorker captions, GPT-4-Turbo ranks funniness at 67% vs a former editor at 94%, crowd workers at 62%; RLHF/DPO on Mistral-7B yields only ~9% win rate vs top-10 human captions; and a few thousand expert pairwise labels (5,580) lift GPT-4o from 67.3% to 82.4% (experts avg 78%).
findings.source_title: Humor in AI: Massive Scale Crowd-Sourced Preferences and Benchmarks for Cartoon Captioning (Zhang et al., NeurIPS 2024) + Bridging the Creativity Understanding Gap (arXiv 2502.20356)
findings.numbers: 284,183,913 ratings, 2.2 M+ captions, 365 contests, 6,044 captions/contest, 1-3 scale; GPT-4-Turbo 67%, crowd 61.67±3.45, editor 94.28±2.79; Mistral-7B DPO 9.34% / RLHF 8.79% win rate; Claude-3-Opus 54.40%, GPT-4o 44.51%; crowd prefers Claude 35.4% vs expert 1.6%; Bridging: zero-shot GPT-4o 67.3%, fine-tuned on 5,580 pairs 82.4% easy / 63.2% hard; experts 78% / 61.6%, Mankoff 85.33% / 68%, majority 84% / 66%
findings.relevance: Funniness is not a stable scalar to regress; but small-scale per-domain preference alignment does work, which is the per-owner setting.

findings.claim: Zero-shot LLM funniness judgments barely correlate with humans: Spearman 0.17-0.27 on Oogiri responses (LLMs rate irrelevant answers 2.4-3.3/4 vs humans 0.68), and 13-18% accuracy at predicting the human pick in Cards Against Humanity rounds, below a 19% popularity baseline.
findings.source_title: Cards Against LLMs: Benchmarking Humor Alignment in LLMs (2026) + Assessing the Capabilities of LLMs in Humor: Oogiri (arXiv 2511.09133)
findings.numbers: CAH: 148,497 games, 4,947 rounds, 10 candidates; Claude ~18%, Grok ~17%, Gemini ~16%, DeepSeek ~14%, GPT ~13%; random 10%, popularity 19.11%; inter-model agreement 21.4-44.9%; Oogiri: 200 topics x 8 responses, 4 raters; Overall Funniness rho Claude Sonnet 4 0.266, GPT-4.1 0.224, Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.169; GPT-4.1 Relevance 0.441, Clarity 0.379, Novelty 0.361, Intelligence 0.352, Empathy 0.303
findings.relevance: Rules out the hosted text model as the 'was it funny' reward; keeps it only for joke generation and slow rapport scoring.

findings.claim: Voice Activity Projection (self-supervised, no labels) predicts upcoming backchannels from raw audio with weighted F1 0.723 (vs 0.685 independent, 0.333 majority) using a frozen CPC encoder plus a 4-layer, 256-hidden causal transformer trained on 2,438 Switchboard dialogs.
findings.source_title: Voice Activity Projection: Self-supervised Learning of Turn-taking Events (Ekstedt & Skantze, Interspeech 2022)
findings.numbers: Switchboard 2,438 dialogs (98 excluded, 135 test, 11 folds 2000/205); CPC 100 Hz 256-d; transformer 256 hidden, 4 layers, 4 heads; 256-way 2 s projection; weighted F1: S/H .899 (SHIFT .510), S/L .786, S-pred .733*, BC-pred .723* (p<0.025); code github.com/ErikEkstedt/conv_ssl
findings.relevance: The timing primitive for when a nod/chuckle/backchannel is appropriate; tiny enough for one CPU core on Orin.

findings.claim: Fine-tuning VAP for continuous backchannel timing+type runs in real time on a CPU (RTF<1, 10 Hz, ~5 s context) after pre-training on ~35 h and fine-tuning on 109 sessions with 13,601 backchannels, but timing+type F1 is still only 38% (vs 34% baseline).
findings.source_title: Yeah, Un, Oh: Continuous and Real-time Backchannel Prediction with Fine-tuning of Voice Activity Projection (Inoue et al.)
findings.numbers: Japanese; pre-train ~35 h; fine-tune 109 sessions (87/11/11), 13,601 backchannels (11,371/1,139/1,091); continuers vs assessments; frozen CPC, 1 channel-wise + 3 cross-attention layers, 4 heads, 512-d fused, 256-d state; continuer timing+type F1 38.11% (P 29.89 / R 52.58) vs 34.13% baseline / 36.10% single-task; 10 Hz; RTF<1.0 on Intel i7-11700; Morency et al. 2010 (HMM/CRF on prosody, words, gaze) is the canonical precursor
findings.relevance: For a dog the 'type' is a body cue with a wide tolerance window, so this level is sufficient; trainable on ~1 day of dialogue.

findings.claim: Stand-up comedy data shows performers go still before the punchline: kinetic energy negatively predicts audience laughter rate (r = -0.75), and Whisper-AT gives 0.8 s laughter detection over 90 specials / 5,400+ segments.
findings.source_title: TIC-TALK: Pipeline and Database for the Multimodal Study of Comedic Timing
findings.numbers: 90 specials (2015-2024), 5,400+ aligned topic segments; BERTopic, Whisper-AT (0.8 s), YOLOv8-cls, YOLOv8s-pose; r = -0.75, N = 24
findings.relevance: Ready corpus of (speech, gesture, laughter-onset) triples for pre-training a 'when will they laugh' predictor; motion should hold still through the punchline and react after.

findings.claim: Owner vocal valence/arousal can be read with very small models: Wav2Small has 72K parameters (120 KB ONNX) distilled from a teacher at valence CCC 0.676 on MSP-Podcast; emotion2vec (93.8 M) reaches IEMOCAP WA 71.79% vs WavLM-base 65.94% after 262 h of self-supervised emotion pre-training.
findings.source_title: Wav2Small: Distilling Wav2Vec2 to 72K parameters for Low-Resource Speech Emotion Recognition + emotion2vec (arXiv 2312.15185, ACL 2024 Findings)
findings.numbers: Wav2Small 72K params vs MobileNet-V4-Small 3.12 M; ONNX 120 KB; teacher valence CCC 0.676; emotion2vec 93.79 M + 0.20 M head, 262 h pre-training, IEMOCAP WA 71.79 / UA 72.69 / WF1 71.80, WavLM-base 65.94, HuBERT-base 64.92, 10 languages / 13 datasets
findings.relevance: Cheap second approval channel (sign of vocal valence on 'good boy' vs 'stop'); use as coarse sign only since valence CCC is ~0.68 at SOTA.

design_implications: Do not use an LLM (hosted or local) as the 'was that funny' reward: zero-shot LLM-human agreement is rho 0.17-0.27 and 13-18% vs a 19% popularity baseline; text-only funniness models cap at ~13.5% over predicting the mean. Keep the text model for joke generation and a once-per-session rapport score (CCC ~0.58).

The funniness reward is the owner's vocal laughter credited to a specific event: r_funny = mean over [t_punch, t_punch+3 s] of P(laugh_owner) weighted by smile delta, gated by mic-array DoA + speaker ID = owner, baseline-subtracted per owner, zeroed if laugh onset precedes the punchline. This is the Weber 2018 Reeti design (laugh+smile probability averaged from punchline to end) that already worked on a robot.
