Retrain the laughter detector in-domain with the Omine synthetic recipe (inject open laughter clips into recordings of the owner's room; no labels): expect detection F1 0.78-0.94 and ~0.3 s onset error versus F1 ~0.6 / precision ~0.5 for off-the-shelf Gillick or AudioSet taggers in the wild. Operate at high threshold (precision >= 0.8); a false 'laugh' reinforces the wrong action.

Discount polite laughter: short laughs without a co-occurring smile (MediaPipe mouthSmileL/R, cheekSquint in [0,1]) should get low weight; laughter type is learnable (F1 0.81) but a duration x smile proxy is the cheap first version.

Owner approval must be an episode-level, aggregated score, not a frame-level reward: faces rank outcomes only weakly per event (EMPATHIC tau ~0.2 per subject, 0.70 after aggregation), whole-interaction face+voice models beat human observers (70% vs 64%), and explicit verbal praise / petting (aibo's channels) should be logged as separate high-weight events.

Use a robot-POV engagement scalar (Del Duchetto model: rho 0.63, cross-robot AUC 0.89, 5 Hz) as the state feature for 'owner is no longer with me'; its drop triggers look-back and its recovery after look-back is the reward. Recalibrate at home (MultiMediate shows face-feature CCC collapsing 0.81 -> 0.28 across setups; audio features transfer better).

Learn preferences over a small action set, not a dense policy: pairwise/bandit preference over expression variants (which chuckle, when, whether to look back) with the pre-trained motion kept fixed and only a latent steered (PbARL/HAPI pattern); the deterministic safety layer keeps final authority.

Timing comes from VAP-style voice-activity projection (CPC + 4-layer 256-hidden transformer, BC-pred F1 0.72, RTF<1 on one CPU core): chuckle/nod inside the backchannel-appropriate window and hold the body still through the punchline (kinetic energy r = -0.75 with laughter rate).

Compute fits Orin beside the 50 Hz lane: YAMNet/PANNs-MobileNetV1 (~4-5 M params) or Whisper-AT (<1% over the Whisper ASR encoder) for laughter tags, a Gillick-size ResNet or wav2vec2-base frame model for onsets, MediaPipe blendshapes on CPU, engagement at 5 Hz on GTX-1060-class budget, Wav2Small (72K params) for vocal valence.

Gate every social signal on identity in multi-person scenes: video rapport CCC fell 0.50 -> 0.04 with three people and engagement rho lost 0.14 in multi-party; use XVF3800 DoA + face ID before any reward is credited.

Simulation plan: a scripted owner whose laugh/smile probability depends on joke type x expression variant with habituation and noise (use Gillick/Omine precision-recall figures to add realistic detector noise); train the bandit/Q-table for 'chuckle if funny' and the engagement-recovery look-back policy there, then transfer the reward-window logging format unchanged to hardware.

trainable_options.name: Omine-style synthetic-data laughter segmenter (wav2vec2 frame classifier, or Gillick ResNet trained on the same synthetic data)
trainable_options.what_it_is: Frame-level laughter detector/segmenter trained on unlabeled base audio with synthetically injected, augmented laughter; predicts laughter/no-laughter every ~20 ms with ~0.3 s onset error
trainable_options.size_params: ~315 M (wav2vec2-large-xlsr-53); wav2vec2-base variant ~95 M; Gillick ResNet-18-style variant small (unstated, MIT repo)
trainable_options.inputs: raw 16 kHz audio, 7 s windows (overlap 2 s)
trainable_options.outputs: per-20 ms laughter probability; onset/offset segments
trainable_options.train_recipe: Inject 0-4 laughter episodes (VocalSound etc.) into laughter-free base audio (own room recordings; filter with YAMNet laughter prob < 0.05), pitch/speed/reverb/compressor/bit-depth augment, BCE + dice loss, AdamW lr 5e-6, 2,500 steps; ~75 min on one RTX 2080 Ti; evaluate P/R/F1 + onset MAE on Gillick's 1,000+1,000 AudioSet clips and own held-out room recordings
trainable_options.license: Pre-trained checkpoint jonatasgrosman/wav2vec2-large-xlsr-53-english (HF); Gillick repo MIT; paper code per repo
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Large model segments 1 h audio/min on RTX 2080 Ti (offline); for streaming on Orin use wav2vec2-base or the ResNet variant with 1 s windows at ~10-40 Hz; feasible alongside 50 Hz lane

trainable_options.name: AudioSet tagger laughter head (YAMNet / PANNs MobileNetV1 / Whisper-AT)
trainable_options.what_it_is: Pretrained 521/527-class audio event tagger giving a per-~1 s 'Laughter' probability; Whisper-AT rides on the duplex stack's Whisper encoder
trainable_options.size_params: YAMNet 3.7 M; PANNs MobileNetV1 4.8 M / MobileNetV2 4.1 M / CNN14 80.8 M; Whisper-AT tiny/base heads on top of Whisper (<1% extra compute)
trainable_options.inputs: 16 kHz mono audio (YAMNet 0.96 s patches; PANNs 10 s / 32 kHz; Whisper-AT 30 s Whisper frames)
trainable_options.outputs: class probabilities incl. Laughter (AudioSet mAP: YAMNet 0.306 balanced, MobileNetV1 0.389, CNN14 0.431, Whisper-AT 36.5-41.7)
trainable_options.train_recipe: Use frozen; optionally fine-tune the final layer on own laughter clips; calibrate threshold per owner
trainable_options.license: YAMNet Apache 2.0 (tensorflow/models); AST BSD-3; Whisper-AT BSD-2; PANNs repo licence not verified in this pass
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Trivial (YAMNet 69.2 M multiplies per frame; MobileNetV1 3.6 GFLOPs); Whisper-AT adds <1% to ASR

trainable_options.name: MediaPipe Face Landmarker blendshapes + HSEmotion FER (feature extractors, not retrained)
trainable_options.what_it_is: On-device smile/AU-like coefficients (52 blendshapes in [0,1], mouthSmileLeft=44, mouthSmileRight=45) and a lightweight 7-class FER model; provide the visual co-signal for laugh weighting and approval
trainable_options.size_params: BlazeFace + FaceMesh-V2 + blendshape head (float16, sizes small, exact MB not stated); HSEmotion MobileNet 14 MB / EfficientNet-B2 30 MB
trainable_options.inputs: RGB frames (192x192 detector, 256x256 mesh; blendshape input 146 landmarks)
trainable_options.outputs: 478 3-D landmarks; 52 blendshape scores in [0,1]; FER 7/8-class probabilities (AffectNet 64.7-66.3%)
trainable_options.train_recipe: No retraining; learn per-owner baseline and thresholds; feed smile delta into reward and into the episode-level approval model
trainable_options.license: MediaPipe Apache 2.0; HSEmotion Apache-2.0
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Runs on phone CPUs (HSEmotion MobileNet 16 ms on a Samsung Fold 3); Jetson TX2 ran a full smile pipeline at 20-25 fps

trainable_options.name: Robot-POV engagement regressor (Del Duchetto et al.)
trainable_options.what_it_is: ResNeXt-50 + LSTM regressor mapping the robot's own camera stream to a continuous engagement scalar in [0,1]; released model and code
trainable_options.inputs: 10-frame video samples from the robot's camera
trainable_options.outputs: engagement in [0,1] at 5 Hz
trainable_options.train_recipe: Trained on 5 h 50 min of continuously annotated museum-robot video (3 coders); transfers zero-shot to UE-HRI (AUC 0.89); fine-tune on a few hours of Parcel POV footage with owner self-report or coder labels
trainable_options.license: Model/code released to the HRI community (licence not stated on the fetched page)
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: <=200 ms per 10-frame sample on a GTX 1060 (5.4 GB); Orin 64 GB can run it at 5 Hz

trainable_options.name: Voice Activity Projection backchannel/timing model (Ekstedt & Skantze; Inoue et al. fine-tune)
trainable_options.what_it_is: Self-supervised model predicting the next 2 s of both speakers' voice activity from raw audio; zero-shot backchannel-appropriate and turn-shift signals; can be fine-tuned for backchannel timing+type
trainable_options.size_params: Frozen CPC encoder + causal transformer (256 hidden, 4 layers, 4 heads); Inoue variant 1 channel-wise + 3 cross-attention layers
trainable_options.inputs: 16 kHz mono (or stereo) audio, ~5-10 s context
trainable_options.outputs: 256-way projection of future voice activity; BC-pred weighted F1 0.723; fine-tuned timing+type F1 38%
trainable_options.train_recipe: Self-supervised on Switchboard (2,438 dialogs) or any dialogue audio; fine-tune on ~109 sessions with backchannel annotations (Inoue); evaluate BC-pred F1
trainable_options.license: github.com/ErikEkstedt/conv_ssl (licence not verified in this pass)
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: RTF < 1 on an Intel i7-11700 CPU at 10 Hz; easily fits on Orin CPU

trainable_options.name: Reaction-to-reward mapping (EMPATHIC recipe)
trainable_options.what_it_is: Supervised temporal network from OpenFace/blendshape facial features to reward class / positivity score, used to rank outcomes and update a belief over reward functions online
trainable_options.size_params: Small (OpenFace AU + head-pose features -> temporal net; parameters unstated)
trainable_options.inputs: 30 fps facial AU + head pose features aggregated over a window after each event
trainable_options.outputs: P(reward class) or positivity score per aggregated frame; trajectory ranking (tau 0.70 across 8 trajectories)
trainable_options.train_recipe: Collect owner reactions while the dog performs candidate behaviours with known ground-truth (e.g., scripted outcomes); train with reward-classification + auxiliary gesture loss; validate with Kendall tau on held-out sessions
trainable_options.license: GitHub repo (licence not verified)
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Negligible compute; needs the blendshape/AU stream

trainable_options.name: Weber-style humour/expression bandit (Q-learning with linear FA over laugh/smile state)
trainable_options.what_it_is: The 2018 Reeti design: state = (P(laugh), P(smile)), actions = sound/grimace/joke-type variants, reward = mean laugh+smile probability from punchline to end; adapts the robot's sense of humour to one user
trainable_options.inputs: laugh/smile probabilities per reaction window; context features (joke type, expression variant)
trainable_options.outputs: choice of expression/joke variant; learned per-owner preference table
trainable_options.train_recipe: Simulate a scripted owner with variant-dependent laugh probability + habituation + detector noise (use Gillick/Omine P/R figures); run epsilon-greedy / UCB; then continue online on hardware with the same reward-window log
trainable_options.license: Design pattern (paper on ACM DL, cited via survey); no code
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Trivial

trainable_options.name: Wav2Small / emotion2vec vocal valence-arousal head

open_questions: Can mirthful vs polite laughter be separated from audio alone on a single owner (SMILE-Next used video+LLM); is duration x smile co-occurrence enough? No audio-only numbers were found.
Habituation/non-stationarity: none of the robot RL papers report reward decay for repeated jokes/expressions; the simulation owner model needs a novelty term and the learner a non-stationary bandit.
Multi-person homes: rapport video CCC fell 0.50 -> 0.04 with three people and engagement rho dropped 0.14 in multi-party; how reliable is XVF3800 DoA + face ID gating in practice?

Weber et al. ICMI 2018 and Vilk & Fitter HRI 2020 are cited only via the Akalin & Loutfi survey and the OSU lab page (ACM DL 403, Semantic Scholar API 429); the Reeti paper's participant count and effect sizes still need to be read from the primary.
No primary source with a learning claim was fetched for Loona, MiRo-E or Moxie (search budget exhausted); what they learn online remains unknown.
Per-class 'Laughter' AP of the small AudioSet taggers (YAMNet/PANNs-MobileNet) was not extractable (figure-only); measure locally on Gillick's 1,000 + 1,000 annotated AudioSet clips.
Can the 315 M-parameter Omine frame model be distilled to <= 20 M for streaming on Orin without losing the ~0.3 s onset accuracy?

How much owner-specific reaction data is needed before the aggregated approval signal becomes reliable (EMPATHIC needed 14-17 people to reach tau 0.70 across trajectories; per-owner curves are unreported)?

results.claim: The canonical open laughter segmenter (ResNet-18-style on spectrograms, 1 s context, 43.1 fps) reaches F1 0.75 on clean Switchboard telephone speech but drops to F1 0.61 (precision 0.51) on in-the-wild AudioSet audio; MFCC-era detectors produced up to 10x more false positives than true laughs in some real recordings.
results.evidence_quote: Table 2: "ResNet + Augmentation 0.676 (±0.022) 0.847 (±0.018) 0.752 (±0.016) | 0.508 (±0.020) 0.759 (±0.017) 0.608 (±0.015)" | "The second model we examine is an adaptation of ResNet-18 [28] for binary audio classification, using 128-dimensional mel spectrograms as features." | "a sliding window that contains a total of 1 second of surrounding audio as context. We use the default frame rate of 43.1 fps as implemented in the Librosa library" | "In some recordings, these false positives outweighed the correctly identified laughter by as much as a factor of 10, calling into question the practical utility of existing methods for laughter detection."
results.correction: All numbers check out (SWB P .676 R .847 F1 .752; AudioSet P .508 R .759 F1 .608; MFCC baseline F1 .688 on SWB, .359 on AudioSet; 260 h / 543 speakers; 1000 laughter + 1000 negative AudioSet clips; 95.2% inter-annotator agreement; 8000 Hz). One attribution nuance: the 'factor of 10' false-positive figure is Gillick et al. reporting Ryokai et al. [7]'s mobile-phone deployment of published (MFCC/pitch-based) detectors, not a measurement made in this paper. The PDF itself is fetchable but only parses via pdftotext.

results.claim: Synthesizing laughter into unlabeled base audio (no human annotation) and fine-tuning a wav2vec2-large-xlsr-53 frame classifier gives a segmenter that beats Gillick's model on every test set (detection F1 0.78-0.94 vs 0.58-0.90) and cuts laughter start-time error from 1.5-2.1 s to 0.3-1.1 s; the same synthetic data also improves Gillick's small architecture.
results.evidence_quote: Table 1 F1 (Gillick / Ours): AMI "0.583" / "0.784"; MAHNOB "0.618" / "0.890"; Gillick set "0.844" / "0.865"; Ours set "0.897" / "0.943" | Table 2 start-time MAE: Gillick set "Gillick ... 2.070(±0.132)" vs "Ours ... 1.085(±0.098)"; Ours set "Gillick ... 1.500(±0.209)" vs "Ours ... 0.314(±0.106)" | "The model trained on our data using Gillick's architecture achieved better performance than Gillick's model with respect to many metrics, particularly in segmentation." | footnote 3: "https://huggingface.co/jonatasgrosman/wav2vec2-large-xlsr-53-english"
results.correction: Numbers are accurate (also confirmed: ~315 M params, 7.0 s input, class every ~0.02 s, 75 min training, 1 min per hour of audio on i9-9900K + RTX 2080 Ti, VocalSound 21,024 clips, 1,456 podcast episodes from 764 programs, segmentation F1 0.617→0.789, end MAE 0.573 s). Two nuances: (1) the checkpoint is jonatasgrosman/wav2vec2-large-xlsr-53-english (an English-ASR-fine-tuned xlsr-53), not the raw xlsr-53; (2) 'improves Gillick's architecture' is the paper's own qualified claim ('with respect to many metrics') — it holds for 5 of 6 F1 comparisons, but on the authors' own podcast test set Gillick's architecture trained on synthetic data scored detection F1 0.837 vs 0.897 for the original Gillick model.

results.claim: A robot-POV engagement regressor (ResNeXt-50 + LSTM) trained on a museum tour-guide robot reaches Spearman 0.63 (0.76 single-party) against 3 coders and transfers zero-shot to a different robot/dataset (UE-HRI) with AUC 0.89, at 5 Hz on a GTX 1060.
results.evidence_quote: "a ResNetXt-50 Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) pre-trained on the ImageNet dataset" ... "a single layer Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) with 2048 units followed by a Fully Connected (FC) layer" | Table 4: "test loss (MSE)" "0.126", "Correlation ρ" "0.634"; Table 5 single-party ρ "0.758" | "Three annotators took part in the coding process" | "The trained model is generic enough to be successfully applied in a completely different scenario, here the UE-HRI dataset, showing the applicability of the model also in different environments, on a different robot with a different camera" | "The area under the Receiver-Operator Curve (ROC) of 0.89" | "taking at most 200ms, allowing real-time estimation of engagement at 5 frames per second" ... "GPU GeForce GTX 1060" ... "Memory usage: 5.4 GB"
results.correction: No correction needed. All stated numbers match (ρ 0.634 overall, 0.758 single-party, 0.622 multi-party; MSE 0.126/0.087/0.136; inter-rater ρ 0.56–0.72; AUC 0.89 on UE-HRI with no retraining; 278 days, 556 km; 94 unique annotated videos totalling 5 h 50 min, 227 people; model+code at github.com/LCAS/engagement_detector). Minor: 5 Hz is the rate implied by a ≤200 ms forward pass over 10 consecutive frames.

results.claim: Facial reactions of untrained observers carry enough information to rank an agent's outcomes above chance, but weakly per person: a learned OpenFace-AU mapping beats random ranking (p=0.0024), improves an online policy for 9/10 new users, and ranks 8 robot trajectories with Kendall tau 0.70 only after aggregating across 14 people.
results.evidence_quote: "the mappings' performance on the holdout set is significantly better than uniformly random guessing (τ = 0), supporting H1; p = 0.0024 with the annotation-reliant auxiliary task and p = 0.0207 without it." | "human observers, none of whom created data within the stage-1 training set. 9 of the 10 participants' interactions achieved a better return than that of a random policy, and 7 of the 10 participants' interactions ended with the probability of reward mappings that lead to optimal behaviors being the highest" | "17 human participants observed 3 episodes of Robotaxi, and 14 of the participants observed 7 episodes of the robotic task." | "For each trajectory, we compute an overall (cross-subject) positivity score as the mean of the trajectory's per-subject positivity scores. After ranking the 8 trajectories by these scores, Kendall's τ independence test yields τ = 0.70 (p = 0.034)" | "were told that their 'reactions are being recorded for research purposes', and nothing more was said"
results.correction: All numbers match. Clarifications: p=0.0024 is with the annotation-reliant auxiliary loss (p=0.0207 without); each of the 14 participants watched 7 of the 8 predetermined trajectories and the τ=0.70 is for the cross-subject mean positivity ranking (per-subject τ values appear only in Fig. 7, not numerically in the text); the online result is described by the authors as a 'preliminary evaluation' run informally in participants' homes with unpaid subjects (Appx. J). Human-proxy baseline: mean τ 0.209 (p=.078), best 0.569 (p=.004).

results.claim: On physical social robots the working pattern for learning humour/affect from social signals is tabular or linear-FA Q-learning over a tiny action set with reward = mean laugh/smile (or valence/engagement) probability in a fixed post-action window: Weber et al. (Reeti) used laugh+smile probabilities from the SSI framework averaged from punchline to end; Gordon et al. (Tega) used SARSA with Affectiva valence+engagement; Park et al. personalised tabular Q-learning over 6-8 sessions.
results.evidence_quote: Survey: "they used a two-dimensional vector containing probabilities of laughs and smiles for state representation, and the action space consisted of sounds, grimaces and three types of jokes. They used an average reward based on all samples from the punchline to the end with a predefined punchline for every joke. The human social signals were captured and processed by using the Social Signals Interpretation (SSI) framework [77]." ... "the Reeti robot adapted its sense of humor ... by using Q-learning with a linear function approximator." | "They used the SARSA algorithm where the reward was a weighted sum of valence and engagement. Both valence and engagement values were obtained from the Affectiva software." | "A personalized policy was trained through 6–8 sessions of interaction by using a tabular Q-learning algorithm." | Weber 2018 primary (OPUS postprint): "we decided to compute an average reward based on all samples from the punchline to the end"; "action space A: sounds, grimaces and three types of jokes and the combination of them"; "we use a linear function approximator"
results.correction: The three attributions are accurate in the survey, and I additionally verified them against the Weber et al. ICMI 2018 postprint (https://opus.bibliothek.uni-augsburg.de/opus4/files/47626/47626.pdf; ACM DL returned 403). Nuances for the generalisation: (1) Weber's 'tiny action set' is tiny only at the category level — the paper lists 3 joke categories, 19 grimaces and 23 sounds, giving 437 grimace-sound and 2052 grimace-joke combinations, with SSI smile/laugh probabilities sampled at 2.5 Hz; (2) Gordon's and Park's rewards are weighted sums (valence+engagement; engagement+learning gains [-100,0,+50,+100]) and the survey does not describe a fixed post-action averaging window for them — the windowed-mean pattern is documented only for Weber.

results.claim: Even with 284 million crowd ratings on 2.2 million New Yorker captions, GPT-4-Turbo ranks funniness at 67% vs a former editor at 94%, crowd workers at 62%; RLHF/DPO on Mistral-7B yields only ~9% win rate vs top-10 human captions; and a few thousand expert pairwise labels (5,580) lift GPT-4o from 67.3% to 82.4% (experts avg 78%).
results.evidence_quote: Table 1: "Total number of ratings 284,183,913"; abstract: "more than 2.2 million captions" | Table 2 (Pairwise): "Human (worker) GPT4o-vision 61.67±3.45", "GPT4-Turbo GPT4o-vision 67±3.33"; (Group Overall): "Human (expert) Cartoon Image 94.28±2.79", "GPT4-Turbo GPT4-vision 74±3.11", "GPT4-Turbo Hessel et al. [22] 77.5±2.96", "Human (worker) GPT4o-vision 59.23±1.45" | Table 3 Overall Win Rate vs Top 10: "Mistral-7B RLHF 8.79", "Mistral-7B DPO 9.34" | arXiv 2502.20356: "GPT-4o Prompting 67.3±1.5", "GPT-4o SFT w/ Expl. (Ours) 82.4±1.2", "Expert Average Accuracy 78±2.6"; "To construct the training set, for each of the 279 training cartoons, we randomly form 10 pairwise comparisons between captions ranked 1-10 and those ranked 1000-1009, and another ten pairs between 30-39 and 300-309. This in total results in 5580 pairs of captions."; "supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a large corpus of New Yorker caption contest caption ranking data released by Zhang et al. (2024)"
results.correction: Two details are off. (1) The 5,580 fine-tuning pairs are NOT expert labels: they are built from crowd-contest rankings (Zhang et al. 2024 data) — the Bridging abstract itself says 'model finetuning with crowd preferences proved remarkably effective'. Corrected: ~5.6k crowd-ranked caption pairs (279 cartoons × 20) lift GPT-4o from 67.3% to 82.4% on the easy split (rank 1-10 vs 1000-1009; hard split 63.2%), vs expert average 78%, best expert 85.33%, expert majority vote 84%. (2) The 67% / 94% / 62% figures mix paradigms: 67% (GPT-4-Turbo) and 61.67% (crowd) are Pairwise accuracies, whereas the editor's 94.28% is Group (Overall). In the editor's own Group (Overall) paradigm GPT-4-Turbo scores 73–77.5% and crowd workers 57.5–59.2%, so the LLM–expert gap is ~17–21 points, not 27. Remaining figures are correct: 284,183,913 ratings (abstract says 'over 250 million'), 2.2 M captions, 365 contests, 6,044 captions/contest, Mistral-7B DPO 9.34% / RLHF 8.79% overall win rate vs Top-10, Claude-3-Opus 54.40%, GPT-4o 44.51%, expert prefers Claude 1.6% vs workers 35.4%.

sweeps.topic: Deployment reality on Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB (LLM/ASR/TTS/VLM/full-duplex inference numbers) and the Unitree Go2 EDU control surfaces (SDK2 SportClient, MotionSwitcher, LowCmd 500 Hz, unitree_mujoco / unitree_rl_lab / unitree_rl_mjlab)

findings.claim: On Jetson AGX Orin 64GB, llama.cpp (JetPack 6.1, CUDA 12.6, full GPU offload, flash attention) decodes Llama 3.1 8B Q4_K_M at 28 t/s with 1.2 s TTFT, Qwen2.5 7B Q4_K_M at 31 t/s / 1.0 s TTFT, and Phi-3 Mini 3.8B at 47 t/s / 0.7 s TTFT; a second blog on JetPack 6.2 with jetson_clocks measured 52 gen t/s for the same Llama 3.1 8B Q4_K_M, so expect 30-50 t/s for an 8B Q4 model depending on build/clocks.
findings.source_title: LLM Inference Benchmarks on Jetson AGX Orin 64GB (2026); cross-checked with ProventusNova 'Running LLMs on Jetson Orin' (https://proventusnova.com/blog/llm-inference-jetson-orin-llamacpp-ollama)
findings.numbers: AGX Orin 64GB: Llama3.1-8B Q4_K_M 28 t/s (TTFT 1.2 s, 5.8 GB) vs 52 t/s (JP6.2, jetson_clocks, prompt 48 t/s); Qwen2.5-7B Q4_K_M 31 t/s (TTFT 1.0 s, 5.2 GB); Phi-3-mini 47 t/s (TTFT 0.7 s, 2.8 GB). Orin NX 16GB: Llama3.1-8B 18 t/s, Qwen2.5-7B 20 t/s. Orin NX 8GB 11 t/s. Orin Nano 8GB Phi-3-mini 28 t/s. Max model ~40 GB on AGX Orin 64GB.
findings.relevance: Sets the per-token budget for any local conversation/intent LLM on the external Orin: ~20-35 ms/token for 7-8B, so an LM cannot sit inside the 50 Hz body-intent loop; it sets intent at 1-5 Hz.

findings.claim: NVIDIA's own TensorRT-LLM v0.12.0-jetson branch on Jetson Orin 64GB (JetPack 6.1) decodes Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct INT4 at 35.2 tok/s (batch 1, 512/512, 260 ms context phase); INT4-GPTQ 33.7 tok/s; peak ~35.9 tok/s. Support is AGX Orin only; other Orin devices 'undergoing testing'.
findings.source_title: TensorRT-LLM README4Jetson (v0.12.0-jetson); forum announcement https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/tensorrt-llm-for-jetson/313228; archived Jetson AI Lab page https://www.jetson-ai-lab.com/archive/tensorrt_llm.html
findings.numbers: Llama-3-8B INT4 BS1: context 260 ms, decode 35.2 tok/s; INT4-GPTQ: 292 ms, 33.7 tok/s; peak 35.9 tok/s; JetPack 6.1 (L4T r36.4); AGX Orin only.
findings.relevance: Official upper-bound-ish number for an 8B model on the AGX Orin; confirms 30-40 tok/s is the realistic ceiling for single-stream 8B decode.

findings.claim: NVIDIA staff report 225.65 output tok/s for Qwen2.5-VL-3B on AGX Orin 64GB with vLLM at concurrency 8 (ISL/OSL 2048/128); an un-tuned user run on JetPack 6.2.1 got 30 tok/s. Separately NVIDIA staff cite 231 tok/s at concurrency 8 on AGX Orin 64GB with the vLLM r36.4 container, and the GenAI benchmarking tutorial's sample (Llama-3.1-8B W4A16, 2048/128, concurrency 1) shows 44.19 tok/s, TTFT 32 ms, ITL 22.5 ms (device not stated).
findings.source_title: NVIDIA Developer Forums: 'The token speed of qwen 2.5 vl 3b model is very lower on Jetson AGX Orin' (+ https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/llm-library-recomendations-for-maximum-token-speeds/358521 and https://www.jetson-ai-lab.com/tutorials/genai-benchmarking/)
findings.numbers: Qwen2.5-VL-3B: 225.65 tok/s @ conc 8 (NVIDIA) vs 30 tok/s (user, vLLM w4a16, JP 6.2.1); vLLM 231 tok/s @ conc 8 AGX Orin 64GB; Llama-3.1-8B W4A16 44.19 tok/s @ conc 1, TTFT 32.02 ms, ITL 22.47 ms; gpt-oss-20b 40 tok/s on AGX Orin (NVIDIA blog 2025-12-11).
findings.relevance: Shows a ~7x gap between tuned NVIDIA containers and naive installs; batching helps throughput but single-stream latency (ITL ~22 ms for 8B) is what the dog feels.

findings.claim: Vision encoding, not the LLM, dominates per-frame VLM latency on AGX Orin: llama.cpp Qwen3-VL-4B Q4_K_M spends 4,079 ms encoding one image (2,040 tokens) then decodes at 32.7 t/s (prompt eval 359 t/s, 2.38 GB). Moondream 2 in the Kestrel server on AGX Orin sustains 4.63 req/s (P50 5.1 s at batch 64; landing page shows 514 ms P50) for ~3-token answers.
findings.source_title: llama.cpp discussion #17732 (Qwen3-VL on AGX Orin) + m87-labs/kestrel PERFORMANCE.md (https://github.com/m87-labs/kestrel/blob/main/PERFORMANCE.md) + moondream.ai
findings.numbers: Qwen3-VL-4B Q4_K_M on AGX Orin: image encode 4,079 ms (2,040 tokens), decode 32.71 t/s, prompt 359 t/s, 2.38 GB. Moondream 2 AGX Orin batch 64: Direct 4.63 req/s P50 5,111 ms; CoT 3.28 req/s P50 15,141 ms; Thor 15.13 req/s / 1,805 ms; moondream.ai lists 514 ms / 4.6 req/s for AGX Orin. SmolVLM-256M runs one image in <1 GB GPU RAM (Apache 2.0).
findings.relevance: A 'state of the world' VLM tick on the Orin costs 0.2-4 s depending on model/runtime; cap image tokens (Qwen min/max_pixels) and run the VLM at <=1-2 Hz, never in the motion loop.

findings.claim: Small models on the Orin Nano Super (llama.cpp, 25 W, ctx 2048) run SmolLM2-135M at 165 tok/s, Qwen2.5-0.5B Q4_K_M at 92.9 tok/s, Qwen3-0.6B Q8 at 49.4, Llama-3.2-1B Q4_K_M at 47.1, Gemma3-1B at 40.8, with TTFT p50 ~0.4-0.75 s; 25 W is the Pareto sweet spot. Single-stream decode is memory-bandwidth bound (~21% of theoretical compute used).
findings.source_title: Tiny LLM Benchmark: Jetson Orin Nano Super 8GB (+ Eric X. Liu, 'Why Your Jetson Orin Nano's 40 TOPS Goes Unused', https://ericxliu.me/posts/benchmarking-llms-on-jetson-orin-nano/)
findings.numbers: SmolLM2-135M Q4 165.2 t/s (101 MB); SmolLM2-360M Q8 102.2; Qwen2.5-0.5B Q4 92.9 (469 MB, TTFT ~500 ms); Qwen3-0.6B Q8 49.4; Llama3.2-1B Q4 47.1 (771 MB, TTFT ~750 ms); Gemma3-1B 40.8. JetPack r36.4.7, llama.cpp b9292. Liu: Qwen2.5-0.5B Ollama 35 t/s, first token 0.5-1.4 s, 20.8% compute efficiency, 68 GB/s bandwidth.
findings.relevance: A 0.1-0.5B 'intent' model can produce ~100+ tok/s even on the smallest Orin; on AGX Orin (2x bandwidth) a sub-1B model can plausibly emit a few motion tokens every 100-200 ms, but not every 20 ms.

findings.claim: Whisper on Jetson: NVIDIA's whisper_trt transcribes 20 s of audio on an Orin Nano in 0.64 s (tiny.en) / 0.86 s (base.en) vs 0.85 s faster-whisper and 1.74 / 2.55 s PyTorch, using ~3x less time and ~60% memory (RTF ~0.03-0.04). Parakeet TDT 0.6B does NOT run on Jetson CUDA via NeMo ('no kernel image'); Moonshine v2 streaming ASR gives 50-258 ms responses on an M3 CPU at 34-245M params.
findings.source_title: NVIDIA-AI-IOT/whisper_trt README (+ Parakeet HF discussion https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v2/discussions/19; Moonshine v2 arXiv 2602.12241 https://arxiv.org/html/2602.12241v1)
findings.numbers: Orin Nano, 20 s audio: tiny.en whisper 1.74 s / faster-whisper 0.85 s / whisper_trt 0.64 s; base.en 2.55 / n/a / 0.86 s; memory 569/404/488 MB (tiny), 666/-/439 MB (base). AGX Orin whisper tiny.en 10 s clip 1.6 s at 15 W (arXiv 2511.02269, method unstated). Moonshine v2: tiny 33.57M WER 12.01% 50 ms; small 123.36M 7.84% 148 ms; medium 244.93M 6.65% 258 ms (Apple M3); MIT. Parakeet v3 600M CC-BY-4.0 WER 6.32% RTFx 3,332 on datacenter GPUs; sherpa-onnx int8 RTF 0.088 at 4 threads on RK3588 CPU.
findings.relevance: Local ASR with <300 ms latency is feasible on the Orin (whisper_trt or Moonshine) as the fallback/side-channel to the hosted Realtime API; do not plan on Parakeet GPU on Jetson.

findings.claim: TTS on Orin: Piper (now GPL-3.0 as piper1-gpl; original MIT repo archived 2025-10-06) reaches first audible sound ~800-900 ms end-to-end in ROS 2 on an Orin Nano with onnxruntime-gpu; on a single CPU thread Piper medium has RTF 0.114 vs Kokoro-82M RTF 1.128 (fp32), so Kokoro needs the GPU. Kokoro-82M is Apache 2.0, 24 kHz, 54 voices; jetson-containers ships kokoro-tts onnx/hf/fastapi and piper1-tts packages. No Kokoro or Sesame CSM-1B latency measurement on any Jetson was found.
findings.source_title: sherpa-onnx PR #2460 CPU TTS comparison (+ Piper-on-Orin-Nano blog https://thomasthelliez.com/blog/running-piper-tts-on-nvidia-jetson-orin-nano-with-low-latency/, Kokoro-82M card https://huggingface.co/hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, piper1-gpl https://github.com/OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl)
findings.numbers: Single-thread MacBook Pro RTF: Piper medium fp32 0.114 (75 MB), fp16 0.123, int8 0.320; MatchaTTS 0.118; KittenTTS 0.389 (23 MB); Kokoro fp32 1.128 (330 MB), int8 1.972. Orin Nano Piper en_US-amy-low: 800-900 ms to first audio (ROS 2, CUDA). Kokoro: 82M params, Apache 2.0, 24 kHz, 8 languages/54 voices, ~1,000 A100-hours (~$1,000) to train.
findings.relevance: Local TTS fallback is Piper on CPU cores (leaves GPU for LLM/policy); Kokoro only if GPU headroom exists; CSM-1B is unmeasured on Orin.

findings.claim: Moshi is a 7B temporal transformer (Helium 7B, 2.1T tokens) over the Mimi codec at 12.5 Hz (8 codebooks x 2048, 1.1 kbps, 24 kHz) with 160 ms theoretical / 200 ms practical latency on an L4 GPU; PyTorch bf16 needs a 24 GB GPU, int8 exists only via Rust/Candle (int4 via MLX/macOS). Nobody has reported running Moshi on a Jetson AGX Orin (the only forum thread is unanswered; NVIDIA: 'We don't have experience with Moshi'). NVIDIA's Moshi-based PersonaPlex-7B is tested on A100 80GB (170 ms turn-taking, 240 ms interruption latency) with no Jetson mention.
findings.source_title: kyutai-labs/moshi README + Moshi paper (https://kyutai.org/Moshi.pdf) + NVIDIA forum 'Kyutai Moshi Install - Jetson AGX Orin' (https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/kyutai-moshi-install/331658) + nvidia/personaplex-7b-v1 (https://huggingface.co/nvidia/personaplex-7b-v1)
findings.numbers: Moshi 7B; Mimi 12.5 Hz, Q=8 codebooks x 2048, 1.1 kbps, 24 kHz; latency 160 ms theoretical, 200 ms on L4; PyTorch needs 24 GB (no quantization); candle q8 (~8B GGUF int8); weights CC-BY-4.0, code MIT/Apache-2.0. PersonaPlex-7B bf16, NVIDIA Open Model License, A100 80GB, 0.170 s turn-taking, 0.240 s interruption, 95% interruption success. AGX Orin bandwidth 204.8 GB/s => int8 7B at 12.5 Hz needs ~87.5 GB/s (my estimate), bf16 ~175 GB/s.
findings.relevance: A trainable full-duplex speech model of Moshi class is not demonstrably deployable on the Orin; keep duplex speech hosted and make any trainable duplex component a small head, or budget an explicit int8-on-Orin experiment.

The Python SDK mirrors this list.

findings.claim: Commit 0953c60 'update for syncretic_motion_control' (2025-05-21) removed the Go2 sport APIs SwitchGait 1011, Trigger 1012, BodyHeight 1013, FootRaiseHeight 1014, TrajectoryFollow 1018, ContinuousGait 1019, Wallow 1021, WiggleHips 1033, GetState 1034, old EconomicGait 1035, Dance3/4 1037-1038, HopSpinLeft/Right 1039-1040 and legacy 1042-1051, and added the 1061-1063 gaits and 2041-2058 stunts; the go2_trajectory_follow example no longer compiles and is commented out of CMakeLists.

findings.numbers: 9 files changed, +64/-444; 14+ API IDs removed, 15 added; TrajectoryFollow example used 30 PathPoints at 0.06 s spacing (fields timeFromStart, x, y, yaw, vx, vy, vyaw).
findings.relevance: Parcel's motion contracts must not depend on BodyHeight/FootRaiseHeight/WiggleHips/ContinuousGait/TrajectoryFollow; continuous body expression beyond Euler+Move requires the low-level interface.

findings.claim: Go2 low-level control publishes LowCmd_ on 'rt/lowcmd' and subscribes LowState_ on 'rt/lowstate'; LowCmd_ has motor_cmd[20] with fields mode (0x01 = PMSM/servo), q, dq, tau, kp, kd, and a mandatory CRC32; LowState_ gives imu_state, motor_state[20] (q, dq, ddq, tau_est, temperature, lost), foot_force[4], foot_force_est[4], bms, power_v/a, tick. Both official examples run the loop at dt = 0.002 s (500 Hz; comment '0.001~0.01') with stand gains Kp 60 / Kd 5 and require ReleaseMode() on the motion_switcher first.
findings.source_title: unitree_sdk2 example/go2/go2_stand_example.cpp + go2_low_level.cpp + idl/go2/LowCmd_.hpp + LowState_.hpp; Python go2_stand_example.py
findings.numbers: dt = 0.002 s (500 Hz), valid 0.001-0.01 s; Kp 60, Kd 5 (stand), Kp 5, Kd 1 (sine test), README safety test kp 10 kd 1 with 1 N.m; PosStopF 2.146E+9, VelStopF 16000; 20 motor slots (12 used); stand sequence 500+500+1000+900 ms; crc32_core over (sizeof(LowCmd_)>>2)-1 words.
findings.relevance: Defines the joint-level surface any learned whole-body expression policy must target, its cadence (500 Hz command loop, 50 Hz policy in Unitree's own deployer) and the CRC/mode-release preconditions the deterministic safety layer must own.

findings.claim: The motion_switcher service (API IDs CheckMode 1001, SelectMode 1002, ReleaseMode 1003, SetSilent 1004, GetSilent 1005) gates the locomotion services; mode names used in the SDK example are 'ai', 'normal', 'advanced' and 'ai-w' (wheeled). Low-level examples loop on CheckMode/ReleaseMode until no mode is active, the README says 'use the app to turn off the high-level motion service (sport_mode)' first, and the unitree_rl_lab deployer refuses to start if another process owns rt/lowcmd: high-level sport control and low-level joint control are mutually exclusive.
findings.source_title: unitree_sdk2 motion_switcher_api.hpp / motion_switcher_client.hpp + unitree_sdk2_python example/motionSwitcher/motion_switcher_example.py + unitree_sdk2_python README
findings.numbers: Service 'motion_switcher'; 5 API IDs 1001-1005; modes ai / normal / advanced / ai-w.
findings.relevance: Parcel's gateway cannot mix SportClient tricks and rt/lowcmd policies in the same instant; switching modes is a service round-trip that must be part of the safety state machine.

findings.claim: unitree_rl_lab (Apache-2.0, IsaacLab 2.3.0 / IsaacSim 5.1.0) ships a Go2 velocity task with sim.dt 0.005 s and decimation 4 (50 Hz policy), 20 s episodes, 4096 envs, joint-position-offset actions with scale 0.25, observations base_ang_vel, projected_gravity, velocity_commands, joint_pos_rel, joint_vel_rel, actions; actuator Go2HV stiffness 25 / damping 0.5; and a C++ deployer (Passive kd 3 -> FixStand kp 60/80/80, kd 5/4/4 -> RLBase ONNX via onnxruntime 1.22.0, gamepad L2+A then Start). unitree_rl_mjlab reproduces the same recipe on MuJoCo Warp (4096 envs, auto policy.onnx export, PC at 192.168.123.222, L2+R2 debug mode). unitree_rl_gym's deploy_real supports only G1/H1/H1_2, not Go2.

findings.claim: unitree_mujoco (BSD-3) simulates Go2/B2/B2w/H1/Go2w/G1/H1-2/AS2 in MuJoCo and exposes the same DDS LowCmd / LowState / SportModeState messages as the real robot so SDK2, ROS 2 and Python control code runs unchanged (DDS domain 1 on 'lo'; Python bridge SIMULATE_DT 0.005 s, VIEWER_DT 0.02 s; gamepad emulates the WirelessController); it does not emulate the sport service.

findings.claim: Programming access is EDU-only: 'The Go2 Pro model doesn't support any type of programming. Only edu/edu+ versions support it'; CycloneDDS 'works out of the box only with the EDU version', Air/Pro need a custom firmware, and the app's WebRTC path cannot publish rt/lowcmd (lowstate only via rt/lf/lowstate). The EDU adds a separate Jetson (EDU Standard: Orin Nano; EDU Plus: Orin NX 16GB '100 TOPS'), foot force sensors, voice module + mic, optional Mid-360 (360 deg x -7..52 deg, 70 m) or Hesai XT16, 8000 mAh (1-2 h) or 15000 mAh (2-4 h) at 28.8 V; robot controller IP 192.168.123.161, PC on 192.168.123.x/24.

findings.claim: Official Jetson AI Lab AGX Orin LLM/VLM charts cannot be read (SVGs rendered as paths, 0 text nodes) and published MLC numbers are hard to reproduce (jetson-containers issue #532: Llama2-7b on AGX Orin 32GB measured ~19 tok/s vs 47 published, Gemma ~23 vs 75, closed without explanation); the Orin Nano Super HTML table gives Llama 3.2 3B 43.07 tok/s, Llama 3.1 8B 19.14, Qwen2.5 7B 21.75 (MLC INT4). NVIDIA's newer TensorRT Edge-LLM C++ runtime supports all Orin modules (INT4 AWQ, 0.6B-27B, Llama 3.x / Qwen3 / InternVL3 / Phi-4-MM) but requires JetPack 7.2; on an Orin Nano Super it gave Cosmos-Reason2-2B 60 TPS, 17 ms TPOT, 29 ms text TTFT / 420 ms image TTFT in 4.3 GB vs vLLM 56 TPS / 6.9 GB.

TRT Edge-LLM: JetPack 7.2 / R39.2 on Orin; Orin Nano Super Cosmos-Reason2-2B W4A16 60 TPS, TPOT 17 ms, TTFT 29 ms text / 420 ms image, 4.3 GB; vLLM 56 TPS, 6.9 GB; llama.cpp Q4_K_M 38 TPS.

findings.claim: Model facts that constrain the local stack: Llama 3.2 1B/3B are 1.23B/3.21B params under the custom Llama 3.2 Community License (3B SpinQuant decodes 19.7 tok/s on a phone); Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct is 3.09B under the 'Qwen Research License'; Qwen2.5-VL-3B is 4B params with 4-16,384 visual tokens configurable; SmolVLM-256M is Apache 2.0 and needs <1 GB GPU RAM; Sesame CSM-1B ('the 1B CSM variant', Llama backbone + Mimi-code audio decoder, HF reports 2B tensors F32) is Apache 2.0, 24 kHz, English, needs a separate LLM, fine-tunable with HF Trainer, no latency numbers.
findings.source_title: HF model cards: sesame/csm-1b, meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct, HuggingFaceTB/SmolVLM-256M-Instruct
findings.numbers: Llama 3.2: 1.23B / 3.21B, 128k ctx (8k quantized), 3B SpinQuant 19.7 tok/s on OnePlus 12, ~2,435 MB. Qwen2.5-3B: 3.09B total / 2.77B non-embedding, 32k ctx, Qwen Research License. Qwen2.5-VL-3B: 4B params. SmolVLM-256M: SigLIP 93M + SmolLM2-135M, 64 visual tokens per 512x512. CSM-1B: Apache 2.0, 24 kHz, released 2025-03-13.
findings.relevance: License and size screen for what can ship on the dog commercially (Apache: SmolLM2/SmolVLM/Kokoro/CSM; restricted: Qwen2.5-3B research license, Llama community license, GPL piper1).

design_implications: Split the action surface explicitly: (a) SportClient presets (Hello, Stretch, Content, Heart, Pose, Scrape, Dance1/2, FrontJump/Pounce, Sit/RiseSit, flips/gaits) plus the only continuous knobs Euler(roll,pitch,yaw), Move(vx,vy,vyaw), SpeedLevel; (b) rt/lowcmd 500 Hz joint control for anything richer. BodyHeight, FootRaiseHeight, WiggleHips, ContinuousGait and TrajectoryFollow were deleted from the SDK in May 2025 and must not appear in Parcel's contracts.

'Look back at the owner when lost' is learnable today on surface (a): a small policy over owner bearing + localisation confidence emitting yaw/Euler + Move at the 50 Hz body-intent lane; no low-level control, no EDU-only risk, trainable in Parcel's own sim.

'Learn to chuckle if the joke was funny' has a cheap form (learned trigger timing/probability over presets like Content/Heart/Scrape from the affect signal) and an expensive form (a learned whole-body motion on rt/lowcmd). The expensive form should reuse Unitree's own pipeline: unitree_rl_lab or unitree_rl_mjlab Go2 env (50 Hz policy, decimation 4 on 5 ms physics, 4096 envs, action scale 0.25) with added reward terms, ONNX export, C++ FSM Passive->FixStand->RL deploy; validate through unitree_mujoco's identical DDS surface first.

Never place an LLM/VLM in the 20 ms loop: on AGX Orin 64GB an 8B Q4 model decodes at ~30-50 tok/s (20-35 ms/token) with 0.7-1.2 s TTFT, a 0.5B model ~100+ tok/s, and a VLM frame costs 0.2-4 s. The 'state of the world' model ticks at 1-5 Hz (text) / <=1-2 Hz (vision) and writes intents; a sub-1M-parameter ONNX policy owns 50 Hz and the deterministic safety layer owns 500 Hz.

Keep full-duplex speech hosted (<= $300/mo Realtime API). Moshi/PersonaPlex-class 7B models have no reported Jetson run, need 24 GB bf16, and on the 204.8 GB/s AGX Orin bf16 is bandwidth-infeasible at 12.5 Hz while int8 is only borderline on paper. If a trainable duplex component is wanted, train a small listener/turn-taking/backchannel head over codec tokens, not the 7B speech LM, and gate a dedicated int8-Moshi-on-Orin experiment behind a measurement.

Local speech fallback that fits the Orin: whisper_trt (tiny/base.en, RTF ~0.03-0.04 even on Orin Nano) or Moonshine v2 (MIT, 50-260 ms on CPU) for ASR; Piper on CPU cores (RTF ~0.11) for TTS; Kokoro only on GPU (CPU RTF 1.1); Parakeet GPU on Jetson is broken in NeMo (CPU/sherpa-onnx only). Budget a 10-minute first-load for whisper.cpp CUDA engines.

Hardware placement: the Go2 EDU's own Jetson (Orin Nano on EDU Standard, Orin NX 16GB / 102.4 GB/s on EDU Plus) should run LiDAR/perception/SDK bridging; the external AGX Orin 64GB (275 TOPS, 204.8 GB/s, 15-60 W) runs LLM/VLM/policies. Buy EDU (Plus): Air/Pro cannot be programmed, DDS works out of the box only on EDU, and rt/lowcmd is unreachable over the app's WebRTC path.

Safety-layer obligations that fall directly out of the SDK: own motion_switcher CheckMode/SelectMode/ReleaseMode (modes ai/normal/advanced/ai-w), refuse rt/lowcmd while any sport mode is active (they are mutually exclusive), compute the CRC32 on every LowCmd, hold the 1-10 ms command cadence, always pass Passive (kd 3) -> FixStand (kp 60/80/80, kd 5/4/4) before enabling a policy, and treat the app's sport-mode toggle as an external state change.

License screen for on-dog models: Apache 2.0 (SmolLM2/SmolVLM, Kokoro, CSM-1B, unitree_rl_lab/mjlab), BSD-3 (unitree_sdk2, unitree_mujoco), CC-BY-4.0 (Moshi weights, Parakeet), MIT (Moonshine, archived Piper) are clean; Qwen2.5-3B (Qwen Research License), Llama 3.2 (community license), piper1-gpl (GPL-3.0) and PersonaPlex (NVIDIA Open Model License) need review before productisation.

Measure, don't trust charts: published Jetson AI Lab MLC numbers were 2-3x above what users reproduced, and the same llama.cpp model varied 28 vs 52 tok/s across JetPack builds; run Parcel's own AGX Orin benchmark matrix (llama.cpp Q4, TensorRT-LLM INT4, vLLM W4A16, TRT Edge-LLM on JetPack 7.2) before fixing the intent-model size.

trainable_options.name: unitree_rl_lab Go2 velocity policy (IsaacLab) -> ONNX -> C++ FSM on rt/lowcmd
trainable_options.what_it_is: Unitree's official RL locomotion stack: IsaacLab 2.3.0 / IsaacSim 5.1.0 Go2 task with a 50 Hz joint-position-offset policy (decimation 4 on 5 ms physics, action scale 0.25), PPO via rsl_rl, exported to ONNX and run by a C++ finite-state machine (Passive -> FixStand -> RLBase) over unitree_sdk2 at 500 Hz command rate. Extend with reward terms for owner-facing yaw, 'chuckle' bounce amplitude, gaze/head pitch, etc.
trainable_options.license: Apache-2.0 (deployer bundles onnxruntime 1.22.0)
trainable_options.size_params: MLP actor (sub-1M params); 4096 parallel envs during training
trainable_options.inputs: base_ang_vel (x0.2), projected_gravity, velocity_commands, joint_pos_rel, joint_vel_rel (x0.05), previous actions (critic adds joint_effort); 20 s episodes

trainable_options.train_recipe: HF fine-tuning (SmolVLM/Qwen-VL) on Parcel-labelled frames; quantize W4A16 for vLLM / INT4-AWQ for TRT Edge-LLM
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Yes at <=1-2 Hz on AGX Orin with capped image tokens; SmolVLM-256M (<1 GB) could run on the dog's Orin NX.

open_questions: Official Unitree docs (Basic_motion_control, AI_motion_service, Motion Switcher, Motion Services V2.0 notice, Quick_start, expansion-dock config) are a JS-only site and could not be read: confirm the rt/lowstate publish rate (500 Hz assumed from example dt=0.002), whether 'ai' mode is required for FrontFlip/Dance/2000-series APIs, the firmware versions that still serve the removed 1011-1040 APIs, and the on-dog network topology (.161 controller, expansion-dock IP).

Which Go2 EDU SKU Parcel will buy (EDU Standard with Orin Nano vs EDU Plus with Orin NX 16GB), and whether the external AGX Orin 64GB rides on the dog (15-60 W, cabling, mass budget within the 7-12 kg payload) or stays off-board with a wireless link and its latency.
No measured Moshi/PersonaPlex run on any Jetson exists: an int8 Candle Moshi experiment on AGX Orin is the only way to settle whether a trainable full-duplex speech model can ever be local.

Official Jetson AI Lab AGX Orin LLM/VLM numbers are unreadable SVGs and community reproduction fell 2-3x short; Parcel needs its own AGX Orin benchmark matrix (llama.cpp Q4, TensorRT-LLM INT4, vLLM W4A16, TRT Edge-LLM on JetPack 7.2) before fixing the intent-model size.

Riva embedded support on JetPack 6/7 (NVIDIA-supported low-latency ASR/TTS on Orin) is unknown: the support-matrix and embedded quick-start pages returned 404; jetson-containers only documents JetPack 5.

No Kokoro, Sesame CSM-1B or Parakeet-GPU latency measurement on any Orin was found; Moondream's AGX Orin latency is only known at batch 64 (5.1 s P50) plus a landing-page '514 ms'; SmolVLM has no Orin number.

Whether the sport-mode presets (Content/Heart/Scrape/Hello) can be interrupted or blended (e.g. Euler tilt during a preset), and their durations, is undocumented in the SDK; this decides how much 'expression' is possible without low-level control.

The unitree_rl_lab Go2 deployer runs on an x86/ARM PC over Ethernet; whether the 500 Hz LowCmd loop can be hosted on the dog's Orin NX alongside LiDAR/perception without jitter has not been shown in any fetched source.

results.claim: On Jetson AGX Orin 64GB, llama.cpp (JetPack 6.1, CUDA 12.6, full GPU offload, flash attention) decodes Llama 3.1 8B Q4_K_M at 28 t/s with 1.2 s TTFT, Qwen2.5 7B Q4_K_M at 31 t/s / 1.0 s TTFT, and Phi-3 Mini 3.8B at 47 t/s / 0.7 s TTFT; a second blog on JetPack 6.2 with jetson_clocks measured 52 gen t/s for the same Llama 3.1 8B Q4_K_M, so expect 30-50 t/s for an 8B Q4 model depending on build/clocks.
results.evidence_quote: multimodalflow: "JetPack Version: 6.1" / "CUDA Version: 12.6" / "Inference Backend: llama.cpp (CUDA)" / "GPU Offload: Full (-ngl 999)" / "Flash Attention: Enabled (-fa 1)"; table: "Llama 3.1 8B Q4_K_M | 28 t/s | 1.2s | 5.8 GB", "Qwen2.5 7B Q4_K_M | 31 t/s | 1.0s | 5.2 GB", "Phi-3 Mini 3.8B Q4_K_M | 47 t/s | 0.7s | 2.8 GB". ProventusNova: "Benchmarked on JetPack 6.2, jetson_clocks enabled, context=2048"; Llama 3.1 8B Q4_K_M: "AGX Orin 64GB | 48 | 52", "Orin NX 16GB | 15 | 18", "Orin NX 8GB | 10 | 11"; Phi-3 mini on Orin Nano 8GB 22/28; Qwen 2.5 7B on Orin NX 16GB 18/20; "a 64GB AGX Orin can GPU-offload a 40GB model" / "Max model size at Q4 ... ~40GB".
results.correction: No correction needed; every number in the claim and its numbers field matches the two blogs. Caveat only: neither blog states the llama.cpp build/commit, so the 28 vs 52 t/s gap cannot be attributed solely to jetson_clocks/JetPack 6.2 — treat 30-50 t/s as an empirical spread, not a modelled one.

results.claim: NVIDIA's own TensorRT-LLM v0.12.0-jetson branch on Jetson Orin 64GB (JetPack 6.1) decodes Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct INT4 at 35.2 tok/s (batch 1, 512/512, 260 ms context phase); INT4-GPTQ 33.7 tok/s; peak ~35.9 tok/s. Support is AGX Orin only; other Orin devices 'undergoing testing'.
results.evidence_quote: README4Jetson.md: "**Platform**: Jetson Orin 64GB, MAX-N, Jetpack 6.1"; INT4 table rows "| 1 | 128 | 128 | 91 | 35.9 |", "| 1 | 512 | 512 | 260 | 35.2 |", "| 1 | 1024 | 512 | 582 | 34.7 |"; INT4 GPTQ rows "| 1 | 128 | 128 | 105 | 34.5 |", "| 1 | 512 | 512 | 292 | 33.7 |", "| 1 | 1024 | 512 | 337 | 33.3 |". jetson-ai-lab archive: "Jetson AGX Orin *Support for other Orin devices is currently undergoing testing." and "JetPack 6.1 (L4T r36.4)". NVIDIA forum: "Initial support for TensorRT-LLM in JetPack 6.1 has been included in the v0.12.0-jetson branch... for Jetson AGX Orin."
results.correction: No numeric correction. Attribution note: the 'AGX Orin only / other Orin devices undergoing testing' wording and 'L4T r36.4' appear on the jetson-ai-lab archive page and the forum announcement, not in README4Jetson.md itself (which says only 'Jetson Orin 64GB, MAX-N, Jetpack 6.1'). The README numbers were taken with clocks locked to MAX-N, so they are a best-case ceiling.

results.claim: Whisper on Jetson: NVIDIA's whisper_trt transcribes 20 s of audio on an Orin Nano in 0.64 s (tiny.en) / 0.86 s (base.en) vs 0.85 s faster-whisper and 1.74 / 2.55 s PyTorch, using ~3x less time and ~60% memory (RTF ~0.03-0.04). Parakeet TDT 0.6B does NOT run on Jetson CUDA via NeMo ('no kernel image'); Moonshine v2 streaming ASR gives 50-258 ms responses on an M3 CPU at 34-245M params.
results.evidence_quote: whisper_trt README: "When executing the base.en model on NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano, WhisperTRT runs ~3x faster while consuming only ~60% the memory compared with PyTorch."; "Execution time in seconds to transcribe 20 seconds of speech on Jetson Orin Nano": "| tiny.en | 1.74 sec | 0.85 sec | **0.64 sec** |", "| base.en | 2.55 sec | Unavailable | **0.86 sec** |"; memory "| tiny.en | 569 MB | **404 MB** | 488 MB |", "| base.en | 666 MB | Unavailable | **439 MB** |". Parakeet HF discussion #19: "RuntimeError: CUDA error: no kernel image is available for execution on the device"; NVIDIA: "We haven't tried on Jetson."; no confirmed CUDA fix, user switched to sherpa-onnx. Moonshine v2 (arXiv 2602.12241): Tiny 33.57M / WER 12.01% / 50 ms; Small 123.36M / 7.84% / 148 ms; Medium 244.93M / 6.65% / 258 ms on Apple M3; GitHub: "Licensed under the MIT License. The models are MIT by default too". arXiv 2511.02269: "The Jetson AGX Orin edge GPU achieved 1.6 s for both models" on jfk.wav "approximately 10 seconds long", "executed in the lowest power consumption mode" (15-45 W). Parakeet v3 card: CC-BY-4.0, 600M, Mean WER 6.32, RTFx 3,332.74. sherpa-onnx docs: parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v2-int8 on RK3588, 4 threads RTF 0.088.
results.correction: All numbers check out. Two wording refinements: (1) the '~3x faster / ~60% memory' headline is stated for base.en specifically (tiny.en is 2.7x / 86% memory); (2) 'does NOT run on Jetson CUDA' is stronger than the evidence — the thread shows one user's no-kernel-image failure, NVIDIA saying 'We haven't tried on Jetson', and no confirmed CUDA fix; phrase as 'not demonstrated on Jetson CUDA'. The '15 W' figure is inferred from 'lowest power consumption mode' of a 15-45 W range; the paper does not name the backend used on the Orin.

results.claim: Moshi is a 7B temporal transformer (Helium 7B, 2.1T tokens) over the Mimi codec at 12.5 Hz (8 codebooks x 2048, 1.1 kbps, 24 kHz) with 160 ms theoretical / 200 ms practical latency on an L4 GPU; PyTorch bf16 needs a 24 GB GPU, int8 exists only via Rust/Candle (int4 via MLX/macOS). Nobody has reported running Moshi on a Jetson AGX Orin (the only forum thread is unanswered; NVIDIA: 'We don't have experience with Moshi'). NVIDIA's Moshi-based PersonaPlex-7B is tested on A100 80GB (170 ms turn-taking, 240 ms interruption latency) with no Jetson mention.
results.evidence_quote: README: "a large, 7B-parameter Temporal Transformer models the temporal dependencies. Moshi achieves a theoretical latency of 160ms (80ms for the frame size of Mimi + 80ms of acoustic delay), with a practical overall latency as low as 200ms on an L4 GPU."; "Mimi is a neural audio codec that processes 24 kHz audio, down to a 12.5 Hz representation with a bandwidth of 1.1 kbps"; "At the moment, we do not support quantization for the PyTorch version, so you will need a GPU with a significant amount of memory (24GB)." BUT the model list reads: "Moshika for PyTorch (bf16, int8): ... kyutai/moshika-pytorch-q8 (experimental)", "Moshika for MLX (int4, int8, bf16)", "Moshika for Rust/Candle (int8, bf16)". Paper: "Helium, a 7B-parameter text LLM that we pretrain on 2.1T tokens"; "We use Q = 8 quantizers, each with a codebook size of NA = 2048. At 12.5Hz, this represents a bitrate of 1.1kbps." Forum: one reply (AastaLLL): "We don't have experience with Moshi. But based on their GitHub, it seems to use PyTorch as the backend inference library." — unresolved. PersonaPlex card: 7B, Moshi architecture, "NVIDIA A100 80 GB", turn-taking 0.170 s, interruption 0.240 s, success 0.950, BF16, NVIDIA Open Model License, no Jetson mention.
results.correction: Replace 'int8 exists only via Rust/Candle (int4 via MLX/macOS)' with: int8 (q8) weights are published for all three backends — PyTorch (kyutai/moshik{a,o}-pytorch-q8, labelled experimental, while the README still says PyTorch quantization is 'not supported'), MLX (q8) and Rust/Candle (q8); only int4 is MLX/macOS-only. Also the NVIDIA forum thread is 'unresolved with a single NVIDIA reply', not 'unanswered'. All other figures (7B, 2.1T tokens, 12.5 Hz, Q=8 x 2048, 1.1 kbps, 24 kHz, 160/200 ms on L4, 24 GB, PersonaPlex A100 80GB / 170 ms / 240 ms / 95%) are confirmed.
