sweeps.topic: Dog behavior science and character-animation principles for a Unitree Go2 companion dog: what the dog should do (looking back, social referencing, play signals, the dog-laugh, tail/posture signals, greeting/attachment), robot-pet ethograms (Sony AIBO/aibo, MiRo), animation principles for robots, HRI believability instruments, Go2 Sport API action inventory, and a proposed 34-behavior catalog

findings.claim: In the unsolvable task, 'looking back' at the human is driven by giving up: less persistent animals look back sooner and longer regardless of species or socialization; when persistence is controlled, wolf-dog differences disappear. All 44 dogs (pack, pet, free-ranging) and 73% of wolves looked back at least once.
findings.source_title: The role of domestication and experience in 'looking back' towards humans in an unsolvable task (Marshall-Pescini, Rao, Viranyi, Range), Scientific Reports
findings.numbers: N: 15 wolves, 14 pack dogs, 19 pet dogs, 11 free-ranging dogs; 3 solvable 3-min trials then 1 unsolvable 3-min trial; looked back: wolves 11/15 (73%), pack dogs 14/14, pet dogs 19/19, free-ranging 11/11; time on apparatus predicts later look-back (LM F=11.9, p=0.001); more persistent animals look back less often and for shorter.
findings.relevance: Defines the LOOK_BACK trigger for Parcel: a persistence budget on a task/nav goal that, when exhausted with the owner present, releases a body-turn-to-owner display; the threshold is the learnable quantity.

findings.claim: Dog gazing at humans is a social problem-solving strategy only under some conditions: with an alternative reward still available, gazing correlates positively with continued effort (help-seeking); after the alternative is consumed it correlates negatively (giving up). Gazes go overwhelmingly to the person who controls the locked resource.
findings.source_title: Disentangling help-seeking and giving up: differential human-directed gazing by dogs in a modified unsolvable task paradigm (Hirschi, Mazzini, Riemer), Animal Cognition
findings.numbers: N=56 dogs (29 herding, 27 terriers); box interaction vs gazing rs=0.51 (p<0.0001) while food available, rs=-0.42 (p=0.001) over the full 3 min; 'food in box' box-related gazing rs=0.55; 89-96% of gazes to the owner when the owner controlled the box; 48-70% to the experimenter when she did.
findings.relevance: Gives two look-back regimes (help request while still trying vs giving up) and the evaluation metric: proportion of looks directed at the responsible person.

findings.claim: Counter-evidence: in a modified impossible task, pet and free-ranging dogs looked back with similar latencies at a human, a dummy human and an object; the authors conclude looking back is not per se a problem-solving strategy but reflects persistence, stimulus salience and reinforcement history (pet dogs looked longer at humans).
findings.source_title: Why do dogs look back at the human in an impossible task? Looking back behaviour may be over-interpreted (Lazzaroni et al.), Animal Cognition, PMID 32090291
findings.numbers: 20 pet dogs (homes) vs 31 free-ranging dogs (Morocco); 3 possible + 1 impossible trial; 4 conditions (social, asocial, dummy human, object).
findings.relevance: Look-back should be learned from reinforcement history (owner helped before -> sooner/longer), and evaluations must set up context before assuming observers read it as help-seeking.

findings.claim: Dogs socially reference their owner about an ambiguous object: most look at the object then referentially at the owner, and the owner's (not a stranger's) positive vs negative message changes approach latency and proximity.
findings.source_title: Dogs' Social Referencing towards Owners and Strangers (Merola, Prato-Previde, Marshall-Pescini), PLoS ONE 7(10):e47653
findings.numbers: 90 dogs recruited, 57 analysed (29 owner-informant, 28 stranger); referential looking 76% (owner) vs 60% (stranger), p=0.22; gaze alternation 62% vs 52%; with owner positive message: approach fan in 28.84 s vs 54.21 s (negative), p=0.001; touch 35.1 s vs 55.44 s, p=0.002.
findings.relevance: Defines CHECK_IN: look at novel stimulus -> look at owner -> approach/avoid conditioned on owner valence (from voice/face); owner identity matters (owner model).

findings.claim: Canonical result: after learning a manipulation task, dogs facing an insoluble version look/gaze at the human while similarly socialized wolves do not; authors propose the dogs' readiness to look at the human face as the key dog-wolf difference.
findings.source_title: A simple reason for a big difference: wolves do not look back at humans, but dogs do (Miklosi et al.), Current Biology 13:763-766, PMID 12725735
findings.numbers: Abstract only (no N/latencies retrievable); described by Marshall-Pescini 2017 as 4-month-old pet dogs vs same-age pet-raised wolves, dogs looking back 'sooner and for longer'. Companion 2015 study (PMC4614426): 10 pet, 10 shelter dogs, 10 wolves on a solvable box: wolves 80% success vs 5% dogs.
findings.relevance: Origin of the 'look back when it cannot solve the task' behavior the owner asked for.

findings.claim: The 'dog-laugh' is a breathy pronounced forced exhalation produced almost exclusively during play and friendly greeting; it initiates play (listeners respond with play-face, chase or play-bow, whether the producer is dog or human), and recorded playback in a shelter reduced stress behaviors and noise.
findings.source_title: Dog-laughter: Recorded playback reduces stress related behavior in shelter dogs (Simonet, Versteeg, Storie), Proc. 7th Int. Conf. on Environmental Enrichment
findings.numbers: 120 shelter dogs (4 mo-10 y), 6 Sundays, within-subject cross-over, 40-min sessions, 3 min per dog x 3 passes x 3 observers, 2 blind coders, 22-code ethogram; fans 74 dB, playback 84 dB; peak noise 120 dB -> 96 dB; social orienting t=-7.41 p=.0123; silence t=-7.01 p=.0121; play-bow t=-7.31 p=.0123; dog-laugh t=-7.11 p=.013; play-face t=-7.41 p=.0123; puppies answered with play-bows and laughs, dogs >2 y sat/lay down.
findings.relevance: Primary description of what Parcel's 'chuckle' should sound like and do: a play-initiating, affiliative pant, not a humor response.

findings.claim: Confirmation with modern acoustics: dogs produce a domain-specific play pant almost absent during training and rest; it co-occurs with play behaviors (play bow, tickling, cuddling) and is operationally 0-4 kHz, 0.1-0.3 s bursts with no harmonic bands.
findings.source_title: Dogs produce distinctive play pants: Confirming Simonet (Volsche, Gunnip, Brown, Kiperash, Root-Gutteridge, Horowitz), International Journal of Comparative Psychology 35, DOI 10.46867/ijcp.2023.35.5620 (CC BY 4.0)
findings.numbers: 16 dyads, N=14 viable; training ~2 min, play 5-10 min, rest 5 min; inter-rater ICC alpha=0.967 (95% CI 0.942-0.983); 353 target vocalizations averaged across raters, 330 co-occurring with play (R1 96.6%, R2 90.2%); ANOVA across contexts F(2,39)=5.897, p=.006; training p=.018, rest p=.013 fewer; play pants vs play behaviors rs(42)=0.998; only 23 outside play phase, 3 unlinked to play/contact.
findings.relevance: Gives the chuckle audio spec and its trigger statistics (play frame + affiliative contact); the learnable part is which owner cues predict that frame (laughter, playful prosody, petting, play invitations).

findings.claim: Play bows are visual signals sent only when the partner can see, and their main function is to re-initiate play after a pause; the 'clarify misinterpretable bite' hypothesis was not supported in puppies.
findings.source_title: Investigating the Function of Play Bows in Dog and Wolf Puppies (Byosiere et al.), PLoS ONE 11(12):e0168570
findings.numbers: 10 dog puppies (2-5 mo), 15 wolf puppies (2.7-7.8 mo); 136 dog bows, 69 wolf bows; 135/136 (99%) dog bows and 69/69 wolf bows with visual access; bites near bows 13.6% (dogs) / 10.1% (wolves); pauses before bows > after in dog puppies.
findings.relevance: PLAY_BOW trigger: play had been happening, a lull occurs, and the owner is facing the dog.

findings.claim: Dogs send play signals almost exclusively to forward-facing partners and use attention-getting behaviors when the partner faces away, scaling the attention-getter's strength to the partner's inattentiveness.
findings.source_title: Attention to attention in domestic dog (Canis familiaris) dyadic play (Horowitz), Animal Cognition, PMID 18679727
findings.numbers: Abstract-level (natural dyadic rough-and-tumble play; head direction and sequential behaviors coded); no N in abstract.
findings.relevance: Defines the audience-gating rule and the graded ATTENTION_GETTER ladder (soft -> strong) keyed to an owner-attention estimate; a small learnable policy with reward = owner orients.

findings.claim: A robotic dog replica with a single lateralized tail-wag parameter changes how real dogs approach it: dogs approached continuously more often for a left-biased wag than a right-biased wag, replicated across two seasons and dog sizes.
findings.source_title: Behavioural responses of dogs to asymmetrical tail wagging of a robotic dog replica (Artelle, Dumoulin, Reimchen), Laterality, DOI 10.1080/13576500903386700
findings.numbers: Life-size Labrador model, tail amplitude 0-45 deg at 2.5 Hz; 2008: 74 trials, left wag 56% continuous approach vs right wag 31% (chi2=4.66, p=.031); 2009: 198 left / 180 right trials, 37.4% vs 27.8% (p=.047); excluding trials with owners/other dogs 129/107 trials 41.1% vs 28.0% (p=.037); >450 interactions; 15% barked (no side effect). Summarizes Quaranta et al. 2007: right-biased wag for owner/humans/cat, left-biased for unfamiliar dog/neutral.
findings.relevance: Evidence that one expressive DOF with a lateral bias is read by observers; supports a right-biased WIGGLE for approach contexts on a tail-less Go2 (body sway).

findings.claim: Naive people reliably recognize happy dog body language but not fearful; fear recognition rises from about 30% to over 70% with professional experience, and ears are the feature experts use most.
findings.source_title: Human Perception of Fear in Dogs Varies According to Experience with Dogs (Wan, Bolger, Champagne), PLoS ONE 7(12):e51775
findings.numbers: N=2,163 (7% low-experience, 68% owners, 14% professionals <10 y, 11% professionals 10+ y); 9 videos (5 happy, 4 fearful); P(fearful) .30 low-experience to >.70 professionals; P(happy) .90-.93 all groups; ears cited ~80% (professionals) vs ~40% (low-experience) for fearful clips; experienced viewers use ~1 more of 5 features.
findings.relevance: Evaluation design: recruit dog-experienced raters for fear/appeasement states; a Go2 without ears will be under-read on negative states, so carry them with whole-body cues and sound.

findings.claim: Dog facial expressions are subject to audience effects: dogs produce significantly more facial movements when a human is attentive than when turned away, while food (arousing but non-social) has no effect.
findings.source_title: Human attention affects facial expressions in domestic dogs (Kaminski, Hynds, Morris, Waller), Scientific Reports, PMID 29051517
findings.numbers: Abstract-level; attentive vs turned-away demonstrator x food/no food.
findings.relevance: Second audience-effect result: expressive output should be gated by the owner's attention state, not emitted into the void.

findings.claim: Shelter dogs that raise the inner brow (DogFACS AU101) more often are rehomed faster; tail-wagging duration was associated with slower rehoming.
findings.source_title: Paedomorphic Facial Expressions Give Dogs a Selective Advantage (Waller et al.), PLoS ONE 8(12):e82686
findings.numbers: 27 bull-breed shelter dogs, 4 UK shelters, 2-min encounter; AU101 power-curve R2=0.39; 5 AU101 -> ~49.83 days, 10 -> ~34.88, 15 -> ~28.31 days to rehoming.
findings.relevance: Caution: dogs' strongest human-appeal signal is facial and unavailable to a Go2; 'more wagging' is not automatically more likeable.

findings.claim: Adult dogs show attachment to their owner in a modified Ainsworth Strange Situation Test; the human-dog relationship factors into Anxiety, Acceptance and Attachment and dogs can be classified secure/insecure.
findings.source_title: Attachment behavior in dogs (Canis familiaris): a new application of Ainsworth's (1969) Strange Situation Test (Topal, Miklosi, Csanyi, Doka), Journal of Comparative Psychology, PMID 9770312
findings.numbers: 51 owner-dog pairs; 3 factors; 5 clusters; no effect of gender, age, living conditions or breed on most variables.
findings.relevance: An off-the-shelf behavioral evaluation protocol (owner leaves/stranger/owner returns) for greeting, proximity-seeking and exploration behaviors of the companion robot.

findings.claim: At reunion, physical+verbal contact from the familiar person produces a sustained oxytocin rise and larger cortisol decrease and more dog-initiated contact and lip licking; verbal-only contact elicits tail wagging and vocalizations first.
findings.source_title: Dogs' endocrine and behavioural responses at reunion are affected by how the human initiates contact (Rehn, Handlin, Uvnas-Moberg, Keeling), Physiology & Behavior, PMID 24471179
findings.numbers: 12 female beagles; treatments physical+verbal (PV), verbal (V), control (C); oxytocin elevated after PV even post-interaction; cortisol decrease largest in PV. (Rehn & Keeling 2011 on greeting intensity vs 0.5/2/4 h alone: OpenAlex record DOI 10.1016/j.applanim.2010.11.015, 113 citations; abstract not retrievable this session.)
findings.relevance: GREET_OWNER should scale with absence duration and adapt to the owner's greeting style (touch vs voice), using the owner model.

findings.claim: Sony's AIBO architecture was built on a canine ethogram (Scott and Fox): 12 behavioral subsystems organized into modes and modules, homeostatic drives (6 internal variables) with releasing mechanisms, a 3-D emotion space (pleasant, arousal, confidence) hosting Ekman's 6 emotions, and lateral-inhibition action selection.
findings.source_title: An ethological and emotional basis for human-robot interaction (Arkin, Fujita, Takagi, Hasegawa), Robotics and Autonomous Systems 42:191-201
findings.numbers: Subsystems: Investigative, Epimeletic, Et-epimeletic, Allelomimetic, Agonistic, Sexual, Eliminative, Ingestive, Comfort-seeking, Miscellaneous Motor, Play, Maladaptive; Agonistic modes: Fighting-Predation, Defense-Escape, Dominant/Subordinate Attitude; Defense-Escape modules: Sitting, Crouching, Running away, Yelping, Tail between legs, Defensive rolling, Move away, Seek out human, Hair raising; internal variables nourishment, moisture, bladder distension, tiredness, curiosity, affection; instinct variables hunger, thirst, elimination, tiredness, curiosity, affection; behavior value V[I]=f(RM[I], Mot[I]); 3 subsystems implemented (investigative, ingestive, play); 3 detectable objects; 282 citations (OpenAlex).
findings.relevance: Reference architecture for 'state of the world -> behavior': drives + affect + releasers -> arbiter over an ethogram tree; Parcel's reaction arbiter should grow into this with learned thresholds.

findings.claim: MiRo's biomimetic controller represents affect as valence x arousal driven by touch, sound/light and a circadian clock, expresses it through ears/tail/eyelids/lights/voice and by scaling movement speed and posture height, and selects among orient/avert/approach/flee plans from a salience map with a basal-ganglia model.
findings.source_title: MIRO: A Robot 'Mammal' with a Biomimetic Brain-Based Control System (Mitchinson, Prescott), Living Machines 2016, LNCS 9793
findings.numbers: DOF: 3 neck (lift, pitch, yaw), 2 per ear (curl, rotate), 2 tail (droop, wag), 1 eyelids; stereo cameras/mics, sonar, 8 capacitive touch sensors, 4 light, 2 cliff, accelerometers; processors P1 spinal (Cortex M0) ~10 ms, P2 brainstem (M0/M4) ~30 ms, P3 forebrain (A8) ~50-200 ms, off-board 100 ms+; stroking raises valence, head strike lowers it; loud sound raises arousal and lowers valence; low arousal slows movement and lowers neck posture.
findings.relevance: Two directly portable ideas for a neck-less Go2: arousal scales velocity and body height continuously; a salience map plus orient/avert/approach/flee plans with persistent selection fits the 50 Hz body-intent lane.

findings.claim: Sony's current aibo (ERS-1000) is documented with four desires (affection, curiosity, sleep, show feelings), emotions (delight, anger, sorrow, pleasure; sadness when no one to play with; surprise at loud sounds), autonomous behaviors (explore territory, memorize faces, approach, play, self-charge), voice-triggered tricks, and about 3 years of staged growth shaped by praise and scolding.
findings.source_title: aibo (ERS-1000) Help Guide: aibo's desires and emotions (plus pages TP0001970093, TP0001970095, TP0001970101)
findings.numbers: 4 desires; 4 named emotions; ~3 years infancy to maturity; documented commands: Hand/Shake hands, Sit down, Lay down, Let's dance, Learn this, You got it, Don't forget, Show me your new trick, Stop, Show me your face, Come on, Take a picture, Charging station, Pass me the bone, Kick the ball, Look for the ball; praise phrases -> positive reactions, scolding -> sad reactions; expression via eye, ear, tail movement and voice tones.
findings.relevance: The only readable vendor behavior list for a commercial robot dog; shows the layering drives -> emotions -> autonomous repertoire -> mood-gated tricks, versus Parcel's current fixed trick list.

findings.claim: Primary-school children attribute intentions equally well to a Unitree Go1 and a zoomorphic Miro-E, but emotions better to Miro-E (ears, tail); children preferred the Go1 overall.
findings.source_title: Does a 'robot dog' need legs, ears, and tail? A comparative analysis of intention- and emotion-attribution to Miro-E and Unitree Go1 (Lakatos et al.), Biologia Futura, PMID 40461921, DOI 10.1007/s42977-025-00263-5
findings.numbers: 111 children aged 7-10; identical scenarios on both robots; no significant intention-attribution difference; Miro-E better on emotion; Go1 preferred.
findings.relevance: Platform-level guidance: invest Go2 expressiveness in intention readability (anticipation, gaze proxies, approach/retreat) and compensate on emotion with sound, lights and whole-body posture.

findings.claim: Canine-inspired movements on a quadruped were recognized above the average rate reported for robotic body-gesture emotion expression for 'alert', 'neutral' and 'yes/agree'; prior experience with robots or dogs did not affect recognition.
findings.source_title: Conveying Emotion and Intention through Quadruped Robotic Motion: A Validation Study Using Canine-Inspired Movements (Yang, Biernacka, Bruno), IEEE RO-MAN 2025
findings.numbers: 35 participants; recognizable set alert/neutral/yes-agree; KIT SARAI lab.
findings.relevance: First RO-MAN validation of canine-inspired quadruped motion; the recognizable states are intention-like, consistent with Lakatos 2025.

findings.claim: Robot animation should follow 12 adapted principles: Squash and Stretch, Anticipation, Intention (Staging), Animated/Procedural/Ad-hoc Action, Slow In/Out, Arcs, Exaggeration, Secondary Action and Idle Behavior, Asymmetry, Expectation (Appeal), Timing, Follow-Through/Overlapping; timing correlates with perceived arousal and idle 'breathing' plus asymmetry sustain the illusion of life.
findings.source_title: Nutty-based Robot Animation: Principles and Practices (Ribeiro, Paiva), arXiv 1904.02898 (extends Ribeiro & Paiva, HRI 2012 'The Illusion of Robotic Life')
findings.numbers: 12 principles; demonstrated on NAO and EMYS; anticipation example: 10-degree pre-rotation before a 90-degree turn; van Breemen's 'Merging Logic' = slow in/out; follow-through flagged as unsafe for most robots.
findings.relevance: Design vocabulary for Parcel's expression layer; highest-payoff additions on a quadruped: Anticipation, Intention (face the target first), Asymmetry, Timing-as-arousal, slow-in/out filtering on the body-intent lane.

findings.claim: Showing forethought (anticipation) before a task and a goal-oriented reaction after it makes a robot seem more appealing, approachable and confident, even though forethought did not improve literal task readability; success vs failure changes perceived competence.
findings.source_title: Expressing Thought: Improving Robot Readability with Animation Principles (Takayama, Dooley, Ju), HRI 2011
findings.numbers: N=273 online; PR2 video prototypes, 4 tasks; forethought: sureness 5.69 vs 5.20 (F(1,255)=15.95, p<.00001), appeal 4.83 vs 4.27 (F(1,265)=16.51, p<.0001), approachability 5.05 vs 4.54 (F(1,262)=12.48); keyword-match readability n.s. (F(1,271)=0.65, p=.42) but task-dependent (0.84 door, 0.78 power, 0.64 drink, 0.29 ushering); reaction: confidence 4.53 vs 4.14 (F(1,267)=7.51, p<.007); competence after success 4.68 vs failure 3.86.
findings.relevance: Every Parcel behavior should be emitted as anticipation -> action -> reaction; 'look back when lost' is itself a reaction-to-failure display.

findings.claim: Eight animation principles can be implemented as continuous parametric modulations of Dynamic Movement Primitives, and users recognize the six resulting emotional expressions above chance and perceive intensity changes correctly for every principle.
findings.source_title: Interactive Expressive Motion Generation Using Dynamic Movement Primitives (Hielscher, Bulling, Arras), IROS 2025, arXiv 2504.06735
findings.numbers: Principles: Arc, Anticipation, Slow In/Out, Timing, Exaggeration, Secondary Action, Follow Through, Randomization; expressions Joy, Sadness, Anger, Fear, Shame, Hurry; platforms KUKA iiwa (sim), Pepper 17 DoF, Daryl 10 DoF; N=34 (ages 20-60); recognition above chance p<.05; intensity perception p<.05 for all principles.
findings.relevance: A training-free way to expose animation principles as a low-dimensional style action space over Go2 velocity/pose intents.

findings.claim: Disney's bipedal robotic character splits expressive control into an animation engine (perpetual, periodic and episodic motions blended from background, triggered and joystick layers) and an RL tracking policy trained with PPO to execute artist motions robustly on hardware.
findings.source_title: Design and Control of a Bipedal Robotic Character (Grandia, Knoop, Hopkins, Wiedebach, Bishop, Pickles, Muller, Bacher), Disney Research / Walt Disney Imagineering, RSS 2024, arXiv 2501.05204
findings.numbers: 14 actuated DoF (5 per leg + 4 neck/head) + 2 DoF antennas, 15.4 kg, 0.66 m; PPO in Isaac Gym, 8192 envs x 24 steps, 100,000 iterations (~22 days on RTX 4090); 50 Hz policy, 600 Hz actuator bus; joint-tracking weights legs 15, neck 100, survival bonus 20; MAE standing 0.035 rad, walking 0.123 rad, episodic 0.027-0.043 rad; 0.7 m/s forward, 0.4 m/s lateral, 1.8 rad/s turn.
findings.relevance: State-of-the-art recipe for artist-directed expressive motion plus learned robustness; maps onto Parcel's behavior catalog + expression layer over sport mode now and a learned tracker later.

findings.claim: An artist-made expressive clip library on a consumer robot dog (Sony aibo) can be compressed into one RL policy (Deep Fourier Mimic) that blends dances while also doing locomotion and gaze control on hardware.
findings.source_title: DFM: Deep Fourier Mimic for Expressive Dance Motion Learning (Watanabe, Li, Hutter), ICRA 2025, arXiv 2502.10980
findings.numbers: aibo 14 DoF (12 legs + 2 head); 170 clips = 34 dances x 5 speeds (0.5-1.5x), 6 s each; PAE/FLD with prediction horizon N=0; PPO in Isaac Gym, 3x256 MLP, 400 Hz sim / 100 Hz control, 5,000 iterations; tracking MAE 0.094 rad vs 0.132 (FLD); 0.5 s transitions.
findings.relevance: Shows the path from a fixed trick list to a blendable learned expressive policy on a small quadruped; dataset is Sony-proprietary.

findings.claim: Multi-Domain Motion Embedding lets legged robots mimic expressive human and dog motion in real time from a small mocap set, trained with PPO in IsaacLab and deployed zero-shot on quadruped and humanoid hardware.
findings.source_title: Multi-Domain Motion Embedding: Expressive Real-Time Mimicry for Legged Robots (Heyrman, Li, Klemm, Kang, Coros, Hutter), arXiv 2512.07673
findings.numbers: ANYmal D quadruped, Unitree H1 (sim), Fourier N1 (hardware); dog mocap ~10 min augmented to ~52 min; 32-D variational latent + wavelet entropy (13 quadruped / 7 humanoid) + periodic channels (25/15); PPO IsaacLab 30,000 iterations (ANYmal), 24 steps/env, 50 Hz; beats VMP and PAE baselines.
findings.relevance: Closest open recipe for 'dog motion -> quadruped in real time'; code/weight release not confirmed in the text read.

findings.claim: Kine2Go is an openly licensed kinematic dataset of Unitree Go2 gaits generated by RL policies from multi-morphology mocap, intended for motion-conditioned policy learning and behavioral cloning.
findings.source_title: Kine2Go: Kinematic dataset for the Unitree Go2 robot with diverse gaits and motions (Palucki, Siwak, Ciebiera, Cygan), University of Warsaw, arXiv 2606.14433
findings.numbers: 800 trajectories from 40 policies (20 rollouts each, 5-20 s); walk/trot/run/turn/spin/canter/pace/strafe, figure-eight/circle/square paths, crawl (Solo8-derived), horse trot/walk; 60 Hz control with 4x decimation; per-frame joint pos/vel, base quaternion/angular velocity, actions, global positions; CC BY 4.0; excludes jumps and sitting; flat terrain only.
findings.relevance: Immediate Go2 locomotion-style prior for gait-level expressiveness; not for episodic expressive actions.

findings.claim: The Godspeed Questionnaire Series (anthropomorphism, animacy, likeability, perceived intelligence, perceived safety; 5-point semantic differentials) is the de-facto standard HRI perception instrument, with documented reliability ranges and known limits.
findings.source_title: Godspeed Questionnaire Series: Translations and Usage (Bartneck), Springer International Handbook of Behavioral Health Assessment, DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-89738-3_24-1 (plus Bartneck et al. 2009 item page and Weiss & Bartneck 2015 meta-analysis)
findings.numbers: Animacy items: Dead/Alive, Stagnant/Lively, Mechanical/Organic, Artificial/Lifelike, Inert/Interactive, Apathetic/Responsive; original alphas anthropomorphism 0.87-0.92, animacy 0.70, likeability 0.86-0.92, perceived intelligence 0.75-0.76; Ho & MacDorman 2010 ~0.92/~0.88/0.6 (safety); Stroessner 2020 anthropomorphism 0.86-0.93, animacy 0.70-0.76, likeability 0.84-0.92, intelligence 0.75-0.92, safety 0.91; 19 languages; 1,852 citations by 2022; 2015 meta-analysis: 160 citing papers, 69 empirical, 21 same hardware, 18 studies analysed; Hauser et al. 2023 (n=26/22): Godspeed largely insensitive in incidental quadruped encounters.
findings.relevance: Default believability instrument for Parcel sessions (Animacy, Likeability, Perceived Safety), paired with behavioral/physiological measures because it can miss effects in short encounters.

findings.claim: RoSAS measures social perception of robots on 18 items in three factors (Warmth, Competence, Discomfort) and has been validated for physical human-robot interaction.
findings.source_title: Validation of the Robot Social Attributes Scale (RoSAS) for Human-Robot Interaction through a Human-to-Robot Handover Use Case (Pan, Croft, Niemeyer), UBC/Disney Research (validating Carpinella et al., HRI 2017)
findings.numbers: Warmth: Organic, Sociable, Emotional, Compassionate, Happy, Feeling; Competence: Reliable, Competent, Knowledgeable, Interactive, Responsive, Capable; Discomfort: Awkward, Scary, Strange, Awful, Dangerous, Aggressive; 22 participants (11 F, ages 22-52), KUKA iiwa handovers; original RoSAS paper 682 citations (Semantic Scholar).
findings.relevance: Warmth is the closest measure of 'companion-ness' and Discomfort the safety counterpart for a 15 kg quadruped; use alongside Godspeed.

findings.claim: On a constrained low-DoF expressive body, viewers recover coarse valence and arousal about two-thirds of the time but exact emotion labels only about 30%, with anger, interest and sadness far more recognizable than love, pleasure, shame or disgust.
findings.source_title: Emotional Expression in Low-Degrees-of-Freedom Robots: Assessing Perception with Reachy Mini (Rogel, Yadollahi, Laban), arXiv 2605.12786
findings.numbers: 100 participants, within-subjects, 10 clips (6-DoF head + rotating base + antennae + non-verbal audio, Laban-mapped); exact accuracy 30.5% overall: Anger 81.8%, Interest 62.2%, Sadness 55.0%, Amusement 43.4%, Fear 39.8%, Pleasure 3.1%, Shame 2.0%, Love 1.0%, Disgust 0%; valence recovered 65.9%, arousal 67.8%; RoSAS warmth + HRIES animacy used.
findings.relevance: Calibrates expectations and metrics for a face-less Go2: target and measure valence/arousal readability plus a few discrete whole-body states (alert, content, playful, fearful).

findings.claim: The Unitree Go2 SportClient exposes its expressive actions as opaque one-shot RPCs with fixed api_ids and no documented descriptions, durations or blending; only Move is a no-reply streaming call.
findings.source_title: unitree_sdk2_python sport_api.py (SPORT_API_ID constants) plus unitree_sdk2 sport_client.hpp and example go2_sport_client.py
findings.numbers: IDs: Damp 1001, BalanceStand 1002, StopMove 1003, StandUp 1004, StandDown 1005, RecoveryStand 1006, Euler 1007, Move 1008, Sit 1009, RiseSit 1010, SpeedLevel 1015, Hello 1016, Stretch 1017, Content 1020, Dance1 1022, Dance2 1023, SwitchJoystick 1027, Pose 1028, Scrape 1029, FrontFlip 1030, FrontJump 1031, FrontPounce 1032, Heart 1036, StaticWalk 1061, TrotRun 1062, EconomicGait 1063, LeftFlip 2041, BackFlip 2043, HandStand 2044, FreeWalk 2045, FreeBound 2046, FreeJump 2047, FreeAvoid 2048, ClassicWalk 2049, WalkUpright 2050, CrossStep 2051, AutoRecovery 2054/2055, SwitchAvoidMode 2058; header has zero doc comments; example sleeps 1 s between actions and 2-4 s around flag gaits; WiggleHips/Wallow absent from current header and ID list; official support pages are JS-rendered and unreadable; DeepWiki descriptions are AI-generated.
findings.relevance: Episodic Go2 clips must be measured on hardware and treated as non-modulable episodic animations; learned modulation today lives in continuous channels (Euler, body height, speed level, gait, Move).

findings.claim: Purposeful quadruped navigation around people raises physiological stress more than search behavior, and multiple robots more than one, measured with ECG/EDA on Spot and Go1.
findings.source_title: Human Stress Response and Perceived Safety during Encounters with Quadruped Robots (Gupta, Shin, Norman, Stephens, Lu, Sentis), arXiv 2403.17270
findings.numbers: Boston Dynamics Spot and Unitree Go1; ECG + EDA + self-report; 8 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables; no effect sizes in abstract.
findings.relevance: Approach behaviors need anticipation/slow-in and readable intent; physiological measures are a usable objective complement to questionnaires in Parcel evaluations.

findings.claim: C-BARQ is a validated owner-report instrument of dog temperament (not an ethogram) whose factors provide a personality-parameter vocabulary (excitability, attachment/attention-seeking, nonsocial fear, energy, trainability).
findings.source_title: C-BARQ (Canine Behavioral Assessment and Research Questionnaire), University of Pennsylvania; Hsu & Serpell 2003 JAVMA (PMID 14621216)
findings.numbers: Development: 1,851 dogs + 203 clinical cases; 152 items -> 68 items, 11 factors, 57% variance; current site: 14 categories + 22 miscellaneous items; ~50,000 pet dogs, 300+ breeds; 35,000+ assistance-dog assessments.
findings.relevance: Expose C-BARQ-style traits as tunable drives/personality knobs in Parcel's owner-facing settings rather than as behaviors.

design_implications: LOOK_BACK has a precise definition: emit when a per-task persistence budget is exhausted with the owner present (Marshall-Pescini 2017); direct it at the person who can help (89-96% of dog gazes go to the owner who controls the resource, Hirschi 2022); make it sooner/longer when the owner has helped before (reinforcement history, Lazzaroni 2020). On a neck-less Go2 the gaze proxy is StopMove + body yaw toward the owner + Euler pitch-up, optionally alternating between obstacle and owner (gaze alternation, Merola 2012). The persistence threshold and the help-history weight are the learnable quantities; reward = owner responds (speech/approach) within a window.

CHUCKLE is the dog-laugh/play pant, not a humor detector: a breathy forced exhalation, 0-4 kHz, 0.1-0.3 s bursts, no harmonics (Volsche 2023), produced almost only in a play/affiliative frame (93% co-occurrence with play behaviors) and itself an invitation to play (Simonet 2005). Fix the audio primitive; learn the trigger P(chuckle | play frame, high arousal, positive valence, owner attentive), with owner laughter, playful prosody, petting/tickle touch, human play bow and whisper as releasers; a 'funny joke' enters through the conversation LLM's valence/arousal estimate. Evaluate by whether the owner answers with more play.

Adopt the AIBO/MiRo architecture: homeostatic drives (affection, curiosity, fatigue) + 2-3-D affect (valence, arousal, confidence) + perception releasers -> lateral-inhibition/basal-ganglia selection over an ethogram tree (Arkin 2003, Mitchinson & Prescott 2016). Parcel's reaction arbiter and owner model already hold most pieces; add a persistent drive/affect state updated by world events (stroke -> valence up; loud sound -> arousal up, valence down; long owner absence -> affection drive up) and let affect modulate ALL motion continuously (arousal scales speed and body height; low arousal lowers posture) instead of only selecting from a trick list.

Audience-gate every expressive behavior: dogs send play bows only when the partner can see (99% of bows, Byosiere 2016), produce more facial expressions when the human is attentive (Kaminski 2017), and scale attention-getters to the partner's inattention (Horowitz 2009). Implement an owner-attention estimate (face orientation, engagement) that gates displays and drives a soft->strong ATTENTION_GETTER ladder; this is a small, cheaply learnable policy with reward = owner orients toward the dog.

Use the 12 robot-animation principles as the expression grammar (Ribeiro & Paiva 2019): wrap every behavior as [anticipation micro-move] -> [action] -> [reaction to outcome], which raises appeal 4.27->4.83, approachability 4.54->5.05 and confidence 4.14->4.53 on 7-point scales (Takayama 2011, N=273); add slow-in/out filtering, asymmetry and randomization to idle, use timing-as-arousal; expose principles as continuous DMP-style parameters (Hielscher 2025) as a low-dimensional style action space for a learned policy.

Design for the platform's perceptual reality: a Go1/Go2 body without ears/tail/face carries intention as well as a zoomorphic robot but emotion less well (Lakatos 2025, 111 children); naive adults read happy but not fearful dog body language and rely on ears (Wan 2012, N=2,163); low-DoF bodies convey valence/arousal ~66-68% but exact emotions ~30% (Rogel 2026, N=100). So target intention readability and valence/arousal, carry negative states with whole-body cues (crouch, retreat, lowered height) plus a motion-synchronized audio channel (pant, chuckle, whine; cf. Music Mode), and only claim a few discrete states (alert, content, playful, fearful).

Treat Go2 sport-mode expressive actions (Hello 1016, Stretch 1017, Content 1020, Dance1/2 1022/1023, Pose 1028, Scrape 1029, FrontFlip 1030, FrontJump 1031, FrontPounce 1032, Heart 1036, Sit/RiseSit 1009/1010, StandUp/Down 1004/1005) as opaque episodic clips with undocumented durations and no blending; measure each clip's duration and footprint on hardware, keep the deterministic safety layer as final authority over them, and put learned modulation in the continuous channels (Euler, body height, SpeedLevel, gait choice, Move). Follow the Disney split (animation engine composing perpetual/periodic/episodic motion + RL tracker) when replacing clips later; Kine2Go (CC BY 4.0) is an immediate Go2 gait-style prior.

Evaluation protocol per session: Godspeed (Animacy, Likeability, Perceived Safety) + RoSAS (18 items: warmth/competence/discomfort); 2-D valence/arousal clip ratings; a Strange-Situation-style behavioral protocol (owner leaves / stranger / owner returns) coding greeting intensity vs absence duration; a help-seeking readability test (owner watches the 'lost' episode and says what the dog wants); a play test (owner produces a play response within N s of a chuckle/bow); dog-experienced raters for fear/appeasement items; ECG/EDA when testing close-range approach; open-ended interviews because Godspeed can miss effects in short encounters (Hauser 2023).

Greeting and attachment are the next 'state of the world' behaviors after look-back: GREET_OWNER intensity should scale with absence duration and owner identity (owner model), and adapt to the owner's contact style (touch vs voice; Rehn 2014); the 51-pair Strange Situation factor structure (Anxiety, Acceptance, Attachment; Topal 1998) doubles as an evaluation rubric.

trainable_options.name: Drives+affect ethogram arbiter with learned thresholds (AIBO/MiRo-style)
trainable_options.what_it_is: A behavior-selection layer: homeostatic drives (affection, curiosity, fatigue), 2-3-D affect (valence, arousal, confidence) and perception releasers feeding lateral-inhibition / basal-ganglia selection over the 34-behavior catalog; the learnable parts are persistence budgets (LOOK_BACK), chuckle trigger probabilities, attention-getter escalation, and greeting intensity vs absence, trained by contextual bandit / small RL from owner-response rewards in sim and logs.
trainable_options.size_params: Tiny (dozens to thousands of parameters: thresholds, releaser weights, a small policy MLP)
trainable_options.inputs: World state: owner presence/attention, task/nav progress, touch events, sound level, owner voice valence/arousal from the conversation lane, time since owner seen, drive levels
trainable_options.outputs: Behavior id + continuous style parameters (speed level, body height, anticipation/exaggeration intensity, chuckle burst count)
trainable_options.train_recipe: Hand-set priors from the ethology numbers (e.g., look-back after persistence budget; bows only when owner facing), then online bandit/PPO fine-tuning with rewards = owner responds/orients/plays within a window; simulate owner responses with a scripted owner model in MuJoCo; replay owner-consented logs
trainable_options.license: Method-only (paper); Parcel-owned implementation
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Trivial: runs at 50 Hz on CPU alongside the body-intent lane

trainable_options.name: DMP-based expressive motion modulation (Hielscher, Bulling, Arras 2025)
trainable_options.what_it_is: Eight animation principles (arc, anticipation, slow in/out, timing, exaggeration, secondary action, follow-through, randomization) implemented as parametric modulations of Dynamic Movement Primitives; emotions built by tuning principle intensities; recognized above chance by 34 users.
trainable_options.size_params: No learned model required (parametric DMPs); optionally a small policy mapping affect -> principle intensities
trainable_options.inputs: A base trajectory (Go2 velocity/pose intent or Euler/body-height profile) plus a style vector (valence, arousal, intensities)
trainable_options.outputs: Modulated trajectory for the 50 Hz body-intent lane
trainable_options.train_recipe: No training for the modulation; learn the affect->style mapping by preference learning from owner ratings (valence/arousal readability) in sim/hardware
trainable_options.license: Not stated in the HTML read
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Trivial CPU cost

trainable_options.name: Disney-style animation engine + RL motion tracker (Grandia et al. 2025)
trainable_options.what_it_is: Artist/procedural animation engine blending perpetual (balance), periodic (gait) and episodic (expressive clips) motions, executed by a PPO tracking policy trained in Isaac Gym with actuator models; the reference recipe for expressive-yet-robust legged characters.
trainable_options.size_params: Small MLP policy (not stated); 14-DoF biped; training 100,000 PPO iterations, 8192 envs, ~22 days on an RTX 4090
trainable_options.inputs: Animation command signals (target poses/phases) + proprioception
trainable_options.outputs: Joint targets at 50 Hz
trainable_options.train_recipe: Retarget a Go2 expressive clip library (authored or from dog mocap) into per-clip phase-conditioned tracking rewards; PPO in Isaac Gym/IsaacLab or MuJoCo with domain randomization; ~weeks on the RTX 5000 Ada; requires low-level joint control on Go2 EDU+ (bypassing sport mode) and the safety layer as final authority
trainable_options.license: Method-only (Disney Research)
trainable_options.deploy_feasibility_orin: Feasible: 50 Hz MLP inference is cheap on Orin; the hard part is validating low-level control safely without hardware on hand

trainable_options.name: Deep Fourier Mimic (DFM) on Sony aibo (Watanabe, Li, Hutter 2025)
trainable_options.what_it_is: Fourier-latent (PAE/FLD) encoding of 170 artist dance clips + PPO tracking on a 14-DoF consumer robot dog, with smooth 0.5 s transitions and concurrent locomotion/gaze; tracking MAE 0.094 rad on hardware at 100 Hz.
trainable_options.size_params: 3x256 MLP policy; 5,000 PPO iterations in Isaac Gym; dataset 170 x 6 s clips (Sony-proprietary)
trainable_options.inputs: Latent phase/frequency parameters of the target clip + proprioception
trainable_options.outputs: Joint targets at 100 Hz
trainable_options.train_recipe: Build a Go2 clip library (retarget dog mocap or author in MuJoCo), train a PAE/FLD latent, then PPO tracking; blend clips by latent interpolation

open_questions: Go2 sport-mode expressive actions (Hello, Stretch, Content, Heart, Dance1/2, Pose, Scrape, FrontFlip, FrontJump, FrontPounce) have no documented durations, footprints, preconditions or interruptibility anywhere readable (official support pages are JS-rendered; SDK header has no comments); WiggleHips/Wallow are absent from the current header and ID list. Which firmware exposes them, and can they be aborted by StopMove/Damp mid-clip for the safety layer?

Can a neck-less quadruped's body-yaw + pitch 'look back' be read by owners as a gaze/help request? No study measured this on a Go1/Go2; Lakatos 2025 shows intention-attribution parity with Miro-E but did not test help-seeking specifically.

Miklosi 2003 primary numbers (N, latencies) and Rehn & Keeling 2011 greeting-vs-absence numbers, Bekoff 1995 bow-timing percentages, Byosiere 2016 adult-dog bow statistics, and Melson 2009 children/AIBO animacy percentages could not be retrieved this session (paywalls/403s); they are flagged as unread and should be pulled via institutional access before being cited.

Is a synthesized play pant (0-4 kHz, 0.1-0.3 s bursts) from a speaker perceived by owners as affiliative/playful rather than as machine noise, and does it elicit play responses as Simonet's playback did in dogs? Needs a small owner study.
Whether MDME/DFM code or weights are released, and whether any dog mocap dataset with a permissive license exists for retargeting to Go2; Kine2Go covers gaits only (no jumps/sits/expressive clips).

How much of the reference architectures' 'learning' should be online on the owner (aibo claims ~3 years of staged growth) versus offline in sim; and how to simulate owner responses (attention, laughter, touch) faithfully enough to train look-back/chuckle triggers before hardware arrives.

results.claim: In the unsolvable task, 'looking back' at the human is driven by giving up: less persistent animals look back sooner and longer regardless of species or socialization; when persistence is controlled, wolf-dog differences disappear. All 44 dogs (pack, pet, free-ranging) and 73% of wolves looked back at least once.
results.evidence_quote: "In the unsolvable trial, 11/15 wolves, all 14 WSC dogs, all 19 pets and all 11 free-ranging dogs looked back towards a human." ... "the longer an individual spent interacting with the apparatus, the longer it took for them to look back at a person (LM: F = 11.9, p = 0.001)" ... "when persistence is factored into the analyses, group differences in human-directed gazing behaviours do not emerge in our study populations but rather, regardless of group, the less persistent an animal, the sooner, longer and more frequently will it look back."
results.correction: All numbers check out (N = 15 wolves / 14 pack dogs / 19 pets / 11 free-ranging; 3 solvable + 1 unsolvable trial, each up to 3 min; 11/15 = 73% wolves; LM F = 11.9, p = 0.001 for latency; duration LM F = 33.4, p < 0.001; frequency GLM chi2 = 11.39, p < 0.001). Only wording note: the paper says 'regardless of group' (the four groups differ in species and in rearing/experience), which the claim renders as 'regardless of species or socialization'.

results.claim: Dog gazing at humans is a social problem-solving strategy only under some conditions: with an alternative reward still available, gazing correlates positively with continued effort (help-seeking); after the alternative is consumed it correlates negatively (giving up). Gazes go overwhelmingly to the person who controls the locked resource.
results.evidence_quote: "significant positive correlation between interacting with the box and gazing at people (rS = 0.51, p < 0.0001)" [until food consumed]; "negative correlation between interaction time with the box and duration of gazing at people (rS = -0.42, p = 0.001)" [entire 3 min]; "We calculated the proportion of gazing at the owner out of the total time gazing at the two people"; "total gaze duration during the 'toy in box' subtest (Group O: median proportion of gazing directed at the owner = 0.89; Group E: median = 0.48) ... 'food in box' subtest (Group O: median = 0.96; Group E: median = 0.54) ... box-related gazing (Group O: median = 0.92; Group E: median = 0.70) and toy-related gazing (Group O: median = 0.96; Group E: median = 0.30)"; abstract: "In the experimenter-responsible group, dogs preferentially directed box-related gazing (prior to or after looking at or interacting with the box) at the owner. Still, they gazed at the experimenter significantly longer than the owner-responsible group. Conversely, toy-related gazing was directed significantly more at the experimenter."
results.correction: The help-seeking/giving-up part and N = 56 (29 herding, 27 terriers), rs = 0.51 / -0.42 / 0.55, and 89-96% to the owner in the owner-responsible group are all supported. But '48-70% to the experimenter when she did' misreads Table 3: 0.48, 0.54, 0.70 and 0.30 are median proportions of gazing directed at the OWNER in the experimenter-responsible group. When the experimenter controlled the rewards, box-related (help-seeking) gazing still went mainly to the owner (median 70% owner / 30% experimenter; total gazing 48-54% owner), while toy-related (play) gazing went ~70% to the experimenter. So 'gazes go overwhelmingly to the person who controls the locked resource' holds only when that person is the owner; the paper's conclusion is that gaze target depends on both responsibility and the dog's current goal (help-seeking vs play) and on the relationship. Also, the negative correlation (rs = -0.42) is computed over the full 3-min trial, not strictly 'after consumption', and the authors interpret it as 'partly help-seeking and partly giving up'.

results.claim: Dogs socially reference their owner about an ambiguous object: most look at the object then referentially at the owner, and the owner's (not a stranger's) positive vs negative message changes approach latency and proximity.
results.evidence_quote: "Most dogs looked referentially at the informant, regardless of his/her identity." ... "Twenty-two of 29 (76%) dogs in the owner group (positive and negative) and 17 of 28 (60%) dogs in the stranger group (positive and negative) showed referential looking towards the informant. This difference was shown not to be significant (chi = 1.5; p = 0.22)." ... "When the informant was the owner, dogs in the negative group took longer to enter the Fan-zone than dogs in the positive group (mean owner-positive = 28.82 vs. owner-negative = 54.21, p = 0.001)." ... "dogs in the negative group took longer to interact with the fan than dogs in the positive group (mean owner-positive = 35.1 vs. owner-negative = 55.44, p = 0.002)." ... "Fewer differences in the dog's behaviour emerged when the informant was the stranger, suggesting that the dog-informant relationship may influence the dog's behavioural regulation."
results.correction: Numbers verified: 90 recruited, 57 analysed (29 owner / 28 stranger), 76% vs 60% (p = 0.22), gaze alternation 62% vs 52% (p = 0.5), touch 35.1 vs 55.44 s (p = 0.002). Two minor notes: (1) the paper itself prints the owner-positive Fan-zone latency as 28.84 s in one sentence (vs stranger-positive 50.97, p = 0.005) and 28.82 s in the owner-positive vs owner-negative sentence (vs 54.21, p = 0.001), so either figure is citable; (2) the paper phrases the stranger result as 'fewer differences' / 'no such difference emerged in the stranger group' for looking and Fan-zone time rather than reporting an explicit non-significant stranger-positive vs stranger-negative latency test.

results.claim: The 'dog-laugh' is a breathy pronounced forced exhalation produced almost exclusively during play and friendly greeting; it initiates play (listeners respond with play-face, chase or play-bow, whether the producer is dog or human), and recorded playback in a shelter reduced stress behaviors and noise.
results.evidence_quote: "During play encounters dogs vocalize using at least four distinct patterns; barks, growls, whines, and a breathy pronounced forced exhalation (dog-laugh) (Simonet, 2001). Further, dog-laughs are used to initiate play. Upon hearing a dog-laugh subjects use a play-face and chase or play-bow with the individual producing the dog-laugh, whether the individual is dog or human (Simonet, 2001)." ... "only the laugh appears to be exclusively produced during play and friendly greetings, and not during other encounters." ... "One Hundred twenty subject dogs ranged from 4 months of age to 10 years of age." ... "The ambient sound level of the shelter with fans running and no dogs was 74dB. During the playback and no dogs the ambient noise was 84dB." ... "The ambient noise level decreased from 120dB at the peak during baseline to 96dB at peak during playback." ... "S (social orienting to front of kennel), t = -7.41, p = .0123, Q (silence), t = -7.01, p = .0121, and play behaviors (play-bow - PB, dog-laugh - DL, and play face - PF), t = -7.31, p = .0123, t = -7.11, p = .013, t = -7.41, p = .0123, respectively." ... "The young puppies (approximately 4-12 months of age) offered play-bows and dog-laugh vocalizations during the playback. ... Dogs over 2 years of age oriented to the sound or the experimenter and assumed the down or sit position."
results.correction: All listed numbers verified against the PDF text (120 dogs, 4 mo-10 y, six Sundays, within-subjects cross-over, 40-min periods, 3 min per dog repeated three times by three observers, two blind coders, Table 1 has exactly 22 codes, 74/84 dB, 120 -> 96 dB peak, all five t/p values, puppy vs >2 y responses). Caveat for weight-bearing use: the 'exclusively during play and friendly greeting' and 'initiates play whether dog or human' statements are carried over from the authors' own 2001 conference work rather than tested here, the source is a non-peer-reviewed enrichment-conference proceedings paper, and the t-tests are reported on a 34-dog 'sample' table rather than all 120 dogs.

results.claim: Confirmation with modern acoustics: dogs produce a domain-specific play pant almost absent during training and rest; it co-occurs with play behaviors (play bow, tickling, cuddling) and is operationally 0-4 kHz, 0.1-0.3 s bursts with no harmonic bands.
results.evidence_quote: "a domain-specific 'play pant,' which was almost completely absent during training and rest. These vocalizations mostly co-occurred with play behaviors (e.g., play bow) or tickling and cuddling." ... "We can now define the canine play pant as including frequencies between 0-4 kHz; of length between 0.1 and 0.3 s; featuring large, irregular oscillating waveforms and high amplitudes; absent of harmonic bands" ... "A total of 16 dogs participated ... leaving us with N = 14 viable recordings." ... "practicing known training cues (on average, 2 min), play until the human or dog disengaged (approximately 5-10 min), and a timed, 5-min shared rest." ... "(alpha = 0.967) with a 95% confidence interval from 0.942-0.983" ... "a total of 353 target vocalizations were recorded, and an average of 330 of those co-occurred with a play behavior or activity. A one-way ANOVA ... F(2, 39) = 5.897, p = .006. A Tukey post hoc test revealed that significantly fewer 'play pants' occurred during training (p = .018 ...) and shared rest (p = .013 ...)" ... "rs (42) = 0.998, p < .001. Of the average 353 target vocalizations recorded, only 23 occurred outside the play phase and only three were not associated with a play behavior, play activities, or direct human-to-dog contact (e.g., tickling)."
results.correction: All numbers verified against the PDF text (16 dyads, N = 14; R1 96.6%, R2 90.2%; ICC alpha 0.967, CI 0.942-0.983; F(2,39) = 5.897, p = .006; training p = .018, rest p = .013; rs(42) = 0.998; 23 outside play, 3 unlinked). The authors describe it as a pilot study with a small sample; note the play-pant/play-behaviour rs of 0.998 is a correlation of per-session counts.

results.claim: Dogs send play signals almost exclusively to forward-facing partners and use attention-getting behaviors when the partner faces away, scaling the attention-getter's strength to the partner's inattentiveness.
results.evidence_quote: "Play signals were sent nearly exclusively to forward-facing conspecifics" ... "attention-getting behaviors were used most often when a playmate was facing away" ... "stronger attention-getters were used when a playmate was looking away or distracted, less forceful ones when the partner was facing forward or laterally" (Horowitz, Animal Cognition 2009, PMID 18679727).
results.correction: Abstract-level support only, as the claim's 'numbers' field already acknowledges; the Europe PMC record confirms journal (Animal Cognition), year (2009) and PMID 18679727. No sample size is given in the abstract.

gaps.gap: MoshiVis is cited only as an open question, yet it is the concrete precedent for injecting non-speech world state into a duplex model. Spot-check (arXiv 2503.15633 HTML): 206M trainable adapter params, PaliGemma-2 ~400M vision encoder, gate = 2-layer MLP (1/8 hidden) + sigmoid on the self-attention output, +7 ms per inference step on an L4 (51 ms/step at start, 59 ms at 5-min context, under the 80 ms budget at 12.5 Hz), MOSNet 3.59 vs 3.34 for base Moshi; inference code at github.com/kyutai-labs/moshivis (weights license not stated in the paper).
gaps.why_it_matters: It answers the digest's open question about adapter-vs-prompt conditioning with numbers: a gated cross-attention adapter over a world-state feature (owner-visible, DoA, track-loss, memory summary) costs ~7 ms/step and preserves speech quality, which is the recommended path for 'look back when lost'.
gaps.suggested_query: MoshiVis kyutai-labs moshivis weights license gated cross-attention adapter Moshi 2503.15633 huggingface

strongest_designs: A. Native-duplex 'Moshi + act stream' (desktop-trained, hosted-fallback): start from Moshi-7B / PersonaPlex-7B (or personaplex-rl-seamless if its license allows) and add one rate-limited discrete behaviour stream to the Depth Transformer (Moshi-Face / MoshiRAG / DuplexSLA pattern: a small codebook of Go2 primitives such as chuckle, play-bow, look-back-yaw, ear/idle modulations, plus a no-op token) decoded at 12.5 Hz or every 160 ms chunk; inject world state two ways — a refreshed PersonaPlex-style text prompt (owner name, memory summary) plus a MoshiVis-type gated cross-attention adapter (~206M params, +7 ms/step on an L4) over a ~5 Hz world-state feature vector (owner-visible flag, DoA bearing, track-loss age, proprio summary). Train with moshi-finetune LoRA (batch <=4 / clips <=60 s on the 32 GB RTX 5000 Ada) on stereo synthetic dialogues where the act channel is labelled by rules (laugh follows setup+punchline; look-back follows track-loss), then GRPO with rule rewards (owner laughter within 3 s after chuckle, owner re-acquired within N s after look-back, plus Kyutai's pause/backchannel/interruption rewards). Behaviour tokens go to a 50 Hz reference-conditioned tracker under the existing deterministic safety layer; the speech half stays on the desktop GPU until an Orin int8 benchmark exists.

B. Hosted-voice + local 'reaction head' dual-system (lowest latency, license-clean, fits budget): keep OpenAI Realtime / Gemini Live for speech and run locally a 5-10 Hz VAP-class causal transformer (frozen CPC encoder + 4 layers, RTF ~0.19-0.73 on CPU) over the owner-mic + robot-TTS stereo audio, extended with world-state tokens (visibility, DoA, track-loss age), conversation-state tokens from the hosted model's transcript/events (joke-setup, punchline, question), and a memory summary; it emits discrete reaction tokens (K on the order of 20-60 Go2 primitives, VQ-BeT/L2L style) predicted ~500 ms ahead, dispatched to the 50 Hz tracker. WHEN to react is learned online by a NeuralLinear Thompson-sampling contextual bandit over the primitive set (Song 2026 / Weber pattern) with reward = laughter/smile probability in a fixed post-action window, pre-trained in sim against an LLM owner simulator; the VAP/nod/backchannel head gives the ~200-300 ms visible-response timing that humans expect.

C. Small quadruped VLA for the slower semantic layer: an Orin-viable sub-1B VLM head (SmolVLA-class 450M or SmolVLM-256M ~150 ms end-to-end on AGX Orin; Qwen2.5-VL-3B if latency allows) fine-tuned with LoRA on 50-100 sim episodes to emit QUART/NaVILA-style mid-level behaviour tokens at 1-2 Hz from image + LiDAR-derived state + conversation/memory text, into the 50 Hz tracker; it owns per-utterance expression (greeting, social referencing, approach/orient to owner) and 'look back when lost' from vision, while design B's audio head owns sub-second reactions like the chuckle.

D. Shared expression substrate: one reference-conditioned 50 Hz tracking policy on the Go2 (QuadFM Gen2Control / BeyondMimic / unitree_rl_lab recipe) trained in MuJoCo Warp (unitree_rl_mjlab) or Isaac Lab, over a clip library = Quad-Imaginarium/Uni-Mo expressive clips (7,488, 96.7% real success) + a handful of authored primitives (chuckle = play-pant body bounce, look-back = yaw+pitch toward DoA, play-bow, attention-getters), exposed as a discrete latent/one-hot codebook (CAMP/VIM/Walk-Like-Dogs) with AMOR-style continuous intensity; this is the common actuator for A/B/C and the only element that must survive the sport-API vs low-level exclusivity on the real dog.

E. Three-layer sim/training plan: L0 physics + tracker (MuJoCo Warp/mjlab Go2, 4,096 envs) and safety recovery with final authority; L1 owner-in-the-loop kinematic owner avatar (Habitat-3.0-style walking human, occlusion/visibility model, LiDAR track-loss events, DoA noise) generating 'lost' episodes; L2 LLM owner simulator (User-LM fine-tuned on recorded owner sessions, tau2-bench voice mode) emitting utterances, calibrated laugh probability, a habituation/novelty term and synthetic laughter audio (Omine recipe) so audio-level rewards exist; pre-train the bandit/reaction head offline on millions of L2 episodes, run GRPO on the duplex model with rule rewards, then evaluate with an owner-only matched-vs-mismatched reaction A/B in the MuJoCo viewer before any hardware.
risks: License stack is mostly research-only: Seamless Interaction dataset is CC-BY-NC 4.0 (confirmed on the HF page), kyutai/moshika-rl-seamless is CC BY-NC and personaplex-rl-seamless's license is unstated; GR00T N1-2B weights are under the 'NVIDIA OneWay Noncommercial License' (confirmed) and only N1.7 is Open Model License; dog mocap (Zhang 2018 via AI4Animation) is CC BY-NC; NVSpeech and UniAct are CC BY-NC-SA; BayLing-Duplex CC BY-NC-ND; ZeroEGGS proprietary; Piper is now GPL-3.0; Delta-IRIS GPL-3.0; Qwen2.5-3B 'Qwen Research License'; Llama 3.2 community license. Any shippable path must re-run the RL/data pipeline on CC-BY/Apache or synthetic data.

Orin latency/throughput: no native-duplex model (Moshi, MiniCPM-o, PersonaPlex) has been run on any Jetson; 8B int4 decodes at 30-50 tok/s on AGX Orin while Moshi needs a 17-stream step every 80 ms; pi0 takes 920 ms per step on Orin, ELLSA 786-854 ms per 1 s block on an A100, Qwen3-VL-4B spends 4 s encoding one image on Orin; Orin is only credibly viable for sub-1B heads (SmolVLM-256M VLA 150 ms), so the duplex speech model will stay on the desktop GPU or hosted.

Training memory on the single 32 GB card: moshi-finetune peaks at 39.6 GB on an H100 at batch 16 / 100 s clips; pi0.5 LoRA needs >22.5 GB; GR00T N1.7 recommends 40 GB+; GRPO replications used 32 H100 / 64 A800 — small-compute RL on LoRA parameters is unreplicated, and training must be scheduled when Parcel's resident local models are stopped.

Reward reliability for 'funny': laughter detectors fall to F1 0.61 / precision 0.51 in the wild and collapse across languages (F1 0.13-0.29), polite vs mirthful laughter needs video+LLM, zero-shot LLM funniness judges correlate at Spearman 0.17-0.27 with humans, text-only funniness ceilings are low (13.5% over predict-the-mean), engagement/rapport estimators overfit their setup (0.81 to 0.28 CCC) and collapse with three people present, and optimising an implicit engagement/length signal produced more controversial output (Pang 2023). The reward DEFINITION changes what is learned (Song 2026), so it must be fixed and validated on a small owner-labelled paired set first.

Sample efficiency and habituation: the literature implies 30-100 labelled events per behaviour, ~480 bandit pulls per condition, 25-100 episodes over ~41 days for in-home personalisation, and 14-17 people to reach tau 0.70 from facial reactions; real home event rates (jokes/day, lost episodes/day) are unknown, preference RL breaks at teacher error 0.1 (real annotators ~40%), and no robot RL paper models reward decay for repeated jokes, so the owner simulator needs a novelty term and the learner a non-stationary bandit.

Sim-to-real for social behaviour: an 86-study review found no work that trains a robot social policy against LLM-simulated humans and validates it with real humans; LLM users are over-cooperative and drift persona, so an LLM owner will laugh too often and the learned trigger policy will be miscalibrated until recorded-owner calibration data exist.

Safety and control-surface constraints on the Go2: sport-mode presets have undocumented durations and no documented interruptibility, high-level sport control and rt/lowcmd low-level control are mutually exclusive via the motion_switcher, the 2025 SDK commit removed 20+ legacy sport APIs, a 500 Hz LowCmd loop co-hosted with LiDAR on the dog's Orin NX is unshown, and any LM-emitted action token must pass the deterministic safety layer with a recovery policy that has final authority (the only pattern with a hardware safety record: <5 falls in 115 min).

Audio front-end unknowns: the XVF3800 wiki documents AEC/beamforming/DoA/DNS but not the AEC reference path, DoA resolution or update rate; quadruped ego-noise is unstudied; VAP models were trained on clean Switchboard stereo and Kyoto ships noise-augmented variants, implying a real domain gap for the owner-mic + robot-TTS pair.

Availability risk: DuplexSLA ('checkpoints coming soon'), DuplexOmni, QuadFM (empty repo), Quad-Imaginarium (pending), pi0.6 (unreleased), Gemini Robotics On-Device (trusted testers only), ELaTE (no weights), and the Go2 person-following code (TODO) may not ship inside the project window; every plan needs a fallback that uses only Moshi/PersonaPlex, Uni-Mo/unitree_rl_lab, and MIT VAP code.

Privacy/consent: laughter, smile and correction logs used as rewards are biometric-adjacent owner data and must be covered by the existing owner-model consent mechanism; multi-person homes need DoA + face-ID gating before any reward is credited to an individual.
contradictions: Seamless Interaction license: the speech topic (HF dataset page) says CC-BY-NC 4.0, the gesture topic (arXiv 2506.22554) says CC BY-SA 4.0. Spot-check of the HF page confirms CC-BY-NC 4.0 governs the download; treat it as non-commercial.

GR00T N1 license: the world-state topic says 'open checkpoint, data and benchmarks under CC BY 4.0', while the VLA topic says N1.5/N1.6 weights are under a non-commercial NVIDIA License. Spot-check: nvidia/GR00T-N1-2B on Hugging Face carries the 'NVIDIA OneWay Noncommercial License'; CC BY 4.0 can only apply to the data/benchmark, not the weights.

Moshi backchannel rate: Kyutai's GRPO paper reports baseline Moshi backchannels at 0.074/s (rising to 0.101/s), whereas Full-Duplex-Bench reports Moshi backchannel frequency 0.001 ('almost never'). These are different metrics on different data (<=1 s vocalisations on dyadic audio vs FDB's scripted protocol); the digest treats both as 'Moshi backchannel rate'.

Moshi interruption latency: the GRPO paper's Moshi baseline is 1.377 s (improved to 0.409 s) while Full-Duplex-Bench reports 0.257 s for the same model and PersonaPlex reports 0.240 s on FDB — a 5x gap from measurement protocol, so numbers from the two papers cannot be compared directly.

Moshi-Face citation: the gesture topic attributes Moshi-Face to arXiv 2401.01885 (Meta's audio-to-photoreal two-rate paper); the actual Moshi-Face paper is arXiv 2606.21970 (Jun 2026), confirmed via the arXiv API.
Qwen2.5-Omni-7B size: '11B total incl. Talker' (speech topic) vs '7B Thinker + Talker' (world-state topic); the 31.11 GB bf16 footprint supports ~11B total.

Uni-Mo per-clip vs universal tracker: the VLA and motion topics state Uni-Mo trains one PPO policy PER motion (96.7% real success over 392 motions), but the simulation topic generalises this to 'expressive motion on Go2 is a solved tracking problem once a reference exists' and QuadFM's universal tracker reports no real-robot success rate; the 96.7% number does not transfer to a single universal tracker.
Uni-Mo clip frame rate: paper says 50 Hz, README says 24 fps (flagged inside the motion topic but repeated as 50 Hz elsewhere).

Gillick laughter detector accuracy: the world-state and online-learning topics say the repo 'gives no accuracy numbers'; the reward topic gives the paper's F1 0.75 (Switchboard) / 0.61 (AudioSet in-the-wild) and precision 0.51 — the numbers exist and should be the ones used for reward-noise modelling.

Orin viability for the duplex backbone: the speech topic poses running Moshi-7B at 12.5 steps/s on the AGX Orin as open, while the VLA topic's on-robot characterisation names Orin cost-optimal only for sub-1B models and the deployment topic's 30-50 tok/s for 8B int4 leaves at most ~20-30 ms of headroom per 80 ms step before Mimi encode/decode and the 17-stream depth transformer — the evidence points to 'not on Orin' rather than 'unknown'.
